messages.content: In our meeting someone mentioned "the elephant in the room". What was that about?

"The elephant in the room" is a big, obvious problem that everyone knows about but nobody wants to discuss.
Example: Everyone was worried about the missing funds, so the budget was the elephant in the room until Rekha finally raised it.
My uncle said "don't count your chickens before they hatch". Is he talking about poultry?

No. It is a saying that means you should not rely on a good result until it has really happened.
Example: You have not got the offer yet, so do not count your chickens before they hatch.
What does "kill two birds with one stone" mean?

It means to solve two problems or finish two tasks with a single action.
Example: I posted the parcel on my way to school, which killed two birds with one stone.
My manager wrote "we will look into it". Is that a yes?

Not exactly. "Look into" means to investigate or examine something, so she is promising to check, not to agree.
Example: The school is looking into why the bell stopped ringing.
My little sister says she "looks up to" me. Is that a compliment?

Yes, it is. "Look up to" means to admire and respect someone.
Example: Young players often look up to their captain.
Meat or meet: "Let us ___ at the canteen."

Use "meet", which means to come together with someone. "Meat" is the flesh of an animal eaten as food.
Examples: Let us meet at the canteen at noon. The curry has no meat in it.
Access or excess? I want to write about the library.

"Access" means the right or ability to enter or use something. "Excess" means more than is needed.
Examples: Students have access to the library until six. Too much sugar is bad for you; avoid excess.
Is it "sincerly" or "sincerely" at the end of a letter?

Write "sincerely". Keep the e before the -ly: sin-cere-ly.
Example: Sincerely, Rohan Kapoor.
I wrote "reciept" on the bill. Is that right?

No. "Receipt" is the right spelling, and the p is silent. Remember the rule "i before e, except after c".
Example: Keep the receipt in case you need to return the bag.
Do people in England say "lift" or "elevator"?

British English says "lift" and American English says "elevator". Indian English usually follows the British word.
Example: The lift in our building is broken, so we took the stairs to the fifth floor.
What is a "biscuit"? My American cousin means something different.

In British English, a biscuit is a small, crisp, baked snack, which Americans call a cookie. In American English, a biscuit is a soft, bread-like roll. In India, "biscuit" usually has the British meaning.
Example: Dad dipped a biscuit in his tea.
Pavement or sidewalk: which is the walkway beside a road?

British English calls it the "pavement" and American English calls it the "sidewalk". In American English, "pavement" can mean the road surface itself.
Example: Please walk on the pavement, not on the road.
Is "can you" or "could you" better when asking a favour?

Both are fine, but "could you" sounds softer and more polite, so it suits strangers, teachers and managers. "Can you" is fine with friends and family.
Examples: Could you please share the notes, Mr. Iyer? Can you pass the salt, Dad?
How do I end a formal letter: "yours sincerely" or "yours faithfully"?

In British-style letters, use "Yours faithfully" after "Dear Sir or Madam", and "Yours sincerely" when you start with a name, such as "Dear Mr Rao". American letters usually end with "Sincerely".
Example: Dear Ms Khan, ... Yours sincerely, Arjun Nair.
Is it okay to write "gonna" in a message?

"Gonna" is a casual spoken form of "going to". It is fine in texts to friends, but use "going to" in essays, emails to teachers and any formal writing.
Examples: I'm gonna be late, Zoya. I am going to submit the report on Monday.
What does "cry wolf" mean?

It means to raise a false alarm so often that people stop believing you when there is a real problem. It comes from the old story of the boy who cried wolf.
Example: Our neighbour's car alarm goes off daily, so no one reacts any more; it has cried wolf too often.
My dad said I just have to "bite the bullet" about the dentist. What does it mean?

"Bite the bullet" means to do something unpleasant or difficult bravely, because it cannot be avoided.
Example: Isha bit the bullet and told her teacher she had lost the library book.
How many meanings does "work out" have?

It has several. It can mean to exercise, to solve something, or to end well.
Examples: Ben works out every morning. Can you work out this puzzle? I hope everything works out for you.
What does "pick out" mean in a shop?

"Pick out" means to choose something from a group of things.
Example: Farah picked out a blue notebook from the whole shelf.
Between or among: when do I use each one?

The usual rule is "between" for two people or things, and "among" for three or more in a group. People do use "between" for several clearly separate items, so the rule is a guide, not a law.
Examples: Share the sweets between you and your brother. The boy was standing among the crowd.
Favourite or favorite: my cousin in America writes it differently.

Both are correct. "Favourite" is the British spelling and "favorite" is the American one. Indian English usually follows the British spelling.
Example: Mango is my favourite fruit.
Surprize or surprise: which spelling is right?

Write "surprise". It ends in -ise, not -ize, in every variety of English.
Example: The surprise party started at six.
"Maybe" or "may be": which one is right here: "It ___ true"?

Write "may be" there. "May be" is a verb phrase, while "maybe" is an adverb meaning "perhaps" that can stand at the start of a sentence.
Examples: It may be true. Maybe we can leave early.
Assure, ensure, insure: help!

"Assure" means to tell someone confidently that something is true, to calm their doubt. "Ensure" means to make certain that something happens. "Insure" means to cover something with insurance.
Examples: He assured us the bus was safe. Please ensure the door is locked. They insured the shop against fire.
Is "recomend" spelled right?

No. It should be "recommend", with one c and a double m: re-com-mend.
Example: Could you recommend a good book for my little sister?
Should "occured" have two r's?

Yes. The correct spelling is "occurred", with a double c and a double r. The final r doubles when you add -ed.
Example: The accident occurred near the school gate.
What is a "flat" in British English? I read it in a novel.

A "flat" is a set of rooms for living in, on one floor of a building. Americans call this an apartment. In India, "flat" is the usual word.
Example: Nikhil's family lives in a third-floor flat near the park.
How do British and American English differ for "chips" and "crisps"?

In British English, "crisps" are thin fried slices of potato sold in packets, and "chips" are thick fried potato pieces. Americans call the first "chips" and the second "fries".
Example: She ate a packet of crisps with her sandwich.
What do Americans call petrol?

They call it "gas", short for gasoline. British English and Indian English say "petrol".
Example: We stopped at the pump to fill the car with petrol.
Why does my teacher say "I'll ring you" instead of "call you"?

In British English, "ring" means to phone someone. Americans say "call". In India, both are widely understood.
Example: I'll ring you after the match, Danish.
Can I say "trousers" in America, or is it "pants"?

American English says "pants" for the garment, but "trousers" is also understood. In British English "pants" usually means underwear, so be careful.
Example: He wore grey trousers to school.
What is a more polite way to say "I want a glass of water"?

Say "I would like a glass of water, please." "I would like" sounds gentler than "I want".
Examples: I would like some tea, please. I'd like to book a table for four.
My boss writes "kindly do the needful". Is it good English?

It is common in Indian office English, but many readers find it stiff or unclear. A clearer polite version states the action.
Example: Please send me the signed form by Friday.
Should I start an email to my professor with "Hi" or "Dear"?

"Dear Professor Sen" is the safe, formal choice for a first email. "Hello Professor Sen" is also polite. "Hi" alone is better for friends.
Example: Dear Professor Sen, I am writing to ask about the project deadline.
If someone asks "Would you mind opening the window?", what is the polite answer?

Say "Not at all" or "Of course not" if you are happy to do it. "Would you mind" asks if the task would bother you, so "No" means you agree, and "yes" would be a refusal.
Example: "Would you mind moving your bag?" "Not at all, here you go."
What does "ten a penny" mean?

It is a British saying for something very common and not special or valuable.
Example: Pens like these are ten a penny, so do not worry about losing one.
What does "easier said than done" mean?

It means that something sounds simple, but is hard to actually do.
Example: Waking up at five every day is easier said than done.
"Call back" or "call me back": what does it mean?

"Call back" means to phone someone again, or to phone someone who called you earlier.
Example: Dad is in a meeting. Can you call back in ten minutes?
"Speed up" and "slow down": are they just opposites?

Yes, they are opposite phrasal verbs. "Speed up" means to go or happen faster, and "slow down" means to go or happen more slowly.
Examples: The bus sped up on the empty road. Please slow down; I cannot write that fast.
What does "two heads are better than one" mean?

It means that two people working together can solve a problem better than one person alone.
Example: I could not solve the puzzle alone, but two heads are better than one, so we asked Tara.
If a task is "a wild goose chase", should I keep going?

Probably not. A "wild goose chase" is a search or task that is foolish and hopeless, because what you want cannot be found.
Example: We spent the whole day looking for the missing key in the garden, and it was a wild goose chase because it was in the house.
What is the meaning of "slow down"? The sign near my school says it.

"Slow down" means to reduce your speed. Used for people, it can also mean to do less or relax.
Examples: Slow down near the school gate. You work too hard, Sana; slow down a little.
What does "run into" mean? I ran into my old teacher.

"Run into" means to meet someone unexpectedly. It can also mean to hit something while moving.
Examples: I ran into my cousin at the market. The cyclist ran into a parked car.
Could you show me how "get the hang of" is used?

"Get the hang of" means to learn how to do something after some practice.
Example: After a few tries, Meera got the hang of riding a bicycle.
Is "until" spelled with two l's at the end?

No. "Until" has one l at the end, even though "till" has two. Think of "un-til".
Example: Wait here until I come back.
Is "rubbish" the same as "trash"?

They are the same idea in two varieties of English. British English says "rubbish" for waste, and Americans say "trash" or "garbage". Indian English uses "garbage" and "rubbish" both.
Example: Put the rubbish in the bin outside.
What is a "torch" in British English?

In British English, a "torch" is a small hand-held light that runs on batteries. Americans call it a "flashlight". In American English, "torch" refers to a burning stick or a blowtorch.
Example: Take a torch because the power cuts are frequent.
What are polite ways to answer "thank you"?

You can say "You're welcome", "My pleasure" or "Not at all" in polite settings. "No problem" and "No worries" are more casual.
Example: "Thank you for the lift, Asha." "My pleasure!"
Being "on thin ice" sounds dangerous. What does it mean?

It means to be in a risky situation where one more mistake could cause trouble.
Example: After three late submissions, Rohan knew he was on thin ice with his teacher.
My little brother never "gives in". What does that mean?

"Give in" means to stop resisting and agree or surrender, usually after pressure.
Examples: Mum finally gave in and let us watch the film. The team never gives in, even when losing.
Someone said this plan gives us "the best of both worlds". Is that good?

Yes, it is praise. "The best of both worlds" means you get the advantages of two different things at once, without their disadvantages.
Example: Living near the market and the park gives Anita the best of both worlds.
What does "cost the earth" mean? Is it the same as "an arm and a leg"?

"Cost the earth" is a mostly British idiom meaning to be extremely expensive. It is very close in meaning to "an arm and a leg", which also means very expensive.
Example: The designer wedding dress cost the earth, so Pooja chose a simpler one.
Explain "once bitten, twice shy".

It means that after a bad experience, a person becomes careful about trying the same thing again.
Example: Samir lost his phone at a concert, and now, once bitten, twice shy, he leaves it at home.
My grandmother says "the early bird catches the worm". What is she telling me?

She means that people who start early get the best chances or results.
Example: The early bird catches the worm, so let us reach the railway station before the crowd arrives.
What does "barking up the wrong tree" mean?

It means to look for something in the wrong place, or to blame the wrong person.
Example: If you think I took your pen, you are barking up the wrong tree; I do not even use that colour.
My teacher told the class to "pull your socks up". What should we do?

In British English, it means to try harder and improve your behaviour or work. It is informal, and teachers often use it as a mild warning.
Example: Our class must pull its socks up before the final exams.
Can you tell me what it means to "throw in the towel"?

It means to give up or admit defeat. The phrase comes from boxing.
Example: After three failed attempts, Dinesh threw in the towel and bought a ready-made cabinet.
Our plans are "up in the air". Is that bad?

It is neither good nor bad. It means the plans are not yet decided or certain.
Example: Our trip to Jaipur is up in the air because we have not booked the tickets.
Meaning of "at the end of the day"?

It means "when everything is considered" or "in the end". It can also literally mean the last part of the day.
Example: At the end of the day, the decision is yours, so choose what you think is right.
What does "back up" mean for a computer file?

To "back up" a file is to make a spare copy so that you do not lose it. The noun is written as one word: "backup".
Examples: Please back up your project before you close the laptop. I keep a backup on a pen drive.
Can "set up" have different meanings?

Yes. It can mean to arrange or prepare something, or to start an organisation.
Examples: Please set up the chairs for the assembly. Her uncle set up a small bakery.
What does "turn into" mean in this sentence: "The caterpillar turned into a butterfly"?

"Turn into" means to change and become something different.
Example: The small stream turned into a river after the heavy rain.
What does "pay back" mean?

"Pay back" means to return money that you borrowed. It can also mean to take revenge, but that sense is less common.
Example: I will pay you back on Saturday, Rohit.
"Break up": is it only for couples?

No. It can mean to end a relationship, but also to separate into pieces or to end a gathering.
Examples: The school broke up for the summer on Friday. The crowd broke up when the rain started.
What does "dress up" mean for a party?

"Dress up" means to wear special or formal clothes. It also means to wear a costume for fun.
Examples: We dressed up for Diwali. The children dressed up as animals.
What does "cheer up" mean?

"Cheer up" means to become happier, or to make someone feel happier.
Example: We bought flowers to cheer up Nani after her hospital stay.
Is "everyone" singular or plural? I wrote "Everyone are here."

Treat "everyone" as singular, so the verb is "is": "Everyone is here." Though it means many people, the word itself takes a singular verb.
Example: Everyone is waiting for the bell.
Is it "I did good" or "I did well" on a test?

In standard English, say "I did well". "Well" is an adverb that describes how you did something, and "good" is an adjective. "Good" is correct in "I feel good" or "It was a good test".
Example: Maya did well in the maths quiz.
"Sometime", "sometimes" and "some time": what are the differences?

"Sometime" means at an unspecified time. "Sometimes" means on some occasions. "Some time" means an amount of time.
Examples: Let us meet sometime next week. Sometimes we walk home. It took some time to find the key.
Lightning or lightening: which is the flash in the sky?

"Lightning" is the flash of light in a storm. "Lightening" comes from the verb "lighten" and means making lighter or less heavy.
Examples: Lightning struck the old tree. Putting less in the bag is lightening the load.
Was the shirt "hanged" or "hung" on the line?

Say "hung". "Hung" is used for objects. "Hanged" is usually used only for execution by hanging.
Example: Dad hung the washed shirts on the line.
Pair or pear: "I bought a ___ of shoes."

Use "pair", which means two things that go together. "Pear" is the fruit.
Examples: Meena bought a pair of sandals. A ripe pear is soft and sweet.
How do I choose between "site", "sight" and "cite"?

"Site" is a place or location. "Sight" is the ability to see, or something you see. "Cite" means to mention a source.
Examples: The building site is closed. The mountain was a lovely sight. Remember to cite your sources in the essay.
Were, we're, where: please sort them out.

"Were" is the past of "are". "We're" is short for "we are". "Where" asks about a place.
Examples: They were at home. We're ready to leave. Where is the station?
How do I spell conscious? It has a funny middle.

"Conscious" is spelled c-o-n-s-c-i-o-u-s. It has "sc" in the middle, then "ious".
Example: The patient was conscious and able to talk.
Is it dilema or dilemma?

It is "dilemma", with a double m. A dilemma is a difficult choice between two options.
Example: Tara faced a dilemma: go to the party or finish her homework.
I always write "harrass". Is it right?

No. It is "harass", with one r and a double s.
Example: It is wrong to harass anyone online or in person.
How do you spell "immediately"? I keep dropping a letter.

"Immediately" has a double m and then "-diately": im-me-di-ate-ly.
Example: Please come to the office immediately.
Interupt or interrupt?

"Interrupt" has a double r. The meaning is to break into what someone is saying or doing.
Example: Sorry to interrupt, but the bus is here.
Is it langauge or language?

It is "language". The u comes before the a: l-a-n-g-u-a-g-e.
Example: Tamil is the first language of many people in Chennai.
Is it "probly" or "probably"?

"Probably" is the right spelling. People often say it quickly as "probly", but it is written with all three syllables: prob-a-bly.
Example: It will probably rain this evening.
Noticable or noticeable?

"Noticeable" is the right spelling. Keep the e after the c so that the c stays soft.
Example: There was a noticeable change in the weather.
Is a "jumper" the same as a "sweater"?

Yes, mostly. In British English a "jumper" is a knitted garment worn on the upper body, and Americans call it a "sweater". In American English a "jumper" can be a sleeveless dress.
Example: Wear a jumper because it is cold in Shimla.
Do people say "autumn" or "fall"?

British English prefers "autumn", and American English commonly says "fall". Both are understood, and Indian English usually uses "autumn".
Example: The leaves turn orange in autumn.
What does an American mean by "faucet"?

A "faucet" is what British and Indian English call a "tap", the thing you turn to get water.
Example: Please close the tap properly; it is dripping.
Centre or center: which is correct?

Both are correct. "Centre" is British, and "center" is American. Indian English usually follows the British spelling.
Example: The shopping centre is next to the bus stand.
Grey or gray: is one a mistake?

No, both are right. "Grey" is more common in British English, and "gray" is more common in American English.
Example: The grey clouds covered the sun.
In a bank, do I write a "cheque" or a "check"?

The paper that orders a bank to pay is a "cheque" in British and Indian English and a "check" in American English. In both, "check" also means to look at something carefully.
Example: Grandpa wrote a cheque for the school fees.
Programme or program?

In British English, "programme" is used for a plan or a TV show, and "program" for a computer program. American English uses "program" for all. Indian English usually follows British use.
Examples: Our school has a cultural programme. She wrote a program in Python.
Learnt or learned: which is right?

Both are correct. "Learnt" is more common in British English, and "learned" is more common in American English.
Example: I learnt to swim last summer.
Do Americans call football "soccer"?

Yes. In the United States, "football" means American football, so they call the game played with a round ball "soccer". British and Indian English call it "football".
Example: The boys played football after school.
What is the polite way to get someone's attention: "excuse me", "sorry" or "pardon"?

Use "Excuse me" to get attention or to pass by. "Sorry" apologises for a mistake. "Pardon?" asks someone to repeat what they said.
Examples: Excuse me, is this seat free? Sorry, I stepped on your foot. Pardon? I did not hear you.
How can I say no politely with "I'm afraid"?

"I'm afraid" is a polite way to introduce bad news or a refusal. You are not scared; it softens what follows.
Example: I'm afraid I cannot come to the meeting on Friday.
What does "please find attached" mean in an email?

It is a formal phrase meaning that the file is attached for you to look at. A simpler everyday version is "I have attached the form".
Example: Please find attached the invoice for March.
How should I respond when a friend texts "What's up?"

It is a casual greeting, so you can answer "Not much, you?" or "Hi, all good!". It does not usually ask for a detailed report.
Example: "What's up, Karan?" "Not much. Just finished homework."
Do I call a female teacher "Madam" or "Miss" in India?

Both are common in Indian schools. "Madam" or "Ma'am" sounds more formal, while "Miss" is widely used by younger students. In many English-speaking countries, students use "Miss" or the teacher's surname. Follow your school's custom.
Example: Good morning, Madam.
"Ms", "Mrs" and "Miss": how do they differ?

"Mrs" is traditionally for a married woman and "Miss" for an unmarried one. "Ms" is neutral and does not show marital status, so it is a safe choice in writing.
Example: Dear Ms Nair, thank you for your reply.
Is "I was wondering if you could help" polite?

Yes, it is a very polite and indirect way to ask for help. Using the past tense makes the request sound gentler.
Example: I was wondering if you could review my essay.
Any tips for declining an invitation politely?

Thank the person first, then give a short refusal, and keep it kind. You do not need a long excuse.
Example: Thank you for inviting me, Meera, but I will not be able to come. Have a lovely time.
Is "goodbye" more formal than "bye"?

Yes, a little. "Goodbye" is neutral or slightly formal, and "bye" is casual and common. "Bye-bye" is often used with young children.
Examples: Goodbye, Mrs. Thomas. Bye, see you tomorrow!
A colleague asked me to "touch base" next week. Should I touch him?

No. "Touch base" is an informal work idiom meaning to make brief contact to share news or check on progress.
Example: Let us touch base on Monday to see how the project is going.
A teammate was called "on the ball". Is that praise or blame?

It describes a person who is alert, quick to understand and good at dealing with things.
Example: Our captain is really on the ball; she noticed the gap in the field at once.
What does "bury the hatchet" mean?

It means to stop fighting and become friendly again. A hatchet is a small axe.
Example: After years of quarrels, the two neighbours buried the hatchet.
What is meant by "missed the boat"?

It means you were too late to take an opportunity.
Example: By the time Zara applied, all the places in the art class were filled; she had missed the boat.
The batter stayed "cool as a cucumber". Is that a compliment?

Yes. It means that she stayed very calm in a tense situation.
Example: Even with two balls left, Priya was as cool as a cucumber.
Everyone calls the water issue "a hot potato". Why?

A "hot potato" is a controversial subject that is difficult or risky to deal with, so people tend to avoid it.
Example: The school timetable is a hot potato; nobody wants to change it.
What does "back to the drawing board" mean?

It means that an idea or plan failed, so you must start planning again from the beginning.
Example: The first model of the bridge collapsed, so it was back to the drawing board for the team.
My classmate gave me the cold shoulder today. What does that mean?

It means to treat someone in an unfriendly way by ignoring them on purpose.
Example: Dev gave his cousin the cold shoulder after their argument.
I read that families "make ends meet". What does that mean?

"Make ends meet" means to earn just enough money to pay for the basic things you need.
Example: With two small jobs, she managed to make ends meet.
If a car is told to "pull over", what should the driver do?

"Pull over" means to steer a vehicle to the side of the road and stop.
Example: The ambulance was coming, so every car pulled over.
How is "catch on" used?

"Catch on" can mean to understand something, or to become popular.
Examples: Ishaan caught on quickly when the teacher explained fractions. The new game caught on in our school.
What does "log in" mean? And is "log on" the same?

"Log in" means to enter your username and password to use a website or computer. "Log on" means nearly the same. The opposite is "log out".
Example: Please log in to the portal to see your marks.
In a sentence like "It turned out well", what does "turn out" mean?

"Turn out" means to end in a certain way, or to prove to be something.
Examples: The picnic turned out well despite the rain. The strange noise turned out to be a cat.
How do you use "let down" when I fail someone?

"Let down" means to disappoint someone by not doing what they hoped or expected.
Example: I do not want to let down my team, so I will practise tonight.
In a phone call, what does "hang up" mean?

To "hang up" is to end a phone call. It comes from the days of old telephones with hooks.
Example: He hung up and then sent me a message.
Can "switch off" mean something besides turning off a light?

Yes. Besides stopping a machine, it can mean to stop paying attention.
Examples: Please switch off the fan. After a long day, I just switch off in front of the TV.
What does "hand out" mean in a classroom?

"Hand out" means to give something to each person in a group.
Example: Mrs. Das handed out the worksheets.
Do I "fill in" or "fill out" a form?

British English usually says "fill in" a form and American English says "fill out". Both are understood, and Indian English uses both.
Example: Please fill in your name and class at the top.
Hole or whole: "I ate the ___ cake."

Use "whole", which means all of something. "Hole" is an opening or gap.
Examples: Jay ate the whole cake. There is a hole in my sock.
Role or roll? I need to write about my part in the play.

Write "role" for a part someone plays, in a play or in life. "Roll" refers to something that turns, a bread roll or a list of names.
Examples: Neha has the main role in the play. The teacher called the roll.
Bare or bear: which one is for the animal?

"Bear" is the animal, and it is also a verb meaning to carry or tolerate. "Bare" means uncovered or empty.
Examples: A bear walked across the field. The children ran on bare feet.
Weight or wait: I wrote "I can't ___ any longer".

Use "wait". "Wait" means to stay until something happens. "Weight" is how heavy something is.
Examples: Please wait here. The weight of the bag was too much.
Diary and dairy look the same to me. Which is the book?

"Diary" is a book where you write about your days. "Dairy" is about milk products.
Examples: I wrote about the match in my diary. Cheese and curd are dairy products.
Angel or angle in maths: which is correct?

In maths it is "angle", the space between two lines that meet. An "angel" is a spiritual being.
Examples: Measure the angle with a protractor. In the play, Lila was an angel.
When do I use "learn" and when "teach"?

"Learn" means to get knowledge for yourself. "Teach" means to give knowledge to someone else.
Examples: I learn Hindi from my aunt. My aunt teaches me Hindi.
"Speak" or "talk": any difference?

They are close. "Speak" is slightly more formal and is used for languages and one-way talking. "Talk" is more informal and suggests a conversation.
Examples: She speaks three languages. We talked about the match for an hour.
Is "enuf" an acceptable spelling of enough?

No. In standard English, write "enough". "Enuf" appears in informal messages, but it is not accepted in schoolwork.
Example: Do we have enough chairs for everyone?
I write "diffrent" a lot. Is that right?

No. It is spelled "different". Many people skip the first e when they say it, so they write "diffrent", but the word is written dif-fer-ent.
Example: The two sisters look different.
Neighbor or neighbour: which spelling should I use?

Both are correct. "Neighbour" is the British spelling and "neighbor" is the American one. Indian English usually follows the British form.
Example: Our neighbour grows roses on her balcony.
What is the spelling of thorough?

"Thorough" is spelled t-h-o-r-o-u-g-h. It means complete and careful.
Example: The doctor made a thorough check.
Do I keep the e in "truely"?

No. The correct spelling is "truly", without an e. It is an exception to the usual pattern of keeping the e before -ly.
Example: I am truly sorry for the delay.
Twelfth: there is an f before the th, right?

Yes, "twelfth" is spelled t-w-e-l-f-t-h, with an f. The number twelve changes its v to f.
Example: My birthday is on the twelfth of March.
Is it "usualy" or "usually"?

"Usually" has two l's, as in "usual" plus "ly". It is spelled u-s-u-a-l-l-y.
Example: We usually have dinner at eight.
Is "scissors" singular or plural? And how is it spelled?

"Scissors" is spelled s-c-i-s-s-o-r-s, with sc at the start and a double s in the middle. It is a plural noun, so we say "a pair of scissors".
Example: These scissors are very sharp.
In England, is it a "mobile" or a "cell phone"?

British English says "mobile" or "mobile phone". American English says "cell phone" or "cell". Indian English commonly says "mobile".
Example: My mobile is almost out of charge.
Mum or Mom? My cousin in the US writes it differently.

"Mum" is British, and "Mom" is American. Indian English uses "mom", "mum", and "mummy", depending on the family.
Example: Mum picked me up from school.
Why does a British teacher say "maths" and an American say "math"?

British English shortens "mathematics" to "maths", and American English shortens it to "math". Indian English follows the British form.
Example: We have maths homework tonight.
What exactly is a "fortnight"?

A fortnight is two weeks, and it is a British word. In American English, people usually say "two weeks".
Example: We will be in Mysore for a fortnight.
Is a "wardrobe" the same as a "closet"?

Mostly yes. British English says "wardrobe" for a tall cupboard for clothes, while American English says "closet", often a small room or space built into a wall.
Example: She hung the saris in the wardrobe.
Is it "full stop" or "period" for the dot at the end of a sentence?

British and Indian English say "full stop". American English says "period".
Example: Put a full stop at the end of every sentence.
What do British people call a baby's "diaper"?

They call it a "nappy". "Diaper" is American, and Indian English commonly uses "diaper".
Example: The baby needs a clean nappy.
What is a "lorry"?

A "lorry" is a large vehicle for carrying goods. It is British English; Americans say "truck", and Indian English uses both words.
Example: A lorry full of vegetables stopped at the market.
Should I call a teacher "Sir" when I write to him?

In India, "Sir" and "Madam" are polite ways to speak to teachers. In writing, begin with "Dear Sir" for a formal letter, or "Dear Mr. Verma" if you know the name.
Example: Dear Sir, I request leave for two days.
Is "cheers" polite or only for drinks?

In British English, "cheers" is said when drinking, and informally also to mean "thanks" or "goodbye". It is casual, so avoid it in formal emails.
Example: Cheers, Jack, I owe you one.
What does "no worries" mean?

It is a casual reply that means "it is fine" or "do not worry". People say it after thanks or apologies.
Example: "Sorry I am late." "No worries, we just started."
How do I start a letter when I don't know the person's name?

In British-style formal letters, use "Dear Sir or Madam". "To whom it may concern" is also used, mostly in American style.
Example: Dear Sir or Madam, I am writing to ask about the evening course.
I'm late replying. What can I write: "I apologise for the delay"?

Yes, "I apologise for the delay in replying" is polite and suitable for work emails. British English accepts "apologise" and "apologize", and American English uses "apologize".
Example: I apologise for the delay in replying to your message.
Is "could I possibly" too much?

It is very polite and a little formal, so use it with someone senior or when the request is large. For small requests, "could I" is enough.
Example: Could I possibly borrow your notes, Mr. Menon?
May I or can I: which is right to ask permission?

Both are used. "May I" is more formal and traditionally the correct choice for asking permission, while "can I" is common in daily speech.
Examples: May I leave the room, please? Can I borrow your pencil?
Which is right at night: "good evening" or "good night"?

Say "good evening" when you meet or greet someone in the evening. "Good night" is usually said when leaving or going to bed.
Examples: Good evening, everyone, welcome to the show. Good night, Nani, sleep well.
Why would anyone "walk on eggshells" at home?

"Walk on eggshells" means to be extremely careful about what you say or do, because someone is easily upset.
Example: Since the argument, everyone has been walking on eggshells around Uncle Raj.
The waiter said the dessert was "on the house". Do we have to pay?

No. "On the house" means that the restaurant or shop is giving it to you for free.
Example: The owner brought us sweets, on the house.
Is it true that people say it's "raining cats and dogs"?

Yes, it is an old idiom for very heavy rain. Of course, no animals fall from the sky.
Example: It was raining cats and dogs, so the match was stopped.
"You got the wrong end of the stick." What did I do wrong?

It means you misunderstood a situation or what someone said.
Example: Maya thought I was angry, but she had got the wrong end of the stick; I was just tired.
Meaning of "word of mouth" for a shop?

"Word of mouth" is when people learn about something because others tell them, not because of advertising.
Example: The little tailor shop became popular by word of mouth.
What does "in the same boat" mean?

It means that people are in the same difficult situation.
Example: None of us finished the project, so we are all in the same boat.
How is "water under the bridge" used after a quarrel?

It means that something unpleasant happened in the past and is no longer important, so there is no need to be upset about it.
Example: Forget the old argument, Vimal; it is water under the bridge.
If a plan is "a long shot", is it likely to work?

No. "A long shot" is an attempt that has little chance of success, though it is still possible.
Example: Winning against the top team is a long shot, but we will try.
"Off the hook": is that about fishing?

It comes from fishing, but the idiom means to be freed from a duty, blame or a difficult situation.
Example: The teacher forgot to collect the homework, so we were off the hook.
"Wake up" or "get up": are they the same thing?

"Wake up" means to stop sleeping. "Get up" means to leave your bed. You can wake up and then stay in bed for a while.
Example: I woke up at six, but I did not get up until half past six.
Our cook "cut corners" on the sweets. Is that a problem?

It can be. "Cut corners" means to do something in the cheapest or easiest way, often by skipping steps, so the quality suffers.
Example: The builders cut corners and used thin walls, so the room leaks.
Where do I "drop off" a friend?

"Drop off" means to take someone or something to a place and leave them there. It can also mean to fall asleep gradually.
Examples: Dad will drop me off at the station. The baby dropped off in the car.
What does "wear out" mean for shoes?

"Wear out" means to become too damaged or old to use after much use. As a verb, it can also mean to make someone very tired.
Examples: My shoes wore out in one monsoon. The long walk wore us out.
Does "miss out" mean that you feel sad?

Not necessarily. "Miss out" means to lose the chance to enjoy or take part in something.
Example: If you do not join the trip, you will miss out on all the fun.
"Come over" tonight, my cousin said. Does that mean I should visit?

Yes, it is an invitation to visit the speaker's home. "Come over" can also mean to cross to the side where the speaker is.
Example: Come over on Sunday and have lunch with us.
In a meeting someone wrote "put forward" next to my idea. What does it mean?

"Put forward" means to suggest an idea, plan or name for others to consider.
Example: Rina put forward a plan to clean the school garden.
How is "sign up" used?

"Sign up" means to join something by writing your name or registering.
Example: Have you signed up for the quiz club, Arun?
When should I say "much" and when "many"?

Use "many" with countable nouns and "much" with uncountable nouns. In everyday speech, "much" mostly appears in questions and negatives; "a lot of" is more usual in positive sentences.
Examples: How many books do you have? There is not much milk.
What do "i.e." and "e.g." stand for?

"I.e." means "that is" and restates or explains something. "E.g." means "for example" and introduces examples.
Example: Bring a fruit, e.g. an apple or a banana, and meet at the main gate, i.e. the one near the library.
Tall or high: which word fits a mountain and which fits a person?

Use "tall" for people, trees and narrow buildings. Use "high" for mountains and for the position of things above the ground.
Examples: Rohan is tall for his age. The shelf is too high for me.
How do "journey", "trip" and "travel" differ?

"Journey" is the act of going from one place to another, often a long one. "Trip" is a journey with a return, usually short. "Travel" is usually used as a verb or an uncountable noun for travelling in general.
Examples: The journey took six hours. We took a trip to the zoo. Travel broadens the mind.
Formally or formerly: which should I pick for "my ___ school"?

Neither fits exactly. "Former" is the adjective that means earlier, so say "my former school". "Formerly" is an adverb meaning in the past, and "formally" means in a formal or official way.
Examples: She was formerly a teacher. The prize was formally announced today.
"Too", "also" and "as well": which one goes where?

They have similar meaning. "Too" and "as well" usually come at the end of a sentence, while "also" usually comes before the main verb.
Examples: I like tea too. She plays cricket as well. We also saw a film.
Despite or in spite of: do they mean the same?

Yes, they mean the same: "although something is true". "Despite" has no "of", but "in spite of" does, and both are followed by a noun or an -ing form.
Examples: Despite the rain, we played cricket. In spite of feeling tired, she finished the race.
Why does fourth have a u but forty does not?

"Fourth" and "fourteen" keep the u, but "forty" does not. English spelling is irregular here, so just learn it: f-o-u-r-t-h, f-o-r-t-y.
Example: He finished fourth in the race, and he is forty years old.
Possesion or possession?

Spell it "possession", with a double s twice: p-o-s-s-e-s-s-i-o-n. It has four s's.
Example: Please keep your bags in your possession at the station.
I need to write questionnaire, but I'm unsure about the n's and r's.

"Questionnaire" is spelled q-u-e-s-t-i-o-n-n-a-i-r-e, with a double n and a single r. It is a set of questions used to collect information.
Example: Please fill in the questionnaire about your school canteen.
Paralel or parallel? Which one has the double l?

"Parallel" has a double l in the middle: par-al-lel. Parallel lines never meet.
Example: The railway track runs parallel to the road.
Is there a double c in vacuum?

No. "Vacuum" has one c and a double u: v-a-c-u-u-m.
Example: Mum used the vacuum cleaner on the carpet.
Cemetary or cemetery?

Spell it "cemetery", with -ery at the end: cem-e-ter-y. Do not use "-ary".
Example: The old cemetery is quiet and covered with trees.
Is existence spelled with an a or an e at the end?

It ends with "ence": e-x-i-s-t-e-n-c-e.
Example: Scientists study the existence of life on other planets.
"Withold" or "withhold"?

"Withhold" is correct, with two h's. It means to keep something back and not give it.
Example: The school will withhold the certificate until the fees are paid.
Ageing or aging?

Both are correct. "Ageing" is the common British spelling and "aging" is the common American spelling.
Example: Our ageing grandfather enjoys his morning walk.
My aunt calls it "jewellery", but my American friend wrote "jewelry". Who is right?

Both are right. "Jewellery" is the British spelling, and "jewelry" is the American spelling. Indian English usually uses "jewellery".
Example: She wore gold jewellery for the wedding.
Tyre or tire: which one goes on a bicycle wheel?

British and Indian English spell the rubber ring around a wheel "tyre", and American English spells it "tire". In every variety, "tire" is also a verb meaning to become tired.
Example: The scooter has a flat tyre.
Defence or defense?

"Defence" is the British spelling, and "defense" is the American spelling. Indian English usually follows the British form.
Example: Our school team has a strong defence.
Do I say "at the weekend" or "on the weekend"?

British English usually says "at the weekend", and American English says "on the weekend". Both are understood everywhere.
Example: We are visiting my grandparents at the weekend.
Is "gotten" a real word? My teacher says it is wrong.

"Gotten" is the past participle of "get" in American English. British English uses "got". It is not wrong, but Indian schools usually follow British English, so "got" is the usual choice there.
Examples: American: She has gotten better at chess. British: She has got better at chess.
Where is the "ground floor" in a British building?

In British and Indian English, the "ground floor" is the level at street height, and the floor above it is the "first floor". In American English, the street level is the "first floor".
Example: The canteen is on the ground floor.
Different from, different to or different than?

"Different from" is correct in all varieties. "Different to" is also common in British English, and "different than" is common in American English. For exams, "different from" is the safest.
Example: My phone is different from yours.
The date "3/4" confused me. Is it March or April?

It depends. In British and Indian usage, it is day first, so 3/4 means 3 April. In American usage, it is month first, so 3/4 means March 4. To avoid confusion, write the month in words.
Example: The match is on 3 April.
Is "best regards" polite for an email?

Yes. "Best regards" is polite and neutral, so it works for most work emails. "Kind regards" is slightly warmer, and "Yours sincerely" is more formal.
Example: Best regards, Sunita Rao.
What does "I hope this email finds you well" mean?

It is a formal, polite greeting to wish the reader good health before the main message. You can use it in business writing, but a short "I hope you are well" is simpler.
Example: I hope you are well. I am writing about the school fair.
What do I say when I meet someone for the first time: "nice to meet you" or "pleased to meet you"?

Both are polite. "Pleased to meet you" is a little more formal. You can also answer "Nice to meet you too".
Example: "This is my friend, Jana." "Nice to meet you, Jana."
Is "What is your name?" rude? How can I ask more politely?

It is not rude among friends, but it can sound blunt with adults or strangers. Say "May I know your name, please?" or "Could I have your name, please?".
Example: May I know your name, please?
My coach ended an email with "thank you in advance". Is it okay?

Yes, it is a common polite phrase when you ask for something. Some readers find it a bit pushy, so many people write "Thank you for your help" instead.
Example: Please send me the schedule. Thank you for your help.
What is a gentle way to ask for something: "I would be grateful if you could..."?

That is a polite, formal way of asking. It suits letters and emails to someone you do not know well.
Example: I would be grateful if you could send me the application form.
Please tell me a polite way to offer a guest a seat.

Say "Please have a seat" or "Please sit down". For a very formal moment, "Won't you take a seat?" is also polite.
Example: Please have a seat, Mrs. Fernandes. I will bring some water.
How can I interrupt someone politely in a meeting?

Use a short phrase such as "Excuse me" or "Sorry to interrupt" and then wait for a pause. Say your point briefly.
Example: Sorry to interrupt, but may I add one point?
My cousin says he will "cram" for his exam. Meaning?

"Cram" means to study a lot in a very short time, usually just before a test.
Example: Leela crammed all night, but she was too tired to remember much in the exam.
The bus arrived in the nick of time. Is "nick" a person's name?

No. "In the nick of time" means just before it is too late. The "nick" is an old word for a tiny moment, not a person.
Example: We reached the platform in the nick of time, just as the guard raised his green flag.
Mum wants the house "spick and span" before the guests come. What does that mean?

It means perfectly clean and neat.
Example: Neha swept and wiped until the kitchen was spick and span.
Our maths teacher called one problem "a hard nut to crack". Is it about food?

No. A hard nut to crack is a difficult problem, or a person who is hard to persuade or understand. You may also hear "a tough nut to crack".
Example: The last puzzle in the quiz was a hard nut to crack, but Dev solved it.
My landlord bent over backwards to help us move in. Did he hurt himself?

No, it is only an expression. To bend over backwards means to make a very big effort to help someone.
Example: The shopkeeper bent over backwards to find the book we wanted.
In our group project, everybody is passing the buck. What does that mean?

To pass the buck means to give the responsibility or blame to someone else instead of dealing with it yourself. It is informal.
Example: When the printer broke, the clerk passed the buck to the manager instead of calling the repairer.
What is a "rule of thumb"? Does it involve thumbs?

No thumbs are needed. A rule of thumb is a rough guide based on experience, which is usually helpful but not exact.
Example: A good rule of thumb is to leave home early on rainy days, because the traffic is slow.
People say Imran is a dark horse. Is that an insult?

Not usually. A dark horse is a person who has hidden talents or surprises others by doing better than expected.
Example: Nobody knew Kavya could sing until the school contest, where she turned out to be a dark horse.
Why do people complain about "red tape" at government offices?

Red tape means too many official rules and forms that make a simple task slow. It is usually said as a complaint.
Example: Getting the new licence took weeks because of all the red tape.
My colleague said "that's a tall order" when the boss wanted the report tonight. Was that rude?

Not necessarily. A tall order is a request that is very hard to fulfil. It describes the task, not the person, and it can be said politely.
Example: Cleaning the whole house before the guests arrive in an hour is a tall order.
My teacher asked us to "sum up" the chapter. What should I do?

To sum up means to give the main points briefly. At the start of a sentence, "to sum up" also introduces a short conclusion.
Example: Please sum up the story in three sentences.
My cousin backed out of the trip at the last minute. What does "back out" mean?

To back out means to decide not to do something you had agreed to do. It can also mean to reverse a vehicle out of a space.
Example: Sanjay backed out of the trip the night before we left.
Our picnic plan fell through. Can a plan fall?

Yes, in this phrase. If a plan falls through, it fails to happen.
Example: The deal fell through because the buyer could not arrange the money.
The judge said "please stick to the topic". What does "stick to" mean?

To stick to something means to keep following it and not change or leave it.
Example: Please stick to the topic, Rohit; we only have ten minutes.
I messed up the recipe. Is "mess up" polite?

"Mess up" means to do something badly or spoil it. It is informal, so in formal writing you would say "make a mistake" instead.
Example: I messed up the curry by adding salt twice.
After we lost the match, my coach said "let's move on". What did he mean?

To move on means to stop thinking about something that is over and go forward to the next thing.
Example: We lost today, but let's move on and get ready for Saturday's game.
Does "sleep in" mean to sleep inside the house?

No. To sleep in means to sleep later than usual in the morning, often on purpose.
Example: On holidays I sleep in until nine.
Can you explain "stay up"? I asked my parents if I could stay up for the cricket final.

To stay up means not to go to bed at the usual time.
Example: We stayed up until midnight to watch the final over.
The teacher told me off for talking in class. What does "tell off" mean?

To tell someone off means to speak to them angrily because they did something wrong. It is informal, and it is more common in British English.
Example: Dad told us off for leaving the lights on.
My map says "alternate route". Should it be "alternative"?

"Alternative" means another possible choice. "Alternate" usually means every second one, but American English also uses "alternate" for a substitute route, so both appear.
Examples: The road is closed, so take the alternative route. We clean the lab on alternate Fridays.
Is there any difference between "continual" and "continuous"?

Traditionally, "continuous" means without a break and "continual" means repeated again and again with pauses. Many people use them interchangeably.
Examples: The rain fell continuously all night. The phone rang continually during dinner.
The teacher said "lessen the noise". Is that a typo for "lesson"?

No. "Lessen" is a verb meaning to make something smaller. "Lesson" is a noun for a class or something you learn.
Examples: Closing the windows will lessen the noise. Today's lesson is about rivers.
Is it "waist" or "waste" my time?

Use "waste" here. "Waste" means to use something badly or to throw it away, and "waist" is the middle part of the body.
Examples: Do not waste water. He tied a sash around his waist.
Bus fair or bus fare: which spelling is right?

Write "fare". A fare is the money you pay for a journey. "Fair" means just, or a market or event.
Examples: The bus fare is paid to the conductor. The school fair raised money for books.
I saw "stake" on a restaurant menu. Is that right?

The menu word is "steak", a thick slice of meat or fish. "Stake" is a pointed post, or something at risk.
Examples: The cook served a fish steak with lemon. Ravi tied the young plant to a wooden stake.
Moral or morale: which one is the lesson of a story?

"Moral" is the lesson, or something to do with right and wrong. "Morale" is the confidence and spirit of a group.
Examples: The moral of the story is to be honest. Team morale was high after the win.
Is it "everyone" or "every one" in "every one of the sweets was gone"?

Use "every one" here. It means each single item and is usually followed by "of". "Everyone" is one word and means all people.
Examples: Every one of the sweets was gone. Everyone enjoyed the party.
Is it "aquaintance" or "acquaintance"?

The correct spelling is "acquaintance", with a c before the q: ac-quaint-ance.
Example: She is an acquaintance from my yoga class, not a close friend.
I wrote "consience". Is that right?

No. The correct spelling is "conscience". Notice that "science" is hidden inside it.
Example: His conscience told him to return the extra change.
Is it peculier or peculiar?

It is "peculiar", ending in -iar.
Example: The soup had a peculiar smell.
Is it hygine, hygeine or hygiene?

The correct spelling is "hygiene". Remember the "i before e" pattern in "hy-gi-ene".
Example: Washing hands is part of good hygiene.
I spelled my cousin's daughter as "neice". Is it right?

No. The correct spelling is "niece", with i before e.
Example: My niece draws beautifully.
Is it eigth or eighth?

The correct spelling is "eighth": it is "eight" plus the letter h.
Example: She finished eighth in the race.
Is "souvenier" spelled correctly?

No. The correct spelling is "souvenir", ending in -ir.
Example: I bought a small wooden elephant as a souvenir.
The word for "sadly": is it unfortunatly or unfortunately?

It is "unfortunately". It is "unfortunate" with -ly added, and the e stays.
Example: Unfortunately, the library was closed today.
Which word do Britons use for the luggage space at the back of a car?

British English calls it the "boot", and American English calls it the "trunk". Indian English usually says "boot".
Example: Dad put the bags in the boot.
Bonnet or hood: what is the cover over a car engine called?

British English says "bonnet" and American English says "hood". Indian English usually says "bonnet".
Example: The driver lifted the bonnet to check the engine.
Do British people say "holiday" or "vacation"?

British English usually says "holiday" for a break from work or school, and "vacation" mostly for university breaks. American English says "vacation" and keeps "holiday" for a festival or public day. Indian English uses both.
Example: We went to Mysore for the summer holidays.
Is it a "timetable" or a "schedule" for classes?

British English says "timetable" for classes and trains, and American English says "schedule". Indian English usually says "timetable" for school.
Example: Check the new timetable on the notice board.
Is it a "postman" or a "mailman"?

British English says "postman" and "post". American English says "mailman" or "mail carrier" and "mail". Indian English follows the British words.
Example: The postman delivers the letters before ten.
What is a "chemist's" in British English?

A chemist's is a shop that sells medicines and everyday items like soap. Americans say "drugstore" or "pharmacy". In India, "chemist" is common.
Example: I bought soap and toothpaste at the chemist's.
In the US, what is a "zebra crossing" called?

They call it a "crosswalk". British English says "zebra crossing" for a striped crossing.
Example: Always use the zebra crossing when you cross the road.
Is it "coriander" or "cilantro" for the green leaves?

British English and Indian English say "coriander" for the leaves and seeds. American English says "cilantro" for the leaves and "coriander" for the seeds.
Example: Add chopped coriander to the chutney.
Is it too stiff to write "purchase" instead of "buy" in an email?

"Purchase" is more formal than "buy". It suits business or official writing, while "buy" is better for friendly messages.
Examples: The school purchased new computers this year. I bought a bag yesterday.
Should I write "kids" or "children" in my essay?

"Kids" is informal and fine in speech or messages. In a formal essay, "children" is the safer word.
Examples: The kids are playing outside. Children need enough sleep to learn well.
Is "require" better than "need" in a formal letter?

Usually yes. "Require" sounds more formal and is common in rules and notices, while "need" is natural in everyday talk.
Examples: Applicants are required to bring a photo ID. I need a pen.
Can I start a sentence with "But"?

Yes, in everyday and modern writing, it is common. Some teachers prefer "however" in formal essays, so check your teacher's preference.
Examples: I wanted to come. But I had a test. I wanted to come; however, I had a test.
How should I greet a whole team: "Dear all" or "Hi all"?

"Dear all" is a little more formal and suits a manager or a client group. "Hi all" is friendly and fine inside a team you know well.
Examples: Dear all, the meeting is moved to Friday. Hi all, lunch is here.
Should I write "don't" or "do not" in a school essay?

Contractions like "don't" are normal in speech and casual writing. Formal essays and official letters usually avoid them, so write "do not".
Examples: I don't know the answer. The committee does not approve the plan.
Is it better to write "assist" than "help" in a customer email?

"Assist" is a little more formal and is common in service writing. "Help" is just as correct and sounds warmer, so it suits most everyday messages.
Examples: Our team will assist you with the booking. Can you help me carry this bag?
Is it "enquire" or "inquire"? My office uses both.

Both are correct. British English often uses "enquire" for asking and "inquiry" for a formal investigation, while American English uses "inquire" and "inquiry". Indian English usually follows the British pattern.
Example: I called the college to enquire about the course fees.
Half my class bought the same pen after the ad. Dad says they "jumped on the bandwagon". What does that mean?

To jump on the bandwagon means to join something because it is popular or successful, often late and without much thought of your own.
Example: When the new game became popular, half the class jumped on the bandwagon.
Priya told me "keep it under your hat". Does that mean I should wear a hat?

No. To keep something under your hat means to keep it secret.
Example: Keep it under your hat, but we are planning a surprise party for Meera.
What does it mean to "learn the hard way"?

It means to learn something from a bad experience instead of from advice.
Example: Arun learned the hard way that you should save your files before the power goes off.
The clerk said, "Get the promise in black and white." What does that mean?

"In black and white" means in writing, so that it is clear and official. It can also describe something very clear, with no grey area.
Example: Please get the delivery date in black and white before you pay.
My friend said "let me play devil's advocate". Is she calling someone a devil?

No. To play devil's advocate means to argue against an idea, not because you disagree, but to test it.
Example: I'll play devil's advocate: what if it rains on the day of the picnic?
What is "the lion's share" of something?

The lion's share is the biggest part of something.
Example: Aditi did the lion's share of the work on our science model.
Our shop has few customers now. My uncle says "the writing is on the wall". What does he mean?

"The writing is on the wall" means there are clear signs that something bad will happen soon.
Example: After a year of empty seats, the writing was on the wall for the old cinema.
Why shouldn't I "burn bridges" when I leave a job?

To burn your bridges means to end a relationship in such an angry way that you cannot repair it later.
Example: Do not burn your bridges when you leave a job; you may need a reference one day.
How do I use "get across"? My teacher said "get your point across".

To get something across means to make an idea clearly understood by others.
Example: She used a drawing to get her point across to the little ones.
I still haven't got around to cleaning my shelf. Is that phrase right?

Yes. To get around to something means to finally find the time to do it, usually after a delay.
Example: I finally got around to replying to Grandma's letter.
The manager wants to "iron out" the problems. Does anyone need an iron?

No. To iron out problems means to solve small difficulties or differences so that everything works smoothly.
Example: We met on Monday to iron out the last details of the trip.
Our teacher asked who broke the window, and Rahul "owned up". What does that mean?

To own up means to admit honestly that you did something wrong.
Example: Rahul owned up to breaking the window and offered to pay for it.
What does "pull off" mean in "We pulled off a win"?

To pull something off means to succeed in doing something difficult. In a driving context, it can also mean to leave the road and stop.
Example: The students pulled off a perfect concert with only two days of practice.
Does "settle in" mean to sit down?

Not exactly. To settle in means to become comfortable in a new place or situation.
Example: It took a week for Anita to settle in at her new school.
How is "leave out" used? Mum said "don't leave out the date".

To leave out something means not to include it.
Example: Don't leave out your phone number when you fill in the form.
What does "line up" mean at school assembly?

To line up means to stand in a line, one behind another. It can also mean to arrange something in advance.
Examples: Please line up outside the lab. The school has lined up a guest speaker for Friday.
What is the difference between "hoard" and "horde"?

A "hoard" is a hidden store of things you save, and "to hoard" means to keep such a store. A "horde" is a large, noisy crowd.
Examples: The squirrel hoards nuts for the winter. A horde of children ran out of the gate.
Is it "born" or "borne" in "she has borne the cost"?

Write "borne" there. "Borne" is a past form of "bear" meaning carried or put up with. "Born" is used for coming into life.
Examples: She was born in Pune. The pillars have borne the weight of the roof for two hundred years.
My atlas says "capital", but I saw "capitol" in a film. Are they the same?

No. A "capital" is the main city of a country or state, and also a letter in upper case. A "capitol" is the building where a legislature meets, mostly in the United States.
Examples: Delhi is the capital of India. Write your name in capital letters.
Is it the "sole" or the "soul" of a shoe?

It is the "sole". "Sole" means the bottom of a foot or shoe, and also "only". "Soul" means the spirit of a person.
Examples: The sole of my shoe came off. Music feeds the soul.
Heal or heel: which one is the back of my foot?

The back of your foot is the "heel". "Heal" is a verb meaning to become well again, and it is also used for hurt feelings.
Examples: She wore shoes with a low heel. Time can heal a broken friendship.
I wrote "good mourning" on a card. Is that right?

No, the greeting is "good morning". "Mourning" means grieving for someone who has died.
Examples: Good morning, everyone! The family stayed in mourning for a week.
Are "disinterested" and "uninterested" the same?

Traditionally, "disinterested" means fair, with nothing to gain, and "uninterested" means not interested. In casual use, many people use "disinterested" for both.
Examples: A judge should be disinterested. Ravi was uninterested in the film.
Precede or proceed: which one means "go ahead"?

"Proceed" means to go ahead or continue. "Precede" means to come before something.
Examples: Please proceed to gate five. Lightning usually precedes thunder.
Flaunt or flout: I want to say someone ignored a rule.

Use "flout". To flout a rule means to disobey it openly. "Flaunt" means to show something off proudly.
Examples: The driver flouted the traffic rules. She flaunted her new bag.
Is it "curiousity" or "curiosity"?

The correct spelling is "curiosity". The noun drops the u of "curious" (-ous becomes -os), giving cur-i-os-i-ty.
Example: Her curiosity made her read the whole encyclopedia.
I wrote "desparate" in my story. Is that right?

No. The correct spelling is "desperate", with an e in the middle: des-per-ate.
Example: The farmers were desperate for rain.
Is "disasterous" spelled right?

No. The correct spelling is "disastrous". The e of "disaster" disappears before -ous.
Example: The flood was disastrous for the harvest.
Is it familar or familiar?

The correct spelling is "familiar", ending in -iar: fa-mil-iar.
Example: Her face looks familiar, but I cannot remember her name.
I keep writing "flourescent". What is the right spelling?

It is "fluorescent". The u comes before the o: fluor-escent.
Example: The classroom has a fluorescent tube light.
Irresistable or irresistible?

The correct spelling is "irresistible", ending in -ible.
Example: The smell of fresh jalebi was irresistible.
Is "marraige" correct?

No. The correct spelling is "marriage": mar-riage, with the i before the a, and a double r.
Example: Their marriage was celebrated in the spring.
I need to spell "medival" for my history project. Is that right?

No. The correct spelling is "medieval", with a second e: me-di-e-val.
Example: We visited a medieval fort on the hill.
In Britain, is it "film" or "movie"?

British English usually says "film" for what Americans call a "movie". Indian English uses both, and "film" is very common.
Example: We watched a film at the cinema on Sunday.
Do I say "sweets" or "candy" for sugary treats?

British English and Indian English say "sweets", and American English says "candy". In India, "sweets" can also mean mithai.
Example: She gave each child a sweet at the door.
Is a "dustbin" the same as a "trash can"?

Yes. British English says "dustbin" and American English says "trash can" or "garbage can". Indian English usually says "dustbin".
Example: Please put the wrapper in the dustbin.
What does a British person call a "parking lot"?

British English says "car park" and American English says "parking lot". Indian English uses both, and "parking" is common too.
Example: Meet me in the car park near the gate.
Is a "motorway" the same as a "highway"?

A motorway is the British word for a major fast road with several lanes. Americans say "highway" or "freeway". Indian English usually says "highway" or "expressway".
Example: The motorway was empty at dawn.
What is an "aubergine"? My recipe book is British.

It is a purple vegetable that Americans call an "eggplant". In India it is usually called "brinjal".
Example: Mum cooked aubergine with garlic and tomatoes.
Do British schools have a "headmaster" or a "principal"?

British English often says "headteacher" or "headmaster", and American English says "principal". Indian English usually says "principal".
Example: The headmaster spoke to the school at assembly.
My pen pal in England asked for a "rubber". What does she want?

In British English, a "rubber" is a pencil eraser. Americans say "eraser", and Indian English uses both words.
Example: Can I borrow your rubber? I made a mistake.
What are "trainers" in British English?

"Trainers" are soft shoes for sport and everyday wear, which Americans call "sneakers". In India, people often say "sports shoes".
Example: She wore white trainers for games class.
When should I use "regarding" instead of "about"?

"Regarding" is more formal and suits letters, emails and notices. "About" is natural in everyday speech.
Examples: I am writing regarding your advertisement. Tell me about your trip.
Is "reside" better than "live" on a form?

"Reside" is formal and common in official papers. In normal speech, "live" is better.
Examples: Applicants must reside in this district. We live near the park.
Can I write "obtain" instead of "get" in my application?

Yes. "Obtain" is more formal than "get" and suits official writing. In friendly speech, "get" is more natural.
Examples: You can obtain the form from the office. Can you get me a pen?
Is "therefore" too formal? Can I just write "so"?

"Therefore" is more formal and common in essays and reports. "So" is fine in speech and friendly writing.
Examples: It was raining; therefore, the match was cancelled. It was raining, so we stayed home.
Can I say "yeah" in a job interview?

It is better to say "yes". "Yeah" is casual, and an interview is usually a formal setting.
Examples: Yes, I have two years of experience. Yeah, I'll be there at six.
My manager wrote "FYI" in a message. What is it?

"FYI" means "for your information". It is a short, informal workplace phrase, so in a formal letter you should write the words.
Example: FYI, the meeting has moved to ten o'clock.
Can I say "guys" to a mixed group?

In casual speech, "you guys" is often used for a mixed group, especially in American English. In formal speech or writing, say "everyone" or "colleagues".
Examples: Are you guys ready to leave? Good morning, everyone.
Should I write "attempt" or "try" in a report?

"Attempt" is more formal and is common in reports and exams. "Try" is the normal everyday word.
Examples: Students may attempt all five questions. Please try the sweets.
I can't come to the party tonight. Can I "take a rain check"?

Yes. To take a rain check means to politely refuse now and suggest doing it another time. It is informal.
Example: I can't come tonight, but may I take a rain check and visit next week?
The guard "turned a blind eye" to the children playing. What does that mean?

To turn a blind eye means to pretend not to notice something that is wrong or not allowed.
Example: The cashier turned a blind eye when the little boy took a free sweet from the bowl.
My coach tells us to "keep our cool" when the score is close. What does it mean?

To keep your cool means to stay calm in a difficult or stressful moment. It is informal.
Example: Keep your cool, Zara; the bus will come soon.
Why did my uncle say the council is "dragging its feet" about the road?

To drag your feet means to be slow in doing something, usually because you do not really want to do it.
Example: The council dragged its feet on repairing the road for months.
After the trek I "slept like a log". Is that good?

Yes. To sleep like a log means to sleep very deeply, without waking up.
Example: After the long trek, Kabir slept like a log.
In our family, who "calls the shots"? My dad says it is Grandma.

To call the shots means to make the important decisions and be in charge. It is informal.
Example: In our house, Grandma calls the shots about festival plans.
His name "rings a bell", but I can't remember where from. What does that mean?

If a name or fact rings a bell, it sounds familiar and reminds you of something you have heard before.
Example: Her name rings a bell, but I cannot remember where we met.
Before the results, we were "on pins and needles". Were we hurt?

No. To be on pins and needles means to feel nervous and excited while waiting for something.
Example: We were on pins and needles until the results appeared on the board.
The bus was "held up" by a traffic jam. Does "hold up" mean to lift something?

In this sentence it means to delay. "Hold up" can also mean to support something or, in talk about arguments, to remain true when tested.
Examples: The bus was held up by a traffic jam. Your argument holds up well.
My teacher asked Ravi to "show me around" the school. What does it mean?

To show someone around means to take them through a place and explain what is there.
Example: Ravi showed the new student around the school.
The flood "cut off" the village. What does "cut off" mean here?

Here it means to separate a place so that people cannot enter or leave. It can also mean to stop something, like a supply, or to interrupt a speaker.
Examples: The flood cut off the village for two days. Please do not cut me off while I speak.
What does "tear up" mean? I heard it twice in a day.

It has two meanings. It can mean to rip something into small pieces. In informal speech, it can also mean to start crying a little.
Examples: She tore up the old notes and put them in the bin. Grandma teared up at the farewell song.
My coach asked us to "build up" our stamina slowly. How is the phrase used?

To build up something means to increase it gradually.
Example: Build up your stamina slowly by walking a little farther each week.
The committee "watered down" the rule. What does "water down" mean?

To water something down means to make it weaker, either by adding water or by changing it so that it has less force.
Example: The committee watered down the rule so that more students could take part.
What does "run away" mean in "the puppy ran away"?

To run away means to leave a place quickly, often from fear or danger. It can also mean to leave home in secret.
Example: The puppy ran away when it heard the thunder.
The captain "stepped down" after the tournament. Did he fall?

No. To step down means to leave an important position, such as captain, manager or head.
Example: The captain stepped down after the tournament and a new player took over.
Elicit or illicit: which one means "to draw out"?

"Elicit" means to draw out a response or information. "Illicit" means forbidden or against the law.
Examples: The teacher asked questions to elicit ideas. The police stopped the illicit trade in fake tickets.
Is it "idle" or "idol" for someone I admire?

For someone you admire, write "idol". "Idle" means not working or not busy.
Examples: Her idol is a champion archer. The machines stood idle during the strike.
Coarse or course: "The cloth is ___."

Write "coarse". "Coarse" means rough, and "course" means a path, a set of lessons, or a part of a meal.
Examples: This cloth feels coarse. She joined a drawing course.
Is it "tide" or "tied": "The ___ came in"?

Write "tide". The tide is the regular rise and fall of the sea. "Tied" is the past tense of "tie".
Examples: The tide came in slowly. He tied his laces tightly.
Taught or taut: "The rope was ___."

Write "taut", which means pulled tight. "Taught" is the past tense of "teach".
Examples: The rope was taut. Mr. Rao taught us geometry last year.
Do I "pour over" a book or "pore over" it?

The correct phrase is "pore over", meaning to study something closely. "Pour" is for liquids.
Examples: Aisha pored over the old atlas for an hour. Please pour the tea slowly.
Canvas or canvass: which one is about asking people for votes?

"Canvass" is the verb for asking people for votes or opinions. "Canvas" is a strong cloth used for tents and bags.
Examples: Volunteers canvassed the neighbourhood before the election. The tent was made of canvas.
Wary or weary: how do I say I am very tired?

Use "weary" for tired. "Wary" means careful because you suspect danger.
Examples: The travellers were weary after the long journey. Be wary of crossing the river after heavy rain.
I wrote "persue" in my notes. Is it right?

No. The correct spelling is "pursue": p-u-r-s-u-e.
Example: She wants to pursue her dream of becoming a pilot.
Is it refrence, referance or reference?

The correct spelling is "reference", with an e in each part: ref-er-ence.
Example: Please add a reference to the book you used.
Is it sargent or sergeant?

The correct spelling is "sergeant", with an e after the s and the letters "ea" before the nt.
Example: The sergeant led the parade on Republic Day.
Is "stomache" spelled correctly?

No. The correct spelling is "stomach", ending in -ach with no e.
Example: The warm soup comforted my stomach on the cold day.
Is it "strenth" or "strength"?

The correct spelling is "strength", with a g before the th: str-eng-th.
Example: The wrestler's strength amazed the crowd.
Suttle or subtle: which is the word for something fine and not obvious?

It is "subtle", with a silent b.
Example: There was a subtle difference between the two shades of blue.
Is "threshhold" right?

No. The correct spelling is "threshold", with one h in the middle: thresh-old.
Example: She stepped across the threshold with a lamp in her hand.
The word for what "time" and "lime" share: is it rhime?

The correct spelling is "rhyme", beginning with rh and with a y before the m and a silent e at the end.
Example: "Cat" and "hat" rhyme.
I want to write "yot" for a sailing boat. Is it spelled right?

No. The correct spelling is "yacht". The ch is silent, so it sounds like "yot".
Example: The yacht sailed out of the bay at sunrise.
Are school years split into "terms" or "semesters" in Britain?

British English uses "terms", usually three in a year. American English uses "semesters", usually two. In India, schools use "term" and many universities use "semester".
Example: The first term exams begin in September.
Is a "tin" only a metal? My mum keeps tea in a "tin".

"Tin" is a metal, but in British English it is also a container, like a can. Americans usually say "can" for a food container.
Example: Mum keeps the tea leaves in a tin.
In Britain, what is a baby "stroller" called?

British English says "pram" or "pushchair". American English says "stroller".
Example: The baby slept in the pram on the way to the park.
Pyjamas or pajamas: which is correct?

Both are correct. British English spells it "pyjamas" and American English spells it "pajamas". Indian English usually follows the British spelling.
Example: He changed into his pyjamas and went to bed.
Is it "analyse" or "analyze"?

British English writes "analyse" and American English writes "analyze". Indian English usually follows the British spelling.
Example: Please analyse the results of the survey.
What is a "flyover"? My American friend says "overpass".

They mean the same: a road that crosses over another road. "Flyover" is the British and Indian word, and "overpass" is the American word.
Example: The new flyover reduced traffic near the market.
A board outside the building said "To let". What does that mean?

"To let" means that the property is available to rent. It is used in British and Indian English, and Americans write "For rent".
Example: A "To let" sign hung outside the second-floor flat.
Is the letter Z said differently in Britain and America?

British English says "zed" and American English says "zee". Indian English usually says "zed".
Example: Zebra begins with zed.
My office emails say "please revert by Friday". Is that standard English?

In standard British and American English, "revert" means to go back to an earlier state. In Indian workplaces it often means "reply", which can confuse readers elsewhere, so "reply" is safer.
Example: Please reply by Friday.
Can I say "prepone the meeting"?

"Prepone" is widely used in Indian English to mean "move earlier", the opposite of "postpone". It is not standard elsewhere, so a safer phrase for international readers is "move to an earlier time".
Example: Can we move the meeting to an earlier time on Thursday?
My cousin says "I'm out of station". Is that correct English?

"Out of station" is common in Indian English and means away from the city or town. In other varieties, people usually say "out of town" or "away".
Example: I am out of town until Monday.
Is "stuff" okay in an essay?

"Stuff" is informal and vague. In an essay, use a more exact word like "items" or "materials".
Examples: Put your stuff in the bag. The kit includes all the materials for the project.
Is "really" too casual for an essay?
