"Really" is common in speech and informal writing. In essays, "very" or a stronger word like "extremely" usually sounds better.
Examples: It was really hot yesterday. The weather was extremely hot yesterday.
Can I say "awesome" in a formal letter?

"Awesome" is a casual word for "very good". In a formal letter, choose "excellent" or "impressive".
Examples: The match was awesome! The school's performance was excellent.
Is "OK" acceptable in an email to my manager?

Yes, "OK" or "okay" is common in work messages, though in a very formal letter you might prefer "agreed" or "that is fine".
Examples: OK, I will send it today. That is fine; I will send the file today.
When is "sufficient" better than "enough"?

"Sufficient" is more formal and suits reports and instructions. "Enough" is the usual word in conversation.
Examples: The funds are sufficient for the repairs. We have enough chairs.
Is "numerous" better than "many" in a report?

"Numerous" is more formal and means "many". In everyday talk, "many" or "a lot of" is more natural.
Examples: The report mentions numerous complaints about the bus service. Many students walk to school.
The class got out of hand when the teacher left. What does that mean?

If something gets out of hand, it becomes too wild or difficult to control.
Example: The noise got out of hand when the whole class started singing at once.
We found a cheap flat near the school, and Dad said we "hit the jackpot". Did we win money?

Not necessarily. To hit the jackpot means to have a big piece of luck or success. It can also mean winning a very large prize.
Example: We hit the jackpot when we found a cheap flat near the school.
What does "by and large" mean in "By and large, the trip was good"?

"By and large" means generally or in most cases.
Example: By and large, the students enjoyed the trip to the museum.
My aunt says my little cousin is "full of beans" today. Is he hungry?

No. To be full of beans means to be lively and full of energy. It is informal and mostly British.
Example: The puppy is full of beans this morning and will not sit still.
Our manager said a new project is "in the pipeline". Where is the pipeline?

There is no real pipeline. If something is in the pipeline, it is being planned or prepared and will happen soon.
Example: A new library is in the pipeline for our town.
My brother says filling in the form twice is "a pain in the neck". Does his neck hurt?

No. A pain in the neck is an informal way to say that something, or someone, is very annoying.
Example: Standing in two queues for one ticket is a pain in the neck.
My cousin is going to "tie the knot" in December. What does that mean?

To tie the knot means to get married.
Example: My cousin will tie the knot in December, and the whole family is invited.
My friends called me a "wet blanket" at the party. What does it mean?

A wet blanket is a person who spoils other people's fun by being gloomy or negative. It is informal.
Example: Don't be a wet blanket, Tara; come and join the game.
When the cart arrived, the kids "made a beeline" for it. Where did they go?

To make a beeline for something means to go straight towards it, without stopping.
Example: The children made a beeline for the ice-cream cart.
I heard "blow up" used for balloons and for an argument. Is that right?

Yes. "Blow up" can mean to fill something with air, to explode, or, informally, to lose your temper suddenly.
Examples: We blew up balloons for the party. Dad blew up when he saw the broken window.
My friend "came down with" a cold before the exam. What does that phrase mean?

To come down with an illness means to start to suffer from it.
Example: Meena came down with a cold the day before the exam.
What does "fill up" mean? The driver said "let's fill up before the highway".

To fill up means to make something completely full, such as a car's fuel tank or a bottle.
Example: Please fill up the water bottle before we start the trek.
I went along with my friends' plan. Does "go along with" mean I walked with them?

Not here. To go along with an idea means to agree to it or accept it. It can also mean to go somewhere together.
Example: I went along with their plan, though I preferred a different route.
What does "knock down" mean? They are going to knock down the old shed.

To knock down a building means to destroy it so that the ground is clear. In shops, it can also mean to reduce a price.
Example: They knocked down the old shed to make room for a garden.
The factory in our town "shut down". What does that phrase mean?

To shut down means to stop operating, either for a time or for ever. It is also used for computers and machines.
Examples: The factory shut down last year. Please shut down the computer before you leave.
Does "wash up" mean the same in British and American English?

No. In British English, "wash up" usually means to wash the dishes after a meal. In American English, it usually means to wash your hands and face.
Example: After dinner, we all helped to wash up.
Could you show me "set aside" in a sentence?

To set something aside means to keep it apart for a special purpose or for later.
Example: Meera sets aside ten minutes every night for reading.
Does "give out" mean to give something away?

It has two meanings. It can mean to hand things to people, and it can mean to stop working or run out.
Examples: The teacher gave out the books. Our old engine finally gave out on the hill.
Do I write "insight" or "incite" in "The book gave me ___ into village life"?

Write "insight", which means a deep understanding of something. "Incite" means to urge people to do something bad or violent.
Examples: The book gave me insight into village life. He was warned not to incite trouble between the neighbours.
Prophecy or prophesy: why do both exist?

They are different parts of speech. "Prophecy", with -cy, is the noun for a statement about the future, and "prophesy", with -sy, is the verb.
Examples: The old prophecy came true. Some storytellers claim to prophesy the future.
Flour or flower: which one goes into chapatis?

"Flour" is the powder from ground grain, used for chapatis and bread. A "flower" is the colourful part of a plant.
Examples: Mix the flour with water to make dough. The flower opened in the morning sun.
I want to "die" my kurta blue. Is that right?

No. Use "dye" for changing the colour of cloth. "Die" means to stop living.
Examples: She dyed the cloth yellow with turmeric. The plant will die without water.
Tale or tail: I want to write about a story.

For a story, write "tale". A "tail" is the part at the back of an animal.
Examples: Grandpa told a tale about a clever crow. The dog wagged its tail.
Is it "scene" or "seen" in "Have you ___ my pen?"

Write "seen". "Seen" is the past participle of "see", and "scene" is a place where something happens or a part of a play.
Examples: Have you seen my pen? The first scene of the play takes place in a market.
Sail or sale: "The shop has a ___ on shoes."

Write "sale", meaning a time when goods are sold cheaply. "Sail" is the cloth on a boat, or the verb for travelling by boat.
Examples: The shop has a sale on shoes. We set sail at dawn.
Hire or higher: "We ___ a car for the trip."

Write "hired". "Hire" means to pay to use something or to employ someone. "Higher" means more high. Americans usually say "rent" for cars.
Examples: We hired a car for the trip to Mysore. The shelf is higher than my head.
Is it "pasttime" or "pastime"?

The correct spelling is "pastime", with only one t in the middle: pas-time.
Example: Reading is her favourite pastime.
Is it oportunity or opportunity?

The correct spelling is "opportunity", with a double p: op-por-tu-ni-ty.
Example: This trip is a good opportunity to practise English.
I wrote "predjudice" in my essay. What is the right spelling?

The correct spelling is "prejudice": pre-ju-dice, with no d before the j.
Example: She had no prejudice against newcomers to the town.
Is "secretery" spelled correctly?

No. The correct spelling is "secretary", ending in -ary: sec-re-tar-y.
Example: The school secretary answered the phone.
Is it sacrafice or sacrifice?

The correct spelling is "sacrifice", ending in -ifice: sac-ri-fice.
Example: He made a sacrifice and gave up his seat to an older woman.
I keep writing "minature". Is that how it's spelled?

No. The correct spelling is "miniature", with an i before the a: min-i-a-ture.
Example: She collects miniature clay animals.
The dark shape of a person against light: silouette or silhouette?

It is "silhouette", with an h after the l: sil-hou-ette.
Example: We saw the silhouette of a tree against the evening sky.
Is "vehical" right?

No. The correct spelling is "vehicle", with a silent h: ve-h-i-cle.
Example: No vehicle may enter the park after dark.
Mould or mold: my science book uses one, my friend's uses the other.

Both are correct. British English spells it "mould" and American English spells it "mold". Indian English usually follows the British spelling.
Example: Mould grew on the old bread.
Catalogue or catalog: which one should I write?

Both are correct. British English usually writes "catalogue" and American English usually writes "catalog", though "catalogue" is also used in the US.
Example: The library has an online catalogue.
Do I write "Monday to Friday" or "Monday through Friday"?

British English usually says "Monday to Friday". American English often says "Monday through Friday". Indian English usually follows the British form.
Example: The office is open Monday to Friday.
Is it "in hospital" or "in the hospital"?

British English usually says "in hospital" when talking about a patient, and American English says "in the hospital". Indian English often follows the British form, but both are heard.
Example: My uncle is in hospital this week, so we visit him every evening.
Do I order a "takeaway" or a "takeout"?

British English says "takeaway", and American English says "takeout". In India, "parcel" is also widely used.
Example: We ordered a takeaway because nobody wanted to cook.
At a restaurant, do I ask for the "bill" or the "check"?

British and Indian English say "the bill". American English usually says "the check".
Example: Could we have the bill, please?
Is it a "ladybird" or a "ladybug"?

British English says "ladybird" and American English says "ladybug".
Example: A ladybird landed on the leaf.
My American cousin says he is "mad at me". Does that mean crazy?

In American English, "mad" usually means angry. In British English, it more often means crazy or very foolish, so "angry" is clearer.
Example: My cousin is mad at me because I forgot his birthday.
Is "request" more formal than "ask"?

Yes. "Request" sounds formal and suits letters and rules. "Ask" is the natural everyday word.
Examples: Students may request extra time in writing. Ask Dad for the keys.
When can I use "prior to" instead of "before"?

"Prior to" is formal and appears in notices and official letters. In everyday speech, "before" is better.
Examples: Please arrive prior to the start of the exam. Wash your hands before lunch.
Should I write "approximately" or "about" in my report?

"Approximately" is more formal and suits reports and exams. "About" is natural in conversation.
Examples: The trip takes approximately three hours. It takes about three hours.
My friend wrote "btw" in a message. What does it stand for?

"BTW" means "by the way". It is an informal short form for messages to friends, not for formal letters.
Example: BTW, I found your pen under the desk.
Can I use "lol" in an email to my teacher?

Better not. "LOL" means "laughing out loud" and is for casual chat with friends. In an email to a teacher, use full sentences.
Examples: Your photo is so funny, lol. That story made me laugh.
Is "folks" a rude word for people?

No. "Folks" is a friendly, informal word for people. In a formal speech, "ladies and gentlemen" or "everyone" fits better.
Examples: Thanks for coming, folks. Good evening, ladies and gentlemen.
Can I call my teacher "dude"?

No. "Dude" is very casual slang, used mostly between close friends. Use "Sir", "Madam" or the teacher's name instead.
Examples: Dude, did you see that catch? Excuse me, Madam, may I ask a question?
In a message to my teacher, can I write "pls" and "thx"?

It is better to write "please" and "thank you" in messages to teachers. Short forms like "pls" and "thx" are for quick chats with friends.
Examples: Pls call me, thx. Please send me the notes. Thank you.
I told Asha her new haircut made her look older, and she went quiet. My friend said I "put my foot in my mouth". Why?

It means to say something careless that embarrasses or upsets someone. You did not mean to hurt her, but the words came out wrongly.
Example: I put my foot in my mouth when I asked Tara how her old job was going, not knowing she had lost it.
The storm will "blow over" by evening, the radio said. Does it blow something over?

Here it means that the storm will pass and end. "Blow over" is also used for an argument or a scandal that fades away and is forgotten.
Examples: The storm blew over by dusk. The quarrel will soon blow over.
My history book mentions a "prophet", but my business book says "profit". Same word?

No. "Profit" is money gained after costs are paid. A "prophet" is a person believed to speak for God or to predict the future.
Examples: The shop made a good profit this month. Many people followed the teachings of the prophet.
Is "speach" the right spelling?

No. It is "speech", with double e. The verb is "speak", but the noun changes.
Example: Rahul gave a speech on Independence Day.
A British recipe site says "washing-up liquid", but an American blog says "dish soap". Same?

Yes. Both mean the liquid soap used to clean plates and pans. "Washing-up liquid" is British, and "dish soap" is American. In India, you may also hear "dishwash liquid".
Examples: We ran out of washing-up liquid. (British) We ran out of dish soap. (American)
My manager wrote "Please advise" at the end of his message. What should I do?

"Please advise" is a formal way of asking you to tell him what to do, or what you think about the matter. It is common in business emails.
Example: The supplier has a delay. Please advise whether we should wait.
My aunt will cook for fifty people "at the drop of a hat". Does she drop hats?

No. "At the drop of a hat" means immediately, without needing much time or persuasion.
Example: Our neighbour will help you at the drop of a hat if you need anything.
The teacher said, "Hold out your hand." Is it only for the hand?

"Hold out" has more than one meaning. Hold out your hand means to stretch it forward. It can also mean to last or to keep resisting, for example when supplies are limited.
Examples: Hold out your hand to receive the prize. Our water won't hold out for another week.
Is the word "humane" a way of saying "human"?

No. "Human" means relating to people. "Humane" means kind and showing compassion, especially towards people and animals.
Examples: Humans need water to live. The shelter takes a humane approach to stray animals.
Is it "rythm" or "rhythm"?

It is "rhythm". It has two h letters and no vowel except y: r-h-y-t-h-m.
Example: The drummer kept a steady rhythm.
Is the word "aeroplane" wrong because my book says "airplane"?

No, both are correct. "Aeroplane" is the British spelling and "airplane" is American. Many Indian schools follow the British "aeroplane", although "airplane" is widely understood.
Examples: The aeroplane landed on time. (British) The airplane landed on time. (American)
Which is warmer to write at the end of a letter to a friend, "Best wishes" or "Regards"?

"Best wishes" is warmer and friendlier, and good for birthdays and good news. "Regards" is more neutral and common in work emails. Both are correct.
Examples: Best wishes for your exams, Priya. Regards, Mr Khan.
The guard told all the passengers to "sit tight" during the delay. Does it mean sitting in a fixed position?

Not exactly. "Sit tight" means to stay where you are and wait patiently until something happens.
Example: Sit tight for a few minutes; the driver is bringing a new tyre.
Meena wouldn't "back down" in the argument even when she was wrong. What does "back down" mean?

To back down means to give up your position in an argument or a fight, often because the other side is too strong or right.
Example: The shopkeeper refused to back down, so the customer went to another shop.
Do animals "adapt" or "adopt" to a new climate?

They adapt. "Adapt" means to change in order to fit new conditions. "Adopt" means to take something as your own, such as a child, a pet or an idea.
Examples: Camels adapt to desert life. We plan to adopt a puppy from the shelter.
Is the word "mispell" spelled correctly?

No, it is "misspell", with a double s. The word is made from "mis-" meaning wrongly and "spell", so both s letters stay.
Example: Many people misspell "necessary" at first.
The teacher asked me to put the list on the "notice board". Americans call it something else, right?

Yes. A "notice board" is British and Indian English, and in American English it is usually a "bulletin board". Both mean a board where announcements are pinned.
Examples: The exam timetable is on the notice board. (British) The exam timetable is on the bulletin board. (American)
My bank letter starts "With reference to your application". What does it mean?

It is a formal way to say "about" or "regarding" something you wrote or said before. It is common in business letters.
Example: With reference to your letter of 5 May, we are happy to confirm the booking.
My teacher told me to explain the story "in a nutshell". How big is a nutshell?

It means in a few words, giving only the main points.
Example: In a nutshell, the story is about a boy who finds a lost puppy and returns it to its owner.
When he was criticised, he "lashed out" at his friend. What does that mean?

To lash out means to speak or attack suddenly in an angry way, often without thinking.
Example: She was tired and lashed out at her brother over a small mistake.
The king sat on his "thrown". Is that spelled right?

No. A king's seat is a "throne", spelled t-h-r-o-n-e, ending in "-one" plus e. "Thrown" is the past participle of "throw".
Examples: The king sat on his throne. The ball was thrown over the wall.
Is it "offical" or "official"?

It is "official", with a double f and an "i" before "al".
Example: She received an official letter from the school.
My American recipe says to "broil" the fish. In my book, we "grill" it. Same method?

Often yes. In British and Indian English, to "grill" is to cook food under strong heat from above. American English calls this "broil", and its "grill" usually means cooking over an open fire outdoors.
Examples: Grill the paneer until it is golden. (British) Broil the paneer until it is golden. (American)
My friends call each other "bro" and "sis". Can I use these words with teachers?

No. "Bro" and "sis" are casual, friendly words, short for "brother" and "sister", used between friends and family. With teachers or at work, use their titles or names.
Examples: Thanks, bro! Thank you, Mr Desai.
My mother told me not to "cry over spilt milk" after I broke my phone cover. What did she mean?

It means do not feel sad about something that has already happened and cannot be changed. You can only fix it or learn from it.
Example: The vase is broken and nothing will bring it back, so there is no use crying over spilt milk.
The driver almost "ran over" a stray dog. What does it mean?

To run over someone or something means to drive over them with a vehicle. "Run over" can also mean to go over the time limit, as when a meeting runs over.
Examples: The car ran over a nail. The meeting ran over by ten minutes.
I wrote "She sat on the stare". My sister laughed. What's wrong?

The word you wanted is "stair", meaning a step in a staircase. "Stare" is a verb meaning to look at something for a long time.
Examples: She sat on the bottom stair. Do not stare at people.
Is it "seige" or "siege" for a castle surrounded by an army?

It is "siege". The word follows the rule "i before e" in most cases, as in "believe" and "field".
Example: The siege of the fort lasted for months.
My teacher said to put a "tick" next to the right answer. An American website said "check mark".

They are the same: the small mark that shows something is correct or done. "Tick" is British and used in India, and "check mark" is American. In American English, "tick" is mostly the name of an insect.
Examples: Put a tick next to each correct answer. (British) Put a check mark next to each correct answer. (American)
Is "Could you possibly help me?" too polite for a friend?

It is very polite and a little formal. With a friend, "Could you help me?" or "Can you help me?" sounds more natural. "Could you possibly" is useful with a stranger or when you are asking for a big favour.
Examples: Could you possibly lend me your notes for a day? Can you help me with this?
In the detective story, the gardener turned out to be "a red herring". Was he a fish?

No. A red herring is something that misleads you or draws attention away from the real answer. In stories, it is often a false clue.
Example: The torn letter was a red herring; it had nothing to do with the missing necklace.
Leela "broke off" the friendship after the quarrel. Is that the same as breaking a stick?

Both senses exist. "Break off" can mean to separate a part by breaking it. It can also mean to end something, such as a friendship or a talk. In your sentence it means to end the friendship.
Examples: She broke off a piece of chocolate. They broke off their friendship after the quarrel.
The teacher said we'd have an "oral" test and a "aural" test. What is the difference?

"Oral" means spoken or connected with the mouth, so an oral test is speaking. "Aural" means connected with hearing, so an aural test means listening. They sound alike. Also note it is "an aural" test.
Examples: The oral exam was about reading aloud. The aural test was a recording of a story.
I typed "withdrawl" on the bank slip form. Is that right?

No, the word is "withdrawal", with an "al" ending. The verb is "withdraw" and the noun adds "-al".
Example: Please fill the form to request a withdrawal.
My friend says "my cousin sister" in English. Is that correct?

It is common in Indian English, but in standard English the word "cousin" does not show gender. Say "my cousin" or "my female cousin", or use her name.
Example: My cousin, Anita, lives in Pune.
Can an email begin with "Greetings"?

Yes. "Greetings" is a general opening, sometimes used when you do not know the reader's name or when writing to a group. It sounds a bit formal or old, so "Hello" or "Dear" followed by a name is often better.
Examples: Greetings, team. Dear Mr Sharma,
People keep saying "time flies" at my sister's farewell. What does that mean?

It means time seems to pass very quickly, usually when you are busy or enjoying yourself. It is often followed by "when you're having fun".
Example: Time flies; it feels like we joined this school only last week.
Our meetings always "drag on". What does that mean?

To drag on means to continue for too long, in a tiring or boring way.
Example: The speech dragged on until half the audience was asleep.
Is "tomato source" correct for a bottle in the fridge?

No. A liquid you add to food is "sauce". A "source" is where something comes from.
Examples: Would you like some sauce with the noodles? The river's source is high in the mountains.
Is "dissapoint" the right spelling?

No. It is "disappoint": the prefix "dis-" plus "appoint", which gives one s and a double p.
Example: I did not want to disappoint my grandparents.
When I wrote "sceptical" in my essay, spell-check changed it to "skeptical". Which one?

Both spellings are correct. "Sceptical" is British, and "skeptical" is American. Indian English usually follows the British spelling. Both mean doubting whether something is true.
Examples: I was sceptical about the story. (British) I was skeptical about the story. (American)
My old letter-writing book ends a leave application with "Yours obediently". Do people still write it?

It appears in older Indian school and office letters, but it is now rare and sounds very old-fashioned. A modern ending is "Yours sincerely" (when the letter begins with a name, such as "Dear Mr Rao") or "Yours faithfully" (when it begins "Dear Sir or Madam"), or simply "Thank you".
Example: Thank you for considering my request. Yours sincerely, Kiran Rao.
After the model fell apart, our teacher said we have to "go back to the drawing board". Do we need paper?

Not necessarily. It means to start again with a new plan because the first one failed.
Example: The first design was too heavy, so the team went back to the drawing board.
The goalkeeper "fended off" two shots. What does that mean?

To fend off something means to defend yourself against it, especially something that is attacking or annoying you.
Example: She fended off the questions with a smile.
The dog lifted its "pause" to shake hands. Is that spelled correctly?

No, the word is "paws", the feet of an animal. "Pause" means a short stop.
Examples: The puppy has muddy paws. Take a pause before the next question.
Is it "jewlery" or "jewellery"? I've seen two spellings.

It is not "jewlery", which is a misspelling. The standard British and Indian spelling is "jewellery" with a double l, and the American spelling is "jewelry".
Examples: She wore gold jewellery for the wedding. (British) She wore gold jewelry for the wedding. (American)
My cousin from the USA asked for the car's "license plate". I only know "number plate".

They mean the same: the metal or plastic plate with the registration number on a vehicle. British and Indian English say "number plate", and American English says "license plate".
Examples: Note down the number plate of the car. (British) Note down the license plate of the car. (American)
The notice says "as per the rules". Is "as per" good English?

It is correct and formal, and often used in business and official notices. In plain English, "according to" or "under" is simpler.
Example: According to the rules, students must wear a uniform.
My friend texted "hang in there" before my exam. Should I be hanging from something?

No. "Hang in there" is an informal way of saying "keep going and do not give up, even though it is hard".
Example: Hang in there, Dev; the exams finish on Friday.
All my relatives came to the station to "see me off". Why?

To see someone off means to go with them to the place where they leave, to say goodbye.
Example: We went to the airport to see my aunt off.
My teacher called the invention "ingenious" and my friend "ingenuous". Are they the same?

No. "Ingenious" means very clever and inventive. "Ingenuous" means innocent and honest, sometimes too trusting. The two words look similar but are rarely used for the same thing.
Examples: It was an ingenious way to save water. His ingenuous smile showed he had nothing to hide.
Which is right, "incidently" or "incidentally"?

It is "incidentally". The adverb comes from "incidental", so it ends in "-ally".
Example: Incidentally, did you bring the book I lent you?
My sister gave the baby a "dummy". My American friend laughed and asked if I meant a "pacifier".

Yes, they mean the same rubber nipple a baby sucks to calm down. "Dummy" is British, and "pacifier" is American. In Indian English, you may hear either word.
Examples: The baby stopped crying when she got her dummy. (British) The baby stopped crying when she got her pacifier. (American)
The office said, "You will receive your certificate in due course." When will that be?

"In due course" means at the proper time, without a fixed date. It is a formal phrase and does not tell you exactly when, so ask the office if you need a date.
Example: The results will be announced in due course.
The cat was "caught red-handed" with the fish. Was the cat painted red?

No. To be caught red-handed means to be found in the act of doing something wrong.
Example: The boy was caught red-handed taking mangoes from the neighbour's tree.
The tickets "sold out" in an hour. What does that mean?

When tickets or goods sell out, all of them are sold, and none are left.
Example: The new storybook sold out in two days.
Which is correct, "great the cheese" or "grate the cheese"?

Use "grate". To grate means to rub food against a rough surface into small pieces. "Great" is an adjective meaning very good or large.
Examples: Please grate the cheese for the sandwiches. We had a great day at the fair.
My friend writes "publically". Is that a mistake?

Yes. The adverb is "publicly", and it does not follow the "-ally" rule. The word "public" is an exception.
Example: The mayor thanked the volunteers publicly.
My friend said, "I gave my maths exam yesterday." Is "gave" right?

It is common in Indian English, but in standard English a student "takes" or "sits" an exam, and a teacher "gives" or "sets" it.
Examples: I took my maths exam yesterday. The teacher gave the class a short test.
My boss said "I am afraid we cannot approve your leave." Is he scared?

No. In polite English, "I am afraid" softens bad news or a refusal. It does not mean the speaker is really frightened.
Example: I am afraid the shop is closed on Sundays.
My little cousin said Grandpa's old car "kicked the bucket". Should I use that phrase?

It is a very informal, slightly joking way of saying "died", and people also use it for things that stop working. Avoid it when speaking about a person's death, because it can sound disrespectful.
Example: The old scooter finally kicked the bucket last week.
Aunt Rita said she'll "pop in" this evening. Do I need to prepare anything?

No. "Pop in" means to visit someone briefly and without a formal plan. It is informal.
Example: I'll pop in on my way back from the market to say hello.
Is it a "dual" or a "duel" between the two swordsmen?

Use "duel". A duel is a fight or contest between two people. "Dual" is an adjective meaning having two parts or two purposes.
Examples: The two knights fought a duel. The room has a dual use as a study and a guest room.
Can you tell me how "liason" is spelled? It looks odd to me.

It is spelled "liaison", with an extra i before the last syllable: li-ai-son. It means communication or a link between people or groups.
Example: Mina acts as the liaison between the teachers and the parents.
My cousin in England is in "Year 7", but my American friend of the same age is in "seventh grade". Are they the same?

They are similar but not exact. In England, Year 7 is the first year of secondary school at age 11 to 12. In American schools, seventh grade is for children around 12 to 13. School systems differ, so check with each school.
Example: My cousin started Year 7 last September.
On a form I saw "Mr / Ms / Mx". What is "Mx"?

"Mx" is a title, pronounced "mix" or "mux", that people who do not wish to use Mr or Ms can choose. It is used mostly in Britain and some other places, and is not found in every form.
Example: Mx Taylor will give the talk.
The news that the school would close was "a bolt from the blue". Was there lightning?

No. A bolt from the blue is a sudden, completely unexpected piece of news, usually shocking.
Example: The cancellation of the trip came as a bolt from the blue.
My cousin told me to "lighten up" at the party. Does it mean switching on a lamp?

No. "Lighten up" is informal and means to become less serious or less worried. Be careful, as it can sound rude if you say it to someone who is upset.
Example: Lighten up, Ravi; it is only a game.
The market was a "bizarre" full of colours. Am I using the right word?

You mean "bazaar", a market with many small stalls. "Bizarre" means very strange.
Examples: We bought bangles at the bazaar. The bizarre noise from the attic worried us.
Is "agressive" spelled right? My coach wrote it on the board.

The correct spelling is "aggressive", with a double g and a double s.
Example: The aggressive player was warned by the referee.
My grandmother says "open the light" when she wants it on. Should I copy her?

It is used in Indian English, but standard English says "turn on the light" or "switch on the light". "Open" is for doors, windows and books.
Example: Please switch on the light; it is getting dark.
An email ended "Do not hesitate to contact me". Is that an order?

No. It is a polite, formal way to say "please feel free to contact me".
Example: If you need anything else, do not hesitate to contact me.
The teacher said she would "give me the benefit of the doubt" about my late homework. Is that good for me?

Yes. To give someone the benefit of the doubt means to believe their explanation when you cannot be sure whether it is true.
Example: Mr Nair gave Ali the benefit of the doubt and accepted that the bus had broken down.
Can you "ring up" the plumber? Is it the same as "call"?

Yes. "Ring up" is British and Indian English for to telephone someone. Americans more often say "call".
Example: I will ring up the plumber in the morning.
Is a person "averse" or "adverse" to risk? And what is the other word?

A person is "averse" to something they dislike, usually followed by "to". "Adverse" describes things that are harmful or unfavourable, such as weather.
Examples: I am averse to spicy food. Adverse weather delayed the flight.
Is "immediatly" right?

No. It is "immediately". The adjective "immediate" ends in "e", and the e is kept when you add "-ly".
Example: Please reply immediately.
Is it "I dreamt about flying" or "I dreamed about flying"?

Both are correct. "Dreamt" is more common in British English, and "dreamed" is more common in American English. Use whichever you prefer, but be consistent in one text.
Examples: Last night I dreamt about flying. (British) Last night I dreamed about flying. (American)
My British friend greets me with "hiya". Is it a word?

Yes. "Hiya" is an informal British greeting, like "hi". Use it with friends, not in formal messages.
Example: Hiya, Sam! How was your trip?
Grandma says "a leopard cannot change its spots" about my cousin who is always late. Is she being unkind?

It can sound a little unkind. The saying means that a person's basic character does not change, so people who behave in a certain way will probably keep doing so. Use it carefully, because it can sound hopeless about someone.
Example: He promised to stop forgetting things, but a leopard cannot change its spots.
The older boys "pick on" the new student. What does it mean?

To pick on someone means to treat them unkindly again and again, often by teasing or bullying.
Example: Please do not pick on your younger sister.
I wrote "He lead the team yesterday". Teacher circled it. Why?

The past tense of the verb "lead" (pronounced "leed") is "led". The word "lead" is only the present tense. The metal "lead" is pronounced "led" too, which is why the two get mixed up.
Examples: She leads the choir every week. She led the choir yesterday.
Is "fourty" spelled correctly for 40?

No. The number 40 is spelled "forty", without the u. The numbers 4 and 14 keep the u ("four", "fourteen"), but 40 does not.
Example: There are forty students in the class.
My aunt works as an "estate agent". My American friend asked, "A realtor?" Same job?

Yes. An estate agent in Britain and India helps people to buy, sell or rent houses and land. In American English the job is a "realtor" or a "real estate agent".
Examples: The estate agent showed us three flats. (British) The realtor showed us three houses. (American)
A song says "Lemme know." What does it mean?

"Lemme" is how people say "let me" quickly in casual speech. "Lemme know" means "let me know". Avoid writing it in formal texts.
Examples: Please let me know when you arrive. (formal) Lemme know when you reach. (casual)
The teacher asked us to "read between the lines" of the letter. How do I read what is not written?

It means to understand a hidden or unstated meaning from the way things are said. You notice the tone and what the writer leaves out.
Example: She wrote that everything was fine, but reading between the lines, I could tell she was homesick.
When she saw the surprise, the whole class "burst out laughing". Is that a kind of explosion?

It is not a real explosion. "Burst out" followed by "laughing" or "crying" means to suddenly begin to do it, often loudly.
Example: Neeraj burst out laughing when the teacher slipped on the banana peel.
The boss gave his "ascent" to the plan. Is that spelled correctly?

No, the spelling should be "assent", which means formal agreement. "Ascent" is the act of climbing or going up.
Examples: The principal gave her assent to the plan. The ascent of the hill took two hours.
What is the right spelling of the word for general agreement? Is it "concensus"?

It is "consensus", with an s after "con" and no c in the middle. It means the opinion that most people in a group share.
Example: The class reached a consensus about the picnic place.
The bus conductor said, "Kindly adjust." What does he want?

It is used in Indian English to ask people to move up or make room, for example on a seat. Standard English would say "Could you please move along a little?"
Example: Could you please move along a little so that she can sit?
I wrote "Respected Sir" at the start of my application and my teacher changed it. Why?

"Respected Sir" is common in Indian English, but in international English the standard opening is "Dear Sir" or, better, "Dear" with the name and title.
Example: Dear Mr Iyer, I am writing to request a day's leave.
Grandfather calls my little sister "the apple of my eye". Why an apple?

The phrase means a person whom someone loves dearly and treasures above others. Originally "apple" meant the pupil of the eye, which people thought precious and in need of protection.
Example: Her granddaughter is the apple of her eye.
All her hard work finally "paid off". Does that mean she was paid?

Not in money. When effort pays off, it brings a good result. "Pay off" also means to pay a debt in full.
Examples: Years of practice paid off when Deepa won the race. He paid off the loan.
My map shows a "Palk Strait". Is it the same as "straight"?

No. A strait is a narrow stretch of water between two pieces of land. "Straight" means not curved.
Examples: Ships pass through the strait every day. Draw a straight line with the ruler.
What is the correct spelling of "nieghbour"?

It is "neighbour" in British and Indian English and "neighbor" in American English. The letters are "ei", not "ie", before "gh".
Examples: Our neighbour feeds the street dogs. (British) Our neighbor feeds the street dogs. (American)
Is it a "kerb" or a "curb" at the road edge?

For the edge of a pavement, British English writes "kerb" and American English writes "curb". Both are pronounced the same. In both varieties "curb" also means to control something, as in "curb your spending".
Examples: Wait on the kerb before crossing. (British) Wait on the curb before crossing. (American)
An American tourist said "howdy" to us. Should I say it too?

"Howdy" is a friendly, informal greeting, mostly used in parts of the United States. It is fine for a joke or in a casual setting, but "hello" or "hi" is safer.
Example: Howdy, everyone! Welcome to the farm.
Everyone says our new neighbour is "down to earth". Is that a compliment?

Yes. A down-to-earth person is sensible, practical and honest, and does not show off.
Example: Although she is a famous singer, she is very down to earth and chats with everyone.
My mum calls every evening to "check up on" my grandma. What does she do?

To check up on someone means to find out whether the person is well or doing what they should. "Check-up" with a hyphen is also a noun for a routine visit to a doctor.
Example: I will check up on the neighbour, as she has been ill.
Do I write "egg yoke" or "egg yolk"?

The yellow part of an egg is the "yolk", spelled with an l. A "yoke" is a wooden bar placed over the necks of oxen.
Examples: Separate the egg white from the yolk. The farmer put the yoke on the oxen.
My friend wrote "changable weather". Is that correct?

The usual spelling is "changeable", keeping the e after "chang" so the g stays soft.
Example: The weather in the hills is changeable.
At the bank I was told to "fill in the form". An American website says "fill out the form". Any difference?

No difference in meaning. "Fill in" is the usual British and Indian choice, and "fill out" is the usual American one, but both are understood everywhere.
Examples: Please fill in the form in capital letters. (British) Please fill out the form in capital letters. (American)
My uncle starts his emails with "I trust this finds you well". Is it normal in modern English?

It is correct but rather formal and old-fashioned. Many people now use "I hope you are well" instead.
Example: I hope you are well. I am writing about the school fair.
The shopkeeper said a good umbrella is "worth its weight in gold" in the monsoon. Is it really that expensive?

No, it is an exaggeration. It means something is extremely useful or valuable.
Example: A reliable torch is worth its weight in gold during a power cut.
My cousin "dropped out" of college. Does that mean he fell out of a building?

No. To drop out means to leave school or a course before finishing it. As a noun, "a dropout" is the person who left.
Example: Many students drop out of the course because of the heavy workload.
Is it "presence" or "presents" in "Your ___ is requested at the wedding"?

Use "presence". "Presence" means being in a place. "Presents" with an s is the plural of "present", meaning gifts.
Examples: Your presence is requested at the wedding. The children opened their presents.
Is it "basicly" or "basically"?

It is "basically". When an adjective ends in "-ic", add "-ally" to make the adverb: basic becomes basically.
Example: The story is basically about a boy and his dog.
On my jacket I fixed the "zip". My American pen friend calls it a "zipper". Are both fine?

Yes. A "zip" is British, and a "zipper" is American, and Indian English usually follows the British word. Both mean the sliding fastener on clothes and bags.
Examples: My bag's zip is stuck. (British) My bag's zipper is stuck. (American)
A customer said, "I'll get back to you tomorrow." What should I understand?

It means the person will contact you again, with an answer or more information, at a later time. It is informal and polite.
Example: Let me check the stock, and I will get back to you this afternoon.
My colleague told me not to "rock the boat" in the meeting. Am I on a boat?

No. To rock the boat means to cause trouble or upset a calm situation, usually by challenging the way things are done.
Example: Everyone agreed with the plan, and nobody wanted to rock the boat.
I can't "shake off" this cold. What does "shake off" mean?

To shake off something means to get rid of it, such as a cold, a habit or a feeling.
Example: He could not shake off the feeling that he had forgotten something.
On the plane, a man asked for an "isle seat". Was that wrong?

Yes, the correct word is "aisle seat". An "aisle" is the walkway between rows of seats. An "isle" is a small island.
Examples: I prefer an aisle seat so that I can stretch my legs. The Isle of Wight is an island.
Is it "dilemna" or "dilemma"?

It is "dilemma", with a double m and no n before the last letter. It means a difficult choice between two options.
Example: Aarav faced a dilemma: join the picnic or finish his project.
My builder said "skirting board", and a video called it "baseboard". Which is right?

Both are right. "Skirting board" is British and "baseboard" is American. Both refer to the narrow board along the bottom of a wall where it meets the floor.
Examples: The painter coloured the skirting board white. (British) The painter coloured the baseboard white. (American)
Is "I look forward to hearing from you" right for ending a job application?

Yes. It is a standard polite closing for formal letters and emails. Note that "forward" is followed by "to hearing", not "to hear".
Example: Thank you for your time. I look forward to hearing from you.
When the teacher asked me the date of the battle, I "drew a blank". What happened?

To draw a blank means to be unable to remember something or to find nothing, even though you try.
Example: I tried to recall the poem for the contest but drew a blank.
After the rain the noise in the street slowly "died down". Is something dying?

No. "Die down" means to become weaker or quieter.
Examples: The wind died down after midnight. Once the excitement died down, we went back to work.
Is a hotel "suit" or "suite"? I'm confused.

For a set of rooms, the spelling is "suite", pronounced like "sweet". "Suit" is the set of clothes, and also a verb meaning to be right for someone.
Examples: The family booked a suite on the top floor. That colour suits you.
Is it "gaurd" or "guard" for the person at the school gate?

It is "guard", with u coming straight after g.
Example: The guard at the gate checks every visitor's pass.
My class teacher said, "Don't just mug up the answers." Is "mug up" good English?

"Mug up" is informal British and Indian English and means to learn something by repeating it again and again, without really understanding. The standard words are "memorise" or "cram".
Examples: Don't just mug up the dates; try to understand the events. Tara crammed for the test.
In a film, the hero says, "I gotta go." Is "gotta" proper?

"Gotta" is a casual spoken form of "have got to" or "have to". It is common in films and chats but should not be used in formal writing.
Examples: I have to leave now. (formal) I gotta go. (casual)
When I wanted to ask about the old quarrel, my mother said "let sleeping dogs lie". Why?

It means do not stir up an old problem that is quiet now, because you may cause more trouble.
Example: The two neighbours have not argued for years, so let sleeping dogs lie.
The sign said "Keep out". Can I read that as an invitation?

No. "Keep out" is a warning telling people not to enter a place.
Examples: The sign on the gate said "Keep out". Please keep out of my room.
Do farmers grow "maze" or "maize"?

Farmers grow "maize", a cereal crop also called corn. A "maze" is a puzzle of paths where it is easy to get lost.
Examples: Maize grows well in this soil. The children got lost in the garden maze.
Which spelling is correct, "apparantly" or "apparently"?

It is "apparently". The word comes from "apparent", which ends in "-ent", so the adverb is "apparently".
Example: Apparently, the match has been moved to Sunday.
We bought a "cot" for the baby, but my American aunt called it a "crib". Which is correct?

Both are right for a small bed with high sides for a baby. "Cot" is British and used in India. "Crib" is American. In American English, "cot" means a light folding bed.
Examples: The baby sleeps in a cot beside our bed. (British) The baby sleeps in a crib beside our bed. (American)
How do I apologise in an email for answering late? Is "sorry for the delay" enough?

Yes, it is a polite and short way to apologise. For a more formal tone, you can write "I apologise for the delay in replying". Keep it brief, and then give your answer.
Example: I apologise for the delay in replying. The form is attached.
After he pushed his little brother, he got "a taste of his own medicine". What does it mean?

It means someone is treated in the same bad way that they have treated others.
Example: Rohan always teases the new boy, but when the others laughed at his haircut, he got a taste of his own medicine.
I made a small "slip-up" in my test. Does that mean I fell?

No. A "slip-up" is a small mistake. The verb is "slip up", used for making a careless error.
Examples: She slipped up on the last question. It was only a minor slip-up.
The word "guerrilla" sounds just like "gorilla" in speech. How do I keep them apart?

A gorilla is the largest of the apes. A guerrilla is a member of a small group of fighters who use surprise attacks. They sound the same in many accents, so remember that the fighter's word is longer, with "ue" and a double "r".
Examples: The gorilla ate bamboo. The book describes a guerrilla group in the war.
My book says "mathmatics" in the title. Is that how to spell it?

No. It is "mathematics", with "the" in the middle: math-e-mat-ics.
Example: Mathematics is her favourite subject.
I asked a British shopkeeper for a "rubber band" and he gave me a puzzled look, then said "elastic band". Which word is right?

Both are understood. "Elastic band" is the traditional British word for a loop of stretchy material used to hold things together. "Rubber band" is the usual American word and is also widely used in Britain and India. In British English, "rubber" is also a word for an eraser.
Examples: Hold the papers together with an elastic band. (British) Hold the papers together with a rubber band. (American)
Can I end an email to my teacher with "Yours truly"?

It is better not to. "Yours truly" is rather old-fashioned and mostly used in American formal letters, and it can also be a joking way to say "me". For a teacher, "Regards" or "Sincerely" is safer.
Examples: Regards, Ananya. Sincerely, Ananya.
I had "butterflies in my stomach" before my speech. Is that a stomach problem?

No. It describes the nervous, fluttering feeling you have when you are anxious or excited about something. It is not an illness.
Example: Ira had butterflies in her stomach before the first day of school.
Grandpa "nodded off" during the film. Did he nod his head?

He probably did, a little. "Nod off" means to fall asleep, often by accident, when you are tired.
Example: Dad nodded off on the sofa while the news was on.
Is it "vain" or "vein" for the blood tube in my arm?

The blood tube is a "vein". "Vain" means too proud of yourself, or without success.
Examples: The nurse found a vein in my arm easily. He is vain about his hair. She tried in vain to open the old lock.
I wrote "experiance" in my CV. Is that spelled right?

No. It is "experience", with an "-ence" ending. Spell it carefully in a CV.
Example: She has three years of experience in teaching.
At a new class a boy said, "Myself Rahul." Is that correct?

This is a common pattern in Indian English, but in standard English you say "I am Rahul" or "My name is Rahul". "Myself" is used only for emphasis or after a verb about yourself, like "I hurt myself".
Examples: Hello, I am Rahul. I cut myself while peeling the apple.
In a restaurant, should I say "I want a coffee" or "I'd like a coffee"?

"I'd like a coffee" is more polite. "I want a coffee" is correct but sounds direct. In a restaurant or a shop, "I'd like" or "Could I have" is the usual polite choice.
Examples: I'd like a cup of tea, please. Could I have the bill, please?
Just as we were talking about Sana, she walked in, and Dad said "speak of the devil". Was he insulting her?

No. People say "speak of the devil" when the person you were just talking about suddenly appears. It is a light, joking remark, and the meaning is not unkind.
Example: We were wondering who would bring the cake, and, speak of the devil, here comes Asha with a box.
My little brother always "acts up" when we go shopping. Does that mean he is acting in a play?

No. "Act up" means to behave badly, especially for a child, or, for a machine, to work badly.
Examples: The children acted up during the long bus ride. My old laptop is acting up again.
Walking through the stream, I wrote "weighed" in my story: "We weighed across the water." My brother says it is wrong. Is it?

Yes, it is wrong here. Use "waded". To wade is to walk through water, and the past tense is "waded". "Weighed" is the past tense of "weigh", which means to measure how heavy something is.
Examples: We waded across the shallow stream. The shopkeeper weighed the rice.
Is "ocurrence" spelled right?

No. It is "occurrence", with a double c and a double r.
Example: Heavy rain is a common occurrence in July.
In London I should take the "Underground", but my American friend says "subway". Are they the same?

Both mean an underground railway. London calls its system the Underground, or the Tube. In American English it is the subway. In British English, a "subway" is a walkway under a road.
Examples: We took the Underground to the museum. (British) We took the subway to the museum. (American)
The letter said, "Reply at your earliest convenience". Is there a deadline?

No exact deadline is given. The phrase is a polite way to say "as soon as you conveniently can". If time matters, a writer usually adds a date.
Example: Please send me the report at your earliest convenience.
The coach "flew off the handle" when we lost. Is that dangerous?

Not literally. To fly off the handle means to lose your temper suddenly and angrily.
Example: Please don't fly off the handle; it was only a small mistake.
My teacher says I must "live up to" my potential. Up to what?

To live up to something means to be as good as expected or promised.
Example: The film did not live up to the praise it had received.
Which is right: "I was ___ out after the trip"?

Use "worn". It is the past participle of "wear", as in "worn out". "Warn" is a verb meaning to tell someone about danger.
Examples: The old shoes are worn out. Please warn the children about the wet floor.
Is it "collegue" or "colleague" for people I work with?

It is "colleague", spelled c-o-l-l-e-a-g-u-e. A trick: "a colleague" has "ague" at the end, like "league".
Example: My colleague shared her notes with me.
Teachers at the new school keep asking, "What is your good name?" Is that standard?

This question is common in Indian English, but in standard English it sounds unusual. The standard way is "What is your name?" or "May I have your name?"
Example: May I have your name, please?
My friend answers "nope" and "yep". Are those real words?

They are informal replies, meaning "no" and "yes". They are fine with friends but not in formal speech or writing.
Examples: "Are you coming?" "Yep." Would you like more tea? No, thank you. (formal)
The radio said it will "rain cats and dogs" tonight. Will animals fall down?

No. It means it will rain very heavily.
Example: It rained cats and dogs, so the match was stopped.
How do I say I can "cope with" a lot of homework? Is "cope" the same as "manage"?

Yes, they are close. "Cope with" means to deal successfully with a difficult situation or task. Note that "cope" is followed by "with", not by an object directly.
Example: Tina copes well with her heavy workload.
Is it "device" or "devise" in "We need to ___ a plan"?

Use "devise", with an s and a z-like sound. "Devise" is the verb meaning to invent or plan something. "Device" is the noun for a tool or gadget.
Examples: We need to devise a plan for the science fair. A calculator is a useful device.
Is it "gratefull" or "grateful"?

It is "grateful", with only one l at the end. Words that end in "-ful" have one l.
Example: I am grateful for your help.
In my British maths book, "0" is called "nought". In America it's "zero". Which is correct?

Both are correct. "Nought" is mostly British and used for the digit 0. "Zero" is the usual American word and is understood everywhere, and it is also used in Britain, especially in science and temperatures.
Examples: The number is nought point five. (British) The number is zero point five. (American)
The letter was addressed to "The Honourable Mayor". What does that mean?

"Honourable" is a title of respect used for some judges and officials, depending on the country. In American English it is spelled "honorable".
Examples: The Honourable Mayor opened the library. (British) The Honorable Mayor opened the library. (American)
The noise of the mixer drives me up the wall. Is it a rude thing to say?

It is informal but not rude. "Drive someone up the wall" means to annoy or irritate someone very much.
Example: My brother's loud music drives me up the wall when I am studying.
The plan did not "pan out". What does "pan out" mean?

To pan out means to happen or develop in a certain way. In your sentence it means the plan did not succeed. Things "pan out well" or "do not pan out".
Example: I do not know how the match will pan out.
The word for the belly button is "naval", right?

No. The belly button is spelled "navel". "Naval" is an adjective that means connected with a navy.
Examples: Ships of the naval force sailed past. The baby's navel healed quickly.
Is "athelete" the way to write the word for a runner?

It is "athlete", spelled a-t-h-l-e-t-e, with no extra e between the h and the l. People often add one because of the way the word is spoken.
Example: The athlete trained every morning before school.
The book says "The toast was burnt", but my American friend wrote "burned". Which is correct?

Both are correct. "Burnt" is more common in British and Indian English, and "burned" is more common in American English. Burnt is also often used as an adjective.
Examples: I burnt the toast again. (British) I burned the toast again. (American)
My friend texted, "It was kinda fun." Can I write "kinda" in an essay?

No. "Kinda" is a spoken form of "kind of", meaning somewhat. It is fine in a chat but avoid it in essays and formal writing. The same applies to "sorta" for "sort of".
Examples: It was rather fun. (formal) It was kind of fun. (casual)
When I asked what I'd do if I failed, my uncle said "we'll cross that bridge when we come to it". What did he mean?

It means we will deal with a problem only if and when it really happens, and not worry about it now.
Example: I may need more books next term, but I'll cross that bridge when I come to it.
The manager "played down" the problem. What does it mean?

To play down something means to make it seem less important or serious than it really is.
Example: She played down her injury and kept running.
I put "current" in my cake recipe and my sister laughed. Why?

For a dried berry in cakes, the word is "currant". "Current" means happening now, or a flow of water or electricity.
Examples: Add a handful of currants to the dough. The current news is about the match. The river has a strong current.
Is it "vaccum" or "vacuum"?

It is "vacuum", with one c and two u letters side by side: vac-u-um.
Example: The vacuum cleaner is under the stairs.
Our newspaper uses the word "eve-teasing". Is it a term used in other countries?

It is used mainly in India for harassing girls and women in public. Elsewhere people use "street harassment" or "sexual harassment". Because "teasing" sounds light, many writers now prefer the standard words.
Example: The police have started a campaign against street harassment.
My friend wrote "cuz" in a text. Is that short for "because"?

Yes. "Cuz" is an informal short form of "because" used in texts, and it can also mean "cousin" in some places. Use "because" in school work and formal writing.
Examples: I stayed home because it was raining. (formal) I stayed home cuz it was raining. (casual)
I wasn't ready for the question, and the bell rang. A friend said I was "saved by the bell". What does this mean?

It means you were saved from a difficult situation just in time by something unexpected. The expression is often linked to boxing, where a bell ends a round.
Example: The teacher was about to call my name when the lunch bell rang, so I was saved by the bell.
The doctor said my uncle will "pull through". Is something being pulled?

It means that the person is going to survive a serious illness or get through a difficult time.
Example: The team pulled through a hard season and won the cup.
The cliff was "sheer" or "shear"? I've seen both.

For a very steep cliff, the spelling is "sheer". "Sheer" also means complete, as in "sheer joy". "Shear" is a verb meaning to cut wool or hair from an animal.
Examples: A sheer cliff rose beside the road. The farmer will shear the sheep tomorrow.
My friend wrote "She comitted herself to the cause." What is wrong with the spelling?

The word should be "committed", with a double m and a double t. The consonant is doubled because the stress falls on the last part of the verb "commit", before "-ed".
Example: He committed himself to finishing the course.
My friend said, "This is just for timepass." What is "timepass"?

"Timepass" is used mainly in Indian English and means something done only to fill free time, often without a purpose. In standard English you could say "a way to pass the time" or "just for fun".
Example: We played cards just to pass the time while it rained.
Can I write "Please reply back" in an email?

It is common, but "reply back" repeats the idea, because "reply" already means to answer. In careful writing, "Please reply" or "Please write back" is better.
Examples: Please reply by Friday. Please write back when you have the details.
My supervisor says Raj has "a chip on his shoulder". What does that mean?

To have a chip on your shoulder means to feel angry or unfairly treated for a long time and to be quick to argue about it. It is informal and usually critical.
Example: Since being left out of the team, he has had a chip on his shoulder and snaps at everyone.
The clerk said, "Please bear with me while the system loads." Are bears involved?

No. "Bear with" means to be patient with someone. It is a polite request, often used when there is a short delay.
Example: Please bear with us while we find your file.
Is it "envelop" or "envelope" for the thing I put a letter in?

For a letter holder, the spelling is "envelope", with an e at the end, pronounced "EN-vuh-lope". "Envelop" is a verb meaning to cover or surround completely, pronounced "en-VEL-up".
Examples: Please put the card in an envelope. Mist began to envelop the village.
Is it "reccomend" or "recommend"?

It is "recommend", with one c and a double m.
Example: Can you recommend a good book about birds?
My teacher said to turn the knob "anticlockwise" and my American cousin said "counterclockwise". Same thing?

Yes. Both mean in the opposite direction to the hands of a clock. "Anticlockwise" is British and common in India, and "counterclockwise" is American.
Examples: Turn the lid anticlockwise to open the jar. (British) Turn the lid counterclockwise to open the jar. (American)
I want to end a request with "Thanks in advance". Does that sound rude?

Some readers find it presumptuous, as if you are sure the person will help. It is common, though. A gentler line is "Thank you for your help" or "I would be grateful for your help".
Example: I would be grateful if you could send the form by Friday.
He passed the entrance test "by the skin of his teeth". Does that mean something to do with teeth?

Not really. The phrase means by a very small margin, only just.
Example: We caught the train by the skin of our teeth, just as the doors were closing.
I think Rahul "fell for" the joke. What did he fall for?

"Fall for" has two meanings. It can mean to be tricked into believing something, or to begin to feel romantic love for someone. Your sentence is about the first meaning.
Examples: He fell for the trick and gave them his bag. She fell for him at school.
Which spelling is right for changing a dress, "altar" or "alter"?

Use "alter". It is a verb meaning to change something slightly. An "altar" is a table or platform in a place of worship.
Examples: The tailor will alter the dress to fit you. Flowers were placed on the altar.
I wrote "posession" for the things my aunt owns. Is that right?

Not quite. The correct spelling is "possession", with a double s twice: poss-ess-ion.
Example: His most valued possession is an old wooden cricket bat.
My boss's email asked for the "updation" of the file. Is that an English word?

"Updation" is used in Indian English, but standard English does not use it. Say "update" instead: "the update of the file" or "please update the file".
Example: Please update the file by Monday.
My manager wrote "Send it ASAP". How is "ASAP" read, and is it rude?

It stands for "as soon as possible" and is read letter by letter, or sometimes as "ay-sap". It is common in work messages but can sound pushy, so a polite request such as "Could you send it as soon as possible, please?" is gentler.
Example: Could you please send the report as soon as possible?
My coach said I'd "get the hang of it" after a few classes. What is "the hang"?

"Get the hang of something" means to learn how to do it. "Hang" here just means the way it works, and it is informal.
Example: Cycling felt hard at first, but Leena soon got the hang of it.
The boxer was "knocked out" in the second round. What does it mean?

Here it means to hit someone so hard that they fall unconscious. "Knock out" also means to eliminate a team or player from a contest.
Examples: The champion was knocked out in the second round. Our school team was knocked out in the quarterfinal.
My friend asked for a "lone" from the bank. Is that right?

No. It should be "loan", money that you borrow and pay back. "Lone" means alone, as in "a lone tree".
Examples: Her father took a loan to repair the house. A lone cyclist crossed the bridge.
Do I write "existance" or "existence"?

It is "existence", ending in "-ence".
Example: The existence of the old fort surprised the tourists.
The farmer's tool is a "plough" in my book. A website spells it "plow". Which is correct?

Both are correct. "Plough" is British and common in India, and "plow" is American. The word is a noun for a farm tool and also a verb meaning to turn over soil.
Examples: The farmer uses a plough drawn by oxen. (British) The farmer uses a plow drawn by oxen. (American)
My colleague wrote "per my last email" in a message to me. Is this polite?

It can sound slightly cold or impatient, because it suggests the reader should already have read the earlier message. It is correct English, but a softer way is "As I mentioned in my previous email".
Example: As I mentioned in my previous email, the files are in the shared folder.
My mum said "curiosity killed the cat" when I asked about my birthday gift. Is that a warning?

It is a gentle warning. It means that being too curious about other people's business, or asking too many questions, can get you into trouble. People often continue "but satisfaction brought it back".
Example: Stop opening the cupboards; curiosity killed the cat.
The lawyer will "draw up" the contract. Is it a drawing?

Not really. To draw up a document means to prepare or write it formally, such as a plan, a list or an agreement.
Example: The club drew up a list of rules for the new members.
The sign said "tow-away zone". Is that spelled like my "toe"?

No. A "tow-away zone" is spelled with "tow", a verb meaning to pull something along, usually a vehicle. "Toe" is the part of the foot.
Examples: The police will tow the car if it is parked here. I stubbed my toe on the step.
Is it "possibilty" or "possibility"?

It is "possibility", with an "i" before the last "ty". The word has "-bil-i-ty".
Example: There is a possibility of rain this evening.
Is it a "cosy" or a "cozy" room?

Both spellings are correct. "Cosy" is British and "cozy" is American. The word means warm, comfortable and pleasant.
Examples: The reading room was cosy in winter. (British) The reading room was cozy in winter. (American)
A form says "I, the undersigned, declare...". Who is the undersigned?

"The undersigned" is the person who signs the document, so it means "I". It is formal and used in legal and official papers.
Example: I, the undersigned, confirm that the details above are true.
Our teacher said that Nina and Pooja are "birds of a feather". Are they both birdwatchers?

Not necessarily. The full saying is "birds of a feather flock together", and it means that people with similar interests or characters tend to become friends.
Example: Both of them love chess and old films, so they are birds of a feather.
The map says "ring road" but my American friend says "beltway". Do they mean the same?

Yes. Both are roads built around a city so that traffic can avoid the centre. "Ring road" is the British and Indian term, and "beltway" is used in parts of the United States.
Example: Take the ring road if you want to avoid the city centre.
Nina announced her news just before my speech and "stole my thunder". What does that mean?

It means she took the attention or praise that should have gone to you, often by doing or saying something just before.
Example: The little brother stole the thunder by dancing during the speech.
Is "quarentine" correct?

No. It is "quarantine", with "-ntine" at the end.
Example: Travellers were kept in quarantine for a week.
Is it "baited breath" or "bated breath"?

It is "bated breath". "Bated" comes from "abate", meaning to lessen, so it describes holding your breath in suspense. "Baited" is about putting bait on a hook or teasing someone.
Examples: We waited with bated breath for the result. He baited the hook with bread.
Our teacher said it is time to "knuckle down". Does it hurt?

No. To "knuckle down" means to begin to work seriously.
Example: Exams start soon, so I need to knuckle down to my studies.
The shop owner said, "The goods will come through by Friday." What does "come through" mean here?

Here it means to arrive or be delivered after waiting. "Come through" can also mean to survive a difficulty or do what you promised.
Examples: The parcel finally came through. She came through the exam well.
Is it "childrens' toys" or "children's toys"?

It is "children's toys". "Children" is already plural, so you add 's to show possession.
Examples: The children's toys are in the box. The boys' toys are on the shelf.
Should "winter" and "summer" start with capital letters?

Not usually. Seasons are written in lower case unless they start a sentence or are part of a name.
Examples: We went to the hills in winter. The Winter Olympics will be held in February.
Is it "I choose a blue shirt yesterday" or "I chose"?

"I chose" is right for the past. "Choose" (rhymes with "news") is the present form, and "chose" (rhymes with "nose") is the past.
Examples: I chose a blue shirt yesterday. Please choose a card.
We said, "Let's bunk the class." Is that standard English?

In Indian English, "bunk" means to skip class, and informal British English has "bunk off". It is not standard in American English, where people say "skip class" or "cut class". The word "skip" is the safest choice in all varieties.
Example: Don't skip class before the exam.
How do I spell "entrepeneur"?

The usual spelling is "entrepreneur", with "-pre-" in the middle. It is a French word for a person who starts a business.
Example: She became an entrepreneur and opened a small bakery.
I found "peek", "peak" and "pique" in one book. Which is for a quick look?

"Peek" means a quick look, often secret. "Peak" is the top of a mountain or the highest point. "Pique" is a feeling of annoyance, as in "a fit of pique", and as a verb it means to arouse curiosity.
Examples: She took a peek at the gift. The peak was covered in snow.
It took him a year to "face up to" the truth. What does that mean?

It means to accept something unpleasant and deal with it bravely.
Example: You must face up to your mistake and apologise.
The teacher said she would "mark down" untidy work. Does that mean writing it down?

Not here. In this sentence, "mark down" means to reduce marks or prices. It can also mean to write something down.
Examples: She marked down my answer for bad spelling. The shop marked down the shoes.
Is "rediculous" the right spelling?

No, it is "ridiculous", with an "i" after the r. It is linked to "ridicule", which has the same "i".
Example: It would be ridiculous to wear a coat in the summer heat.
Is it "deterioate" or "deteriorate"?

It is "deteriorate". There is an "-ior-" in the middle: deter, io, rate.
Example: The paper began to deteriorate in the damp cupboard.
What does it mean when someone writes "Cc'd" in an email, and when do I use Bcc?

"Cc" means "carbon copy": the people in Cc receive a copy that everyone can see. "Bcc" means "blind carbon copy", where the recipient's name is hidden from others. Use Bcc when you do not want to share addresses.
Example: I have copied the principal on this email.
Is a "comprehensive" explanation the same as a "comprehensible" one?

No. "Comprehensible" means easy to understand. "Comprehensive" means complete and covering many things.
Examples: His answer was comprehensible even to a small child. The teacher gave a comprehensive list of topics.
Dad "hit the roof" when he saw my report card. Did he climb up?

No. It means he became extremely angry, usually suddenly and loudly.
Example: Mum will hit the roof if you break another glass.
The leftover leave days can "carry over" to next year. What does that mean?

"Carry over" means to continue or be moved into the next period, such as leave or marks.
Example: Unused marks cannot carry over to the next test.
Is it "lambs gamble" or "lambs gambol" in a field?

It is "gambol", meaning to run or jump about playfully. "Gamble" means to risk money on a chance.
Examples: The lambs gambol in the field. It is unwise to gamble with your savings.
What is the difference between "respectfully" and "respectively"?

"Respectfully" means with respect. "Respectively" shows that items are matched in order.
Examples: He spoke respectfully to the elders. Anil and Sita are 12 and 14 respectively.
Everyone knows about the new shop, but it is an "open secret". What does that mean?

An "open secret" is something that is officially secret but known by most people.
Example: It was an open secret that the teacher was leaving.
Which one fits: "broach a subject" or "brooch a subject"?

It is "broach", meaning to bring up a topic for the first time. A "brooch" is a piece of jewellery pinned to clothes.
Examples: She wanted to broach the subject of holidays. Grandma wore a silver brooch.
Ms Rao is going to "take over" our class next month. Does that sound unfriendly?

Not at all. "Take over" means to begin to be in charge of something that another person was handling before. The phrase is neutral.
Example: Ms Rao will take over the class when Mr Iyer retires.
When do I write "anyone" and when "any one"?

Write "anyone" when you mean any person. Write "any one" as two words when you mean a single one from a group.
Examples: Is anyone at home? You may choose any one of these books.
We organised the school fair "on a shoestring". Does that involve shoes?

No. Doing something "on a shoestring" means doing it with very little money.
Example: She started her small tailoring shop on a shoestring, using one old machine.
Some workers "walked out" of the meeting. What does that mean?

"Walk out" means to leave suddenly, often to show anger or protest.
Example: The audience walked out in the middle of the speech.
Is "I was tired, I went to bed" a good sentence?

It is a comma splice, which means two full sentences are joined only by a comma. Use a full stop, a semicolon, or a joining word such as "so".
Examples: I was tired, so I went to bed. I was tired; I went to bed.
I answered the phone at the office and said "Who are you?" My boss frowned. What should I say?

That question sounds rude on the phone. Say "May I know who is calling, please?" or "Who is speaking, please?" Both are polite.
Example: Good morning, Sunrise Traders. May I know who is calling, please?
Which words get capital letters in a book title?

In common title style, capitalise the first word, the last word, and the important words. Short words such as "and", "of" and "the" are usually written in lower case in the middle. Some styles differ.
Example: The Man in the Moon
Is it "irrelevent" or "irrelevant"?

It is "irrelevant", ending in "-ant". It has a double r at the start.
Example: Your answer is irrelevant to the question.
Is it "playwrite" or "playwright"?

It is "playwright", a person who writes plays. The "wright" part means a maker, as in "shipwright".
Example: The playwright wrote his first drama at 19.
Is it correct to write "I am writing to follow up on my last email"?

Yes. "Follow up" is a phrasal verb meaning to check on something you asked or said before. As a noun or adjective it is usually written "follow-up".
Example: I am writing to follow up on my email of Monday.
Are sympathy and empathy the same?

Not exactly. "Sympathy" means feeling sorry for someone's trouble. "Empathy" means sharing or understanding how another person feels.
Examples: She felt sympathy for the injured bird. A good friend shows empathy and listens carefully.
The editor asked me to "tone down" the language. What does that mean?

To "tone down" is to make something less strong, harsh or extreme.
Example: Please tone down your reply; it sounds angry.
Is it polite to say "Thank you for getting back to me"?

Yes. It is a friendly and polite reply when someone has answered your message or call.
Example: Thank you for getting back to me so quickly.
How do I spell the breathing problem "asma"?

The spelling is "asthma", with "th" in the middle.
Example: The school nurse keeps an inhaler for students with asthma.
I got a call from an unknown person who asked for someone else. How can I say politely that they have the wrong number?

You can say, "I think you have the wrong number." Or say, "I'm sorry, there is no one here by that name." Both are polite.
Example: I'm sorry, I think you have the wrong number.
The coach told us to "warm up" before the match. Is it only about sport?

No. "Warm up" means to prepare your body for activity, and it can also mean to become warmer or more friendly.
Examples: We warmed up with a short jog. The room will warm up soon.
Can you "look over" my essay before I submit it?

Yes. "Look over" means to check something quickly. It is not as detailed as "go through".
Example: Please look over my letter for mistakes.
Do "censor" and "censure" mean the same?

No. To "censor" is to remove parts of a book, film or message that are thought to be unsuitable. To "censure" is to criticise someone formally and strongly.
Examples: The film was censored before release. The council censured the officer.
When do I write numbers as words and when as digits?

A common rule is to write numbers from one to ten as words and larger ones as digits, but styles differ. Use digits for dates, times and measurements.
Examples: I have three sisters. There are 25 students in the class.
How many dots should I use for an ellipsis and what is it for?

An ellipsis has three dots. It shows that something has been left out or that a thought trails off.
Examples: She said, "I wonder if..." and stopped. The list went on and on...
How is "gauge" spelled? "guage" looks wrong.

Yes, "guage" is wrong. The correct spelling is "gauge", with the a before the u.
Example: The fuel gauge shows the tank is half empty.
Everyone was asked to "weigh in" on the decision. What does that mean?

"Weigh in" means to give your opinion in a discussion.
Example: Several teachers weighed in on the new timetable.
After the film my friend said, "Let's go Dutch." What did he suggest?

He suggested that each person pays for their own share instead of one person paying for everyone. The phrase is informal.
Example: We went Dutch at the cafe, so I paid only for my own tea and snacks.
Is "porridge" the same as "oatmeal"?

Similar but not identical. "Porridge" is the usual word in Britain for a hot cereal made from oats, while "oatmeal" is the usual American word, which can also mean the ground oats themselves. Americans also say "porridge" sometimes, so the words overlap.
Examples: He had porridge for breakfast. He had oatmeal for breakfast.
My brother "pulled an all-nighter" before the exam. Is it a good idea?
