The phrase means he stayed awake all night to study or work. Whether it is a good idea is another matter, because many people concentrate better after sleep.
Example: She pulled an all-nighter to finish the project.
How do I use "on behalf of" in an email?

"On behalf of" means representing another person or a group. It is common in formal messages.
Example: I am writing on behalf of the sports club to invite you.
The bank decided to "write off" the loan. What does that mean?

"Write off" means to accept that something is lost and not to count it any longer. It can also mean to damage a vehicle beyond repair.
Example: The shopkeeper wrote off the unpaid bill.
Is it "a tenant of the faith" or "a tenet of the faith"?

It is "tenet", a belief or principle. A "tenant" is a person who rents a home.
Examples: Honesty is a tenet of the club. The tenant pays rent every month.
Is a "dressing gown" the same as a "bathrobe"?

Largely yes. Both are loose garments worn at home over night clothes or after a bath. "Dressing gown" is British, and "bathrobe" is American.
Examples: She put on her dressing gown. She put on her bathrobe.
Grandfather says "make hay while the sun shines". We have no hay at home!

It is a proverb meaning that you should use a good opportunity while it lasts. It comes from farming, because hay is cut and dried in dry, sunny weather.
Example: The shops are empty today, so let's make hay while the sun shines and finish our shopping.
Is it "recipie" or "recipe"?

It is "recipe", ending in "-pe". There is no "ie" at the end.
Example: My grandmother has an old recipe for lemon rice.
The principal promised new books but did not "follow through". What does that mean?

"Follow through" means to continue with an action until it is completed, especially something that you promised.
Example: She made a plan and followed through on it.
Can you "stick around" after the show? Is that polite?

Yes, it is friendly and informal. "Stick around" means to stay in a place a little longer.
Example: Please stick around after the meeting; we need your help.
Is "nineth" correct for position nine?

No, it is "ninth", without the e. Other ordinals keep the e, such as "eleventh".
Example: She came ninth in the spelling bee.
Is it "James's book" or "James' book"?

Both are accepted. Many style guides prefer "James's" because it shows how you say it, while some prefer "James'" for names ending in s, so choose one and keep it.
Example: This is James's book.
Is "Many thanks" correct, or should I write "Much thanks"?

"Many thanks" is the standard polite phrase and is correct. "Much thanks" is informal and less common.
Example: Many thanks for your help with the form.
The teacher told Arjun to "speak up". Was she angry?

Not necessarily. "Speak up" means to talk more loudly so that others can hear, or to say what you think.
Examples: Please speak up; I cannot hear you at the back. Do not be afraid to speak up in class.
Is "tortuous" a misspelling of "torturous"?

No, they are different words. "Tortuous" means full of twists and turns, and "torturous" means causing great pain or suffering.
Examples: A tortuous mountain road led to the village. The wait was torturous.
Which one is about weather: "climatic" or "climactic"?

"Climatic" is about climate. "Climactic" is about a climax, the most exciting point of a story or event.
Examples: Climatic changes affect farming. The climactic scene of the film was exciting.
Is it "heirarchy" or "hierarchy"?

It is "hierarchy", with "ie" and not "ei". It means a system with people or things ranked above others.
Example: The company has a clear hierarchy.
Is it "sacreligious" or "sacrilegious"?

It is "sacrilegious". The word comes from "sacrilege", which has "-lege", not "-lig".
Example: Damaging the old temple was sacrilegious.
Is it "anonomous" or "anonymous" for a letter with no name?

It is "anonymous", with "-ymous" in the middle. It comes from Greek roots meaning "without a name".
Example: The principal received an anonymous letter.
Neha and I are "on the same wavelength". Is that a radio thing?

The phrase comes from radio, but it means that two people think alike and understand each other easily.
Example: We were on the same wavelength, so we chose the same gift without talking about it.
The new coach wants to "raise the bar". What bar?

It is an idiom, not a real bar. "Raise the bar" means to set a higher standard for yourself or others.
Example: Her excellent performance raised the bar for the rest of the class.
My little brother has "grown out of" his shoes. Does that mean he grew outside them?

It means he has become too big for them. It is also used for habits that a child stops as they grow older.
Examples: She grew out of her fear of the dark. He has grown out of his old school bag.
Are "amiable" and "amicable" the same?

They are related but not the same. "Amiable" describes a friendly person. "Amicable" describes a friendly agreement or relationship.
Examples: He is an amiable neighbour. They reached an amicable settlement.
People say he got the job because someone "pulled strings". Is that a fair way?

To "pull strings" means to use your influence or contacts to get an advantage for yourself or someone else. It often suggests the result was not entirely fair, but that depends on the case.
Example: His uncle pulled strings to get him an interview.
Please "bring me up to speed" on the project. Is that about running?

No. "Bring someone up to speed" means to give them the latest information so that they know what is happening.
Example: Can you bring me up to speed on what I missed yesterday?
My friend asked, "A penny for your thoughts?" Was she offering money?

It is a polite and friendly way of asking what someone is thinking, and she was not offering money.
Example: You look quiet today; a penny for your thoughts?
Is it "miscelaneous" or "miscellaneous"?

It is "miscellaneous", with a double l in the middle: "mis-cel-lan-e-ous". Your spelling is missing one l.
Example: The box contained miscellaneous items.
Is "Sorry to bother you" polite when I ask my teacher a question after class?

Yes, it is polite and common. It shows you respect the other person's time. You can also say "Excuse me, do you have a minute?"
Example: Sorry to bother you, Sir, but could you explain this question again?
He "ticked off" the tasks on the list. Is that the same as "ticked off" in a quarrel?

The first means to mark an item with a tick. "Ticked off" can also mean annoyed, and in British English it also means scolded.
Examples: She ticked off each item on the list. The teacher ticked him off for being late.
Are "ambiguous" and "ambivalent" the same? They look alike.

No. "Ambiguous" means having more than one possible meaning. "Ambivalent" means having mixed feelings about something.
Examples: The instructions were ambiguous. She felt ambivalent about moving.
What is the difference between "perquisite" and "prerequisite"?

A "prerequisite" is something that is required before something else. A "perquisite" or "perk" is an extra benefit from a job.
Examples: Maths is a prerequisite for the course. A company car is a perquisite of the job.
Do I put full stops at the end of bullet points?

Many styles use them when the bullet is a complete sentence and leave them out when it is a short phrase. Be consistent within the same list.
Examples: Bring your ticket. Bring your ID card.
Is "amoral" the same as "immoral"?

No. "Immoral" means knowingly wrong or against good morals. "Amoral" means having no sense of right and wrong at all, or not concerned with morals.
Examples: Cheating is immoral. A robot is amoral because it has no values of its own.
How should I address a woman in a formal letter if I do not know her name?

Write "Dear Madam" when you do not know her name. "Ma'am" is common in India as a respectful way to speak to a woman, but it is less usual as an opening in a formal letter.
Example: Dear Madam, I am writing to enquire about the course.
Is it "offence" or "offense"?

Both are correct. "Offence" is British and Indian, and "offense" is American.
Examples: Cheating is a serious offence. Cheating is a serious offense.
Is it "innoculate" or "inoculate"?

It is "inoculate", with one n and one c, as in "inoculation". It means to give someone a vaccine.
Example: The clinic will inoculate the children next week.
Is the word for a paid driver "chauffer" or "chauffeur"?

It is "chauffeur", from French, with "-eur" at the end.
Example: The hotel sent a chauffeur to meet us at the airport.
Work will "pile up" while I am on leave. What does "pile up" mean?

"Pile up" means to gather in large amounts, so that the quantity increases.
Example: The letters piled up while we were on holiday.
The receptionist said, "Could you hold the line?" What does she want me to do?

She wants you to wait without ending the call while she connects you or checks something. It is a polite phrase.
Example: Could you please hold the line for a moment while I check?
My brother says speaking English is now "second nature" to him. Is it his second language?

Not necessarily. "Second nature" means something is so familiar from practice that you do it without thinking. English may or may not be his second language, because the phrase is about how easy it feels.
Example: After years of practice, typing is second nature to her.
In Britain I asked for a "soda" and got a different drink. What are they called?

British English usually says "fizzy drink" for a sweet carbonated drink. American English says "soda" or "pop". In Britain, "soda water" is plain sparkling water.
Examples: He ordered a fizzy drink. He ordered a soda.
My friend "went back on his word" about the trip. Is that serious?

It depends on the situation, but it is a negative phrase. To "go back on your word" means to break a promise or not do what you said you would.
Example: She went back on her word and did not return the book.
Is it "dependant" or "dependent" in British English?

In British English, "dependant" is the noun for a person who depends on you, while "dependent" is the adjective. American English uses "dependent" for both.
Examples: He has two dependants. The trip is dependent on the weather.
Is "paraphenalia" the right way to spell the word for all the small things needed for a hobby?

No. The correct spelling is "paraphernalia", with an r in the middle. It means all the small things needed for an activity.
Example: The painter's paraphernalia filled the room.
Which word is used for giving up a fee: "waive" or "wave"?

"Waive" means to give up a right or not to demand something, such as a fee. "Wave" means to move the hand in greeting, or a rolling body of water.
Examples: The school waived the late fee. She waved at her friend.
My grandmother calls okra "lady's finger". Is that standard English?

"Lady's finger" is common in Indian English. The standard word in British and American English is "okra", although you may also hear "ladies' fingers" in Britain.
Example: We cooked okra with onions for dinner.
Should I use single or double quotation marks?

Both are used. British English often uses single marks for the main quotation, and American English uses double marks. Indian writing uses either, so pick one style and stay with it.
Examples: She said, 'I am ready.' She said, "I am ready."
Is it "ommit" or "omit"?

It is "omit", with one m. The noun "omission" also has one m.
Example: Do not omit your name on the form.
Is it "mortage" or "mortgage" when talking about a house loan?

The spelling is "mortgage", with a t in the middle that is usually not pronounced.
Example: They are still paying the mortgage on their flat.
Is "return back" correct, as in "Please return back the book"?

The "back" is unnecessary, because "return" already means to give or go back. Standard English says "Please return the book." Some people use "return back" in speech, especially in Indian English.
Example: Please return the book by Monday.
My British book says "drawing pin" and my American book says "thumbtack". Same?

Yes. Both mean a short pin with a flat head used to fix paper to a board. "Drawing pin" is British and Indian, and "thumbtack" is American.
Examples: Fix the notice with a drawing pin. Fix the notice with a thumbtack.
I could not "make out" the sign in the fog. Is "make out" a good phrase here?

Yes. Here "make out" means to see or understand something with difficulty.
Example: I could not make out the number on the bus.
Please "pass on" my message to Dad. Is that polite?

Yes. "Pass on" means to give information or something else to another person. It can also mean to decline an offer.
Examples: I will pass on your message to the teacher. She passed on the extra cake.
Parents can "opt out" of the school trip. What does that mean?

"Opt out" means to choose not to take part in something.
Example: You can opt out of the email list at any time.
Is it "specially" or "especially" in "I like fruits, ___ mangoes"?

It is "especially", meaning above all or particularly. "Specially" means for a special purpose, as in "specially made". The two words overlap a little in speech.
Examples: I like fruits, especially mangoes. This cake was specially made for her.
When I lost the match, my brother laughed. That was "rubbing salt in the wound". Why?

The phrase means to make someone's pain or disappointment worse. The idea is that salt on a cut makes it hurt more.
Example: Telling her about the party she could not attend was rubbing salt in the wound.
I have been "racking my brains" about this riddle. Is that a good phrase?

Yes. "Rack your brains" means to think very hard to find an answer or remember something.
Example: I racked my brains, but I could not recall his name.
I read "waistcoat" in a British book and "vest" in an American one. Same?

Often yes. A "waistcoat" is a sleeveless jacket worn over a shirt, which Americans call a "vest". In British English, a "vest" is an undershirt.
Examples: He wore a waistcoat to the wedding. He wore a vest to the wedding.
I wanted to argue but "bit my tongue". Did I hurt myself?

No. To "bite your tongue" means to stop yourself from saying something you would regret.
Example: She bit her tongue instead of criticising the cook.
Help me spell the word for a system with too many rules and forms: "buraucracy"?

The correct spelling is "bureaucracy". It begins with "bureau", the French-origin word for an office or desk, followed by "-cracy".
Example: Getting the licence involved a lot of bureaucracy.
Does "She asked where I was going" need a question mark at the end?

No. It is an indirect question, reported inside a statement, so it ends with a full stop.
Examples: She asked where I was going. She asked, "Where are you going?"
The school is going to "do away with" paper tickets. What does "do away with" mean?

It means to stop using or get rid of something.
Example: The company decided to do away with the old form.
Do I write "pens, pencils, etc." or "pens, pencils and etc."?

Write "pens, pencils, etc." The abbreviation "etc." already means "and so on", so "and etc." repeats the "and".
Example: Bring pens, pencils, erasers, etc.
Is "miniscule" an error? I see it everywhere.

It is a very common spelling, but "minuscule" is the standard form in careful writing. People often link it with "mini", which is why the mistake spreads.
Example: The difference between the two scores was minuscule.
Should it be "9 AM", "9 a.m." or "9 am"?

All three are seen, and usage varies by publisher and country. "9 a.m." is common in both British and American writing, "9 am" is often used in British and Indian writing, and "9 AM" appears in many American styles. Choose one style and use it throughout.
Examples: The meeting starts at 9 am. The meeting starts at 9 a.m.
Please "give back" the umbrella when you finish. Is it correct English?

Yes. "Give back" means to return something to the person who gave it to you.
Example: Please give back the key when you leave.
Does 04/05/2026 mean April 5 or May 4?

It depends on the country. British and Indian writing usually put the day first, so it means 4 May. American writing puts the month first, so it means 5 April. Writing the month in words avoids confusion.
Example: Please arrive by 4 May 2026.
Do I write "the 1990's" or "the 1990s" for a decade?

Write "the 1990s". An apostrophe is not needed for a plain plural of a year. It is used only to show missing digits, as in "the '90s", or possession.
Example: My parents were children in the 1990s.
Which spelling should I use for a computer, "disc" or "disk"?

Usually "disk" is used for computer storage, as in "hard disk". "Disc" is more common for round media such as CDs or a "disc brake", especially in British English.
Examples: Save the file on the disk. She bought a disc of old songs.
Is "fortuitous" the same as "fortunate"?

Not strictly. "Fortuitous" means happening by chance, while "fortunate" means lucky. Many people use "fortuitous" to mean lucky, so the meanings overlap in practice.
Examples: A fortuitous meeting led to a job. We were fortunate to find a seat.
What is the plural of "quiz": "quizes" or "quizzes"?

It is "quizzes", with a double z, because the final z is doubled before "-es".
Example: We have two quizzes this week.
My friend invited me for a "sleepover". Is it written as one word, and is "sleep over" a verb?

Both forms exist. "Sleepover" as one word is the noun for a night spent at a friend's home. "Sleep over" as two words is the phrasal verb.
Examples: Zoya is having a sleepover on Saturday. Can I sleep over at your house?
My friend wrote that I am "indispensible". Is that the right spelling?

The standard spelling is "indispensable", ending in "-able". The word means so important that you cannot do without it.
Example: A good dictionary is indispensable for a language student.
Is it "exilarating" or "exhilarating"?

It is "exhilarating", with an h after the x. It means very exciting.
Example: The ride on the swing was exhilarating.
Is "batchmate" a proper English word?

It is common in Indian English for a person who joined or passed out in the same year as you. In other varieties, "classmate" or "someone in my year" is more usual.
Example: He is my batchmate from engineering college.
Is it "perseverence" or "perseverance"?

It is "perseverance", ending in "-ance". The verb is "persevere", but the noun takes "-ance".
Example: Her perseverance helped her finish the long climb.
The captain said I "dropped the ball" on the arrangements. Was it a literal ball?

No. To "drop the ball" means to make a mistake or fail to do something you were responsible for. The idiom comes from sports, but it is used everywhere.
Example: Someone dropped the ball, and the invitations were never sent.
Is it "phisician" or "physician"?

It is "physician", beginning with "ph". It is a formal word for a doctor.
Example: The physician checked her pulse.
Which one is right: "repitition" or "repetition"?

It is "repetition". It comes from "repeat", so the second letter is "e", not "i".
Example: Repetition helps me remember new words.
Should "history" and "maths" be capitalised, or only "English"?

Language names such as English and Hindi always take a capital letter. School subjects such as history and maths take a small letter unless they are part of a course title.
Examples: I like history and English. She is in History 101.
Is it right to say "Don't take tension"?

"Take tension" is an Indian English usage, and many people will understand it. Standard alternatives are "Don't worry" or "Don't get stressed".
Example: Don't worry; we have plenty of time.
My mother says, "Keep on trying." Why not just "keep trying"?

Both are correct. "Keep on" gives a little more stress to continuing, especially when the task is hard.
Example: Keep on practising and your handwriting will improve.
My friend says, "I met him yesterday only." Is "only" right here?

It is an Indian English usage meaning "just yesterday". It sounds unusual in other varieties. A standard alternative is "I met him just yesterday".
Example: I met him just yesterday.
I wrote "curiculum" in my report. Is it right?

No. It is "curriculum", with a double r in the middle.
Example: The curriculum includes music and art.
I could not "take in" all that the teacher said. Is that right?

Yes. "Take in" means to understand or absorb information. It can also mean to give shelter to someone or to deceive them, depending on the sentence.
Example: There was so much to take in on the first day of school.
Can I use exclamation marks in a formal email?

You can, but sparingly. One may be fine in a warm greeting or thanks, but too many make an email look unprofessional.
Example: Thank you for your quick reply! I will send the form today.
Which is right for a clever movement: "manoeuvre" or "maneuver"?

Both are correct. "Manoeuvre" is British and Indian, and "maneuver" is American.
Examples: The driver made a quick manoeuvre. The driver made a quick maneuver.
My history book says the king's "rain" lasted forty years. Is that correct?

It should be "reign", meaning the time a king or queen rules. "Rain" falls from clouds, and "rein" is the strap used to guide a horse.
Examples: The queen's reign was peaceful. The rider pulled the rein.
Do "prescribe" and "proscribe" mean the same?

No. "Prescribe" means to recommend or order something, like a rule or a medicine by a doctor. "Proscribe" means to forbid.
Examples: The teacher prescribed three books. The law proscribes smoking in the hall.
Is it "the sun shined" or "the sun shone"?

"The sun shone" is the usual past form when the sun gives light. "Shined" is used when someone polishes something, as in "He shined his shoes". Some speakers also say "shined" for light, but "shone" is the safer choice.
Examples: The sun shone all day. I shined my shoes before school.
Is "inteligence" correct?

No. It is "intelligence", with a double l.
Example: She showed great intelligence in solving the puzzle.
Is "childlike" an insult, like "childish"?

No. "Childish" is usually negative and means silly like a child. "Childlike" is usually positive and means innocent, curious or full of wonder.
Examples: Stop being childish and share the toy. Grandpa has a childlike love for kites.
Is it "Dear Sir," or "Dear Sir:" at the start of a formal letter?

Both are used. "Dear Sir," with a comma is common in British and Indian English. American business letters often use a colon, as in "Dear Sir:".
Example: Dear Madam, I am writing about the missing parcel.
Is it "an illusion to Shakespeare" or "an allusion to Shakespeare"?

It is "allusion", meaning an indirect reference to something. "Illusion" means something that seems real but is not, like a trick of the eye.
Examples: The poem contains an allusion to Shakespeare. The magician created the illusion of floating.
Is it "disburse" or "disperse" when a crowd goes away?

For a crowd, the word is "disperse", meaning to scatter. "Disburse" means to pay out money.
Examples: The crowd dispersed after the show. The office disbursed the salaries on Friday.
The doctor says my grandfather is "not out of the woods yet". What does that mean?

It means the danger or difficulty has not yet fully passed, even if things are getting better.
Example: The company is improving, but it is not out of the woods yet.
Are "masterful" and "masterly" the same?

They overlap, but strictly "masterly" means very skilful, and "masterful" means commanding or controlling.
Examples: The pianist gave a masterly performance. The captain had a masterful manner.
We could not "get through" because the line was busy. Is "get through" correct for a call?

Yes. "Get through" means to reach someone by phone or to pass through a difficult place. It also means to finish a task or survive hard times.
Examples: I could not get through to the helpline. We got through the exam period.
When should I use a semicolon and when a colon?

Use a colon to introduce a list or an explanation. Use a semicolon to join two closely related complete sentences, or to separate items in a long list.
Examples: I need three things: a pen, a book and a bag. The sky was dark; it began to rain.
In a nature book I saw "pray" and "prey". Which is the hunted animal?

"Prey" is an animal hunted by another animal. "Pray" means to speak to God.
Examples: The tiger stalked its prey. They pray at the temple.
My book says the king was "prosecuted" for his beliefs. Is that the right word?

Probably not. "Persecute" means to treat people badly because of who they are or what they believe. "Prosecute" means to bring someone to a court of law.
Examples: Many people were persecuted for their faith. The company was prosecuted for fraud.
After the holidays the teacher said, "Back to the grindstone!" What does that mean?

It means to return to hard work, usually after a break.
Example: The festival is over, so it is back to the grindstone for everyone.
My grandmother said she would "sow" a button. Is she planting it?

She probably means "sew", which is to join with a needle and thread. "Sow" means to plant seeds.
Examples: Please sew this button on my shirt. Farmers sow wheat in their fields.
Does "aggravate" mean "annoy" or "make worse"?

Its original meaning is "make worse", as in "aggravate a problem". In everyday speech, many people also use it to mean annoy, and some careful writers avoid that.
Examples: The delay aggravated the problem. The noise irritated me.
Do I put a full stop after Mr and Dr?

In British English, the full stop is often left out when the last letter of the abbreviation is the last letter of the word, as in "Mr" and "Dr". American English usually keeps it, as in "Mr." and "Dr."
Examples: Dr Sharma is here. Mr. Brown will arrive soon.
My colleague wrote "Apologies for the confusion". Is that a proper apology?

Yes, it is a polite and quick way to say you are sorry that something was unclear. It is formal enough for work emails.
Example: Apologies for the confusion about the meeting time; it is at 3 pm.
Our company decided to "take on" more staff. What does "take on" mean?

"Take on" has two common meanings. It can mean to hire people, or to accept a task or responsibility.
Examples: The shop took on three extra workers for the festival. She took on the job of class monitor.
Is "pidgeon" the right spelling for the bird?

The bird is spelled "pigeon", with no d.
Example: A pigeon sat on the window ledge.
I cannot "tell the twins apart". Is "tell apart" correct?

Yes. "Tell apart" means to see the difference between two similar people or things.
Example: Even their teacher cannot tell them apart.
Is "grizzly" or "grisly" used for horrible things?

"Grisly" means horrible or shocking. "Grizzly" is a kind of bear, and it can also mean grey-haired.
Examples: The newspaper described a grisly crime. A grizzly bear lives in North America.
Is it "allude to" or "elude to" a story?

It is "allude to", meaning to mention something indirectly. "Elude" means to escape from or avoid someone or something.
Examples: The speaker alluded to an old story. The thief eluded the guards.
My teacher said, "I want cent percent attendance." Is "cent percent" standard English?

"Cent percent" is used mostly in India. In standard English, say "one hundred percent" or "full attendance".
Example: The school expects full attendance this week.
I want to "fit in" with my new class. Is it correct?

Yes. "Fit in" means to feel part of a group and be accepted by them. It also means to find time for something in a busy day.
Examples: He fits in well with the team. I can fit in a short meeting at four.
I wrote "Give me leave tomorrow" to my manager. How can I ask politely?

Try "Would it be possible to take leave tomorrow?" It sounds more polite than a direct order.
Example: Would it be possible for me to leave an hour early today?
The boy "got away with" copying homework once. What does the phrase say?

"Get away with" means to do something wrong and escape punishment or notice. The phrase suggests the person was lucky.
Example: He thought he could get away with being late every day, but the teacher noticed.
My teammate said, "Stop beating a dead horse." Why would I hit a horse?

You would not. It is an idiom meaning to keep discussing something that is already settled or cannot be changed, which is a waste of effort.
Example: We have decided on the venue, so there is no point in beating a dead horse.
The shop's accounts are "in the red". What colour should I look for?

You do not need to see any colour. "In the red" means owing more money than you have, because losses are traditionally written in red ink.
Example: The small business was in the red for two years.
He always "stands up for" his friends. Is that a good trait?

Yes. "Stand up for" means to support or defend someone who is being treated unfairly.
Example: It takes courage to stand up for a friend.
The old chair is "falling apart". How is that different from "falling down"?

"Fall apart" means to break into pieces because of age or poor condition. "Fall down" means to drop to the ground.
Example: My old bag finally fell apart on the way to school.
Is it "vegeterian" or "vegetarian"?

It is "vegetarian", ending in "-arian".
Example: Mina is a vegetarian and eats no meat.
Do I capitalise the first word after a colon?

It depends on the style. In British English, the word after a colon usually starts with a small letter, unless it is a proper name. American style often capitalises it when a full sentence follows.
Example: She had one aim: to win the race.
Do I need a comma before "and" in "red, white and blue"?

It depends on the style. The comma before the last "and" is called the Oxford or serial comma. American style usually includes it, British and Indian style often leaves it out, and both are acceptable if you are consistent.
Examples: We bought pens, paper, and glue. We bought pens, paper and glue.
The clerk asked me to "hand over" the form. Is it polite?

It is correct but fairly direct. "Hand over" means to give something to another person, often because they are in charge of it. A polite request needs a "please".
Example: Please hand over your ticket at the gate.
Our group project had "too many cooks". What went wrong?

The full saying is "too many cooks spoil the broth". It means that when too many people try to handle one task, the result gets worse.
Example: Five of us edited the poster at once, and too many cooks spoiled it.
Which one is correct: "The bank is opposite to the school" or "opposite the school"?

The usual standard form is "opposite the school", with no "to". You may hear "opposite to" in Indian English, but it is less common elsewhere.
Example: The bank is opposite the school.
Please explain how "canon" differs from "cannon".

A "cannon" is a large gun. A "canon" is a set of rules or a body of accepted works, such as an author's canon.
Examples: An old cannon stands at the fort. These novels belong to the literary canon.
My boss gave me one day to "think over" the offer. What should I do?

"Think over" means to consider something carefully before you decide. So use the day to weigh the offer calmly.
Example: Let me think over your suggestion and tell you tomorrow.
Is "reticent" the same as "reluctant"?

Not exactly. "Reluctant" means unwilling to do something. "Reticent" means reserved and not telling things readily.
Examples: He was reluctant to sing. The shy boy was reticent about his marks.
Do "credible" and "credulous" mean the same?

No. "Credible" means believable. "Credulous" means too ready to believe things.
Examples: The witness gave a credible story. A credulous person may believe any rumour.
Let's "run through" the speech once before the event. What does that mean?

"Run through" means to practise or read something quickly from beginning to end.
Example: We ran through the dance steps twice before the show.
My mother says I am "burning the candle at both ends" before the exams. Is that a safety warning?

It is advice, not a safety warning. The idiom means you are doing too much, for example by studying late at night and getting up very early, and tiring yourself out.
Example: She was burning the candle at both ends with her job and her evening classes.
My student said, "I am having a doubt in this sum." Is that correct?

In Indian English, "a doubt" often means a question. In standard English, "doubt" means a feeling of being unsure, so "I am having a doubt in this sum" can sound odd. Say "I have a question about this sum" or "I do not understand this step".
Example: I have a question about this sum.
What is the difference between a hyphen and a dash?

A hyphen joins words or parts of words, as in "well-known". A dash is longer and marks a pause or an extra thought in a sentence.
Examples: She is a well-known singer. My brother — the tall one — is a pilot.
People say the old cricket player has "lost his touch". Is that unkind?

It can sound a little unkind. It means a person has lost a skill they once had.
Example: The singer seems to have lost her touch; her last songs were not as good.
Please check the spelling: exagerate or exaggerate?

It is "exaggerate", with a double g.
Example: Don't exaggerate; the fish was not as big as a bus.
Is it "I loath spiders" or "I loathe spiders"?

It is "loathe". The verb meaning to hate strongly ends in -e. The adjective "loath" means unwilling, as in "I am loath to leave".
Examples: I loathe cold coffee. He was loath to say goodbye.
My British uncle talks about the "windscreen" and my American friend about the "windshield". Same thing?

Yes. Both mean the large front window of a car. "Windscreen" is British and also used in India, and "windshield" is American.
Examples: Clean the windscreen before the trip. Clean the windshield before the trip.
Does "humourous" keep the u from "humour"?

No. The noun is "humour" in British English, but the adjective is "humorous" without the u.
Example: He wrote a humorous story about his dog.
Is it "a book entitled Gulliver's Travels" or "titled"?

Both are acceptable. "Entitled" has another meaning, too, which is having the right to something. Some careful writers prefer "titled" for the name of a book.
Examples: She read a book titled Gulliver's Travels. You are entitled to a refund.
Can I "try out" for the school team?

Yes. "Try out" means to test something or to take part in a test for a place.
Example: Many students will try out for the football team on Saturday.
The principal had to "step in" to stop the argument. What does that mean?

"Step in" means to become involved in a situation to help or to stop a problem.
Example: When the two teams argued, the referee stepped in.
I told Meera everything to "get it off my chest". Does that have to do with a cough?

No. It means to talk about something that has been worrying you so that you feel relieved.
Example: She needed to get it off her chest, so she told her friend about the argument.
Is an "ice lolly" the same as a "popsicle"?

Yes. Both are frozen treats on a stick. "Ice lolly" is British, and "popsicle" is American, though that word started as a brand. In India, the word "ice candy" is also used.
Examples: We bought an ice lolly in summer. We bought a popsicle in summer.
We "used up" all the paper. Is that right?

Yes. "Use up" means to finish the whole supply of something.
Example: The children used up all the paint in one afternoon.
Is "camoflage" right?

No. It is "camouflage", with "ou" after the m.
Example: The insect's colour works as camouflage on the leaves.
My cousin told me to "read the room" before telling jokes. What should I do?

"Read the room" means to notice the mood and feelings of the people around you and act in a suitable way.
Example: Read the room first; if everyone looks tired, save the story for later.
I keep writing "supercede". Is it "supersede"?

It is "supersede". It is the only common English verb ending in "-sede". Others like "precede" and "proceed" are spelled differently.
Example: The new timetable will supersede the old one.
When do I write "Mum" with a capital M?

Write it with a capital M when you use it as a name, and with a small m when it follows "my" or "your".
Examples: Mum, can I go out? My mum is a teacher.
Is it a "rucksack" or a "backpack"?

Both words describe a bag carried on the back. "Rucksack" is common in British English, while "backpack" is American and also widely used in India.
Examples: She packed her rucksack for the trek. She packed her backpack for the trek.
When I answer a work call, should I say "I am Anita" or "This is Anita speaking"?

"This is Anita speaking" or just "Anita speaking" sounds natural on the phone. "I am Anita" is understood, but it is less common in a formal call.
Example: Good afternoon, this is Anita speaking. How may I help you?
Which spelling is right in "She has a flair for music"?

"Flair" is right, meaning a natural talent. "Flare" means a bright flame or a sudden burst.
Examples: He has a flair for drawing. The flare lit up the night sky.
My cousin said, "I passed out of college in 2019." Is that right?

In Indian English, it means graduated. In British and American English, "pass out" usually means to faint, so it can confuse people. The standard alternative is "graduated".
Example: She graduated from college in 2019.
My teacher asked us to "dig into" the topic. Do I need a spade?

No. "Dig into" means to look deeply into something, such as a subject or a problem. It can also mean to start eating food eagerly.
Examples: Let's dig into the history of the fort. We dug into the biryani.
Do I write "north" or "North" in "go north to the lake"?

Use a small letter for plain directions, as in "go north". Use a capital letter when it is part of a name or a region, such as "North India".
Examples: Drive north for ten minutes. We travelled to North India.
Mum told me to "dip my toe in" with the music club first. Is it about swimming?

Not here. It means to try something new in a small, careful way before you commit fully.
Example: Dip your toe in by attending one class before you join for the whole year.
Her old anger "flared up" again at dinner. Did something catch fire?

No. "Flare up" means to start again suddenly and strongly, as a feeling, argument or problem does.
Example: The quarrel flared up when they met at the wedding.
I need a "pail" of water, not a "pale" one. Are they different words?

Yes. A "pail" is a bucket. "Pale" describes a light colour or a face that has little colour.
Examples: Fill the pail at the tap. The sky was pale blue at dawn.
How should I spell "disatisfied"?

The correct spelling is "dissatisfied", with a double s. It is the prefix "dis-" joined to "satisfied", and both s letters stay.
Example: The customer was dissatisfied with the late delivery.
The hotel says "city centre" and the American website says "downtown". Are they the same?

Roughly, yes. Both mean the main business and shopping area of a city. "City centre" is British and Indian, and "downtown" is American.
Examples: The hotel is in the city centre. The hotel is downtown.
Does "After the match we had tea" need a comma?

It usually does. Put a comma after an opening phrase, as in "After the match, we had tea." For a very short phrase, the comma is sometimes left out.
Example: After the long journey, we were ready to sleep.
Is "thanks a lot" too casual for a teacher?

It is friendly, but a little casual. For a teacher, "Thank you very much, Ma'am" is safer.
Examples: Thanks a lot for the lift! Thank you very much, Ma'am, for your help.
My friend said "this is the same only". What does "only" add?

In Indian English "only" is added for emphasis, meaning "exactly" or "just". Here it means "this is exactly the same". Standard English says "this is exactly the same".
Example: This is exactly the same as the one I bought.
When the bus broke down, we were left "high and dry". Were we on a hill?

No. It means left alone without help or resources in a difficult situation.
Example: The driver left the group high and dry at the station with no tickets.
I need a good tailor, so my friend said to "ask around". Whom should I ask?

"Ask around" means to ask several people for information or advice. Try neighbours, friends and relatives.
Example: I asked around, and three people recommended the same bakery.
How are "retch" and "wretch" different?

To "retch" is to make the movements of vomiting. A "wretch" is an unfortunate or unhappy person.
Examples: The bad smell made him retch. The poor wretch had lost his home in the flood.
Is "volunteir" correct for someone who offers to help?

No, it is "volunteer". It ends in "-eer", as in "engineer".
Example: Aisha is a volunteer at the school library.
At the fair they sold "candy floss", but the American book calls it "cotton candy". Are they the same?

Yes. It is the fluffy spun sugar sold at fairs. "Candy floss" is British, and "cotton candy" is American.
Examples: The children shared a stick of candy floss. The children shared a stick of cotton candy.
Should I write "principal" or "Principal" in "Our Principal is Mrs Rao"?

Use a capital when the title comes right before a name, as in "Principal Rao". When it is used generally, a small letter is usually better: "Our principal is Mrs Rao."
Examples: Principal Rao welcomed the guests. The principal welcomed the guests.
How do I say well done to my neighbour for her new job? Is it "congratulation" or "congratulations"?

Use "congratulations", always with an s. Follow it with "on" and the thing achieved.
Example: Congratulations on your new job, Mrs Mehta!
My uncle works at a "godown" near the market. What is that?

"Godown" is a word used in India and nearby countries for a warehouse or storeroom for goods. It is not widely used in other varieties of English.
Example: The rice is stored in a godown near the market.
The organisers will "pull out all the stops" for the annual day. Are they pulling something out of a box?

No. It means to make the greatest possible effort. The phrase comes from the stops of a church organ, which are pulled out to make the sound louder.
Example: The class pulled out all the stops to make the farewell party special.
My grandmother says children should never "answer back". Does that mean they cannot answer questions?

No. "Answer back" means to reply rudely to someone, usually an older person or a person in charge. Answering a question politely is fine.
Example: Ravi was sent to his room because he answered his father back.
Is the shellfish called a "muscle" or a "mussel"?

The shellfish is a "mussel". A "muscle" is a part of the body that lets you move.
Examples: The cook added mussels to the soup. Swimming strengthens the muscles in your arms.
How do I spell "alleged": "aleged" or "alleged"?

It is "alleged", with a double l. The word means said to be true without proof.
Example: The alleged mistake turned out to be a printing error.
My hairdresser says "fringe" but my American cousin says "bangs". Are they different?

They are the same: the hair cut straight across the forehead. "Fringe" is British, and "bangs" is American.
Examples: Mira trimmed her fringe before the party. Mira trimmed her bangs before the party.
My friend wrote "two mango's" on the list. Is the apostrophe needed?

No. A plural is made by adding s or es, and no apostrophe is used. The correct form is "two mangoes".
Example: We bought two mangoes and three bananas.
After dinner at my friend's house, what do I say to her mother?

"Thank you for having me" is a polite thing to say to a host. It shows you enjoyed the visit.
Example: Thank you for having me, Aunty; the meal was delicious.
Our college is arranging a party for "freshers". Who are they?

A "fresher" is a student in the first year of college or university. The word is used in British English too.
Example: The freshers met their teachers on the first day.
The teacher wants to "nip it in the bud" when students copy each other. What will she do?

She will stop the problem early, before it grows bigger.
Example: The rumour is spreading, so let's nip it in the bud.
The librarian helped me "track down" an old book. Did she follow footprints?

No. "Track down" means to find something or someone after a careful search.
Example: After a long search, we tracked down the owner of the lost bag.
Which word do I use for someone who digs coal: "miner" or "minor"?

It is "miner". A "minor" is a person under the legal age of adulthood, and as an adjective it means small or not very important.
Examples: The miner went down into the coal pit at dawn. This is only a minor problem.
My son starts "kindergarden" next year. Is that how it is spelled?

The spelling is "kindergarten", ending in "-ten". It comes from German words meaning "children's garden", but the spelling does not use "den".
Example: My son starts kindergarten next year.
In my recipe book it is a "courgette", but the shop label says "zucchini". Are these different vegetables?

No, they are the same long green vegetable. "Courgette" is British, and "zucchini" is American.
Examples: Slice the courgette thinly. Slice the zucchini thinly.
Should I write "a well known author" or "a well-known author"?

Use a hyphen before a noun: "a well-known author". When the phrase comes after the noun, you usually leave the hyphen out, as in "The author is well known."
Examples: She is a well-known author. The author is well known.
My friend said "bless you" when I sneezed. Is it a prayer?

It is a polite habit after a sneeze, said in a kind way. Most people say it without thinking about religion. A short "thank you" is the usual reply.
Example: "Achoo!" "Bless you." "Thank you."
The notice says "reply at the earliest". Is that polite?

It means "as soon as possible", and it is common in Indian business English. It is understood, but it can sound pushy, so "as soon as you can" may be friendlier.
Example: Please send the form as soon as you can.
The children "had a field day" in the puddles. Is that an event?

It means they enjoyed themselves a great deal, often by making the most of a chance.
Example: The puppy had a field day in the garden after the rain.
My father wants to "branch out" into selling spices. What does it mean?

"Branch out" means to start a new kind of activity, usually beyond what you already do.
Example: The bakery branched out into making sandwiches.
My music teacher says "chord" and my mother says "cord". Are they the same?

No. A "chord" is a group of notes played together. A "cord" is a thin rope or string, or an electric wire.
Examples: He played a chord on the guitar. Tie the parcel with a strong cord.
Should "ingredient" end in "ant" or "ent"?

It ends in "-ent": "ingredient". The letters "ie" come before the "nt".
Example: Salt is an important ingredient in most recipes.
The British weather report told people to wear "wellies". What are they?

They are waterproof rubber boots, short for "Wellington boots". "Wellies" is informal and British; Americans usually say "rain boots".
Examples: Put on your wellies before you walk through the puddles. Put on your rain boots before you walk through the puddles.
Does "Thank you Rahul" need a comma?

Yes. A comma is needed before the name of the person you speak to, so write "Thank you, Rahul."
Example: Come here, Rahul, and meet my cousin.
My manager said "if I may" before correcting me. Was she angry?

Not necessarily. "If I may" is a polite way to ask permission before you say or do something. It can be formal.
Example: If I may, I would like to add one more point.
A new boy said "Myself Ravi". Is that correct?

It is common in Indian English, but standard English says "I am Ravi" or "My name is Ravi". "Myself" is not used as a subject in standard English.
Example: Hello, my name is Ravi, and I am new to this school.
Is a mobile phone for a child "a double-edged sword"?

That phrase describes something with both good and bad effects. A phone can help a child stay in touch, but it can also take attention away from study.
Example: Fame can be a double-edged sword, because it brings chances but takes away privacy.
Please do not "butt in" when I am speaking. Is "butt in" rude?

It is informal and a little rude. "Butt in" means to interrupt a talk or join in without being asked.
Example: Sorry to butt in, but the bus is leaving.
Is the shelf above a fireplace a "mantel" or a "mantle"?

The shelf is a "mantel". A "mantle" is a loose cloak, and it is also used for a role or duty that someone takes on.
Examples: The clock stood on the mantel. She took on the mantle of team captain.
How is "pyschiatrist" spelled correctly?

It is "psychiatrist". It begins with "ps", and the p is silent, then "ych".
Example: The hospital has a new psychiatrist on the staff.
Which spelling should I use for the yellow element: "sulphur" or "sulfur"?

Both appear. "Sulphur" is the older British spelling, and "sulfur" is the American one. Many science books now use "sulfur" even in Britain, so follow your textbook.
Examples: Sulphur is a yellow solid. Sulfur is a yellow solid.
Is it "on monday in march" or "on Monday in March"?

Use capital letters: "on Monday in March". The names of days and months are always capitalised in English.
Example: Our exams begin on Monday in March.
What can I say to a friend whose grandfather has died?

You can say "I'm so sorry for your loss" or "My condolences". Keep it short and kind, and offer to listen if the person wishes to talk.
Example: My condolences to you and your family.
Why do some letters say "I am sending the form herewith"?

"Herewith" means "with this letter or message". It is formal and rather old-fashioned. In everyday emails, "attached" or "enclosed" is more natural.
Example: I am sending the form herewith.
The principal wants a "dry run" of the annual day. Will there be rain?

No. A dry run is a practice of an event before the real one, to find problems.
Example: We did a dry run of the speech on Friday and fixed the sound problem.
The whole class "pitched in" to clean the hall. Does that mean they threw something?

No. "Pitch in" means to join others and help with a job.
Example: Everyone pitched in, so the work was done by noon.
Which is right for a bundle of hay: "bail" or "bale"?

It is "bale". A bale is a large, tightly tied bundle of hay, cotton or paper. "Bail" is money paid to free someone from custody until a trial, and it also means to scoop water out of a boat.
Examples: The farmer lifted a bale of hay. We had to bail water out of the boat.
How do I spell "island"? I keep writing "iland".

The spelling is "island", with a silent s. The s is written but not pronounced.
Example: We took a boat to the small island.
Do I dry plates with a "tea towel" or a "dish towel"?

You can use either word. They mean the same cloth. "Tea towel" is British, and "dish towel" is American.
Examples: Dry the glasses with a tea towel. Dry the glasses with a dish towel.
What does the apostrophe do in "don't" and "it's"?

In a contraction the apostrophe shows where a letter or letters have been left out. "Don't" is "do not" and "it's" is "it is" or "it has".
Examples: I don't like cold tea. It's raining outside.
Can I end a message to a friend with "all the best"?

Yes. It is a warm, friendly sign-off that wishes someone well.
Example: I hope the exam goes well. All the best!
What are a "lakh" and a "crore" in English?

They are Indian numbering units. A lakh is one hundred thousand, and a crore is ten million. Many international readers prefer "100,000" and "10 million".
Examples: The car costs about five lakh rupees. The project cost two crore rupees.
The contractor gave me a "ballpark figure". Is that an exact amount?

No. A ballpark figure is a rough estimate, close enough to give you an idea.
Example: Can you give me a ballpark figure for the number of guests?
Rahul said the facts in the story do not "add up". Is he talking about sums?

Not here. When facts do not "add up", they do not make sense together, so something may be missing or wrong. It can also mean to total numbers.
Examples: His excuse does not add up, because the shop was closed. Add up the marks for all four sections.
The carpenter checked the wall with a "plumb line". Is it spelled like the fruit "plum"?

No. A "plum" is a fruit. "Plumb" means exactly vertical, and a "plumb line" is a string with a weight used to check this.
Examples: We bought ripe plums at the market. The carpenter used a plumb line to check the wall.
Is "arcitect" right for the person who designs buildings?

No, it is "architect". It needs an h after the c, so it is "arch" followed by "itect". The "ch" is pronounced like a k.
Example: The architect showed us the plan for the new library.
My teacher wrote "speciality" but my friend's book says "specialty". Which is right?

Both are right. "Speciality" is the usual British and Indian spelling, and "specialty" is the usual American one.
Examples: Biryani is the speciality of this restaurant. Biryani is the specialty of this restaurant.
Should I write "hindi" and "english" with capital letters?

Yes. Names of languages are always capitalised: Hindi, English, Tamil.
Example: Meena speaks Hindi at home and English at school.
The notice said "please be seated". Is that an order?

It is a formal, polite request to sit down. It is used at events and in offices.
Example: Ladies and gentlemen, please be seated; the programme will begin soon.
My aunt introduced him as my "cousin brother". Is that standard English?

It is common in Indian English, where people stress that he is a male cousin. In standard English one word is enough: "cousin". Say "my cousin" and add the name or the age if you want to be specific.
Example: My cousin Arjun is visiting us this week.
My uncle said I "backed the wrong horse" in the school debate. Which horse?

There is no horse. The phrase means you supported a person or a plan that did not win or did not work out.
Example: Our class backed the wrong horse by choosing the caterer who arrived late.
The plan to open a club "fizzled out" after one month. Why was it sad?

"Fizzle out" means to end slowly and weakly, with a disappointing result, after a good start.
Example: The excitement fizzled out when nobody turned up for the second meeting.
Which means a small glass bottle: "vial" or "vile"?

It is "vial". "Vile" is an adjective meaning extremely unpleasant.
Examples: The lab kept the liquid in a small glass vial. The drain gave off a vile smell.
How do I spell "spagetti"?

The correct spelling is "spaghetti", with an h after the g and a double t. The h keeps the g hard.
Example: We cooked spaghetti with tomato sauce.
Should I pack my "swimming costume" or my "bathing suit" for the trip?

They mean the same clothing for swimming. "Swimming costume" is British, and "bathing suit" is American, though Americans also say "swimsuit".
Examples: Pack your swimming costume in the blue bag. Pack your bathing suit in the blue bag.
When should I use brackets like ( ) in a sentence?

Round brackets, also called parentheses, hold extra information that could be removed without breaking the sentence.
Example: My cousin (who lives in Pune) is visiting us this week.
What should I write on a card to a classmate who is ill?

"Get well soon" is the usual kind message. You can add "We miss you in class."
Example: Get well soon, Arun! We miss you in class.
My friend says "I live in Delhi itself". What is "itself" doing there?

In Indian English "itself" is added for emphasis, meaning "right here" or "in that very place". In standard English you can drop it or use "right in".
Example: I live right in Delhi, so the school is close.
All my work in the garden "went down the drain" after the storm. Is the garden flooded?

Maybe, but the phrase is not about water. It means that effort or money was wasted or lost.
Example: All our hard work went down the drain when the file was deleted.
The teacher told us to "cross out" the wrong answers. Do I rub them out?

No. "Cross out" means to draw a line through words so that they are marked as wrong or not wanted. "Rub out" means to remove them with an eraser.
Example: Cross out the wrong word and write the right one above it.
Is it "sleight of hand" or "slight of hand" for a magic trick?

It is "sleight of hand", where "sleight" means skill in quick, clever movements. "Slight" means small or thin.
Examples: The magician used sleight of hand to hide the coin. There is a slight chance of rain.
How do I spell the word that means to fill someone with excitement: "exilarate"?

The correct spelling is "exhilarate". It has an h after the x.
Example: A fast ride on the swing can exhilarate small children.
The mechanic asked for a "spanner", but the American video said "wrench". Same tool?

Yes. It is the tool used to turn nuts and bolts. "Spanner" is British, and "wrench" is American.
Examples: Pass me the spanner, please. Pass me the wrench, please.
Where do commas go in "on 5 March 2025"? Do I need any?

In the British style "5 March 2025", you usually need no commas. In the American style, you write "March 5, 2025", with a comma between the day and the year.
Examples: We met on 5 March 2025. We met on March 5, 2025.
Which is polite at the classroom door: "can I come in" or "may I come in"?

"May I come in?" is the more polite form because "may" asks for permission. "Can" is common in speech and not wrong, but it is less formal.
Example: May I come in, Ma'am?
My neighbour asked me to "close the light". Do I shut a door?

In some Indian English you hear "close the light" for switching it off. Standard English says "turn off the light" or "switch off the light".
Example: Please switch off the light when you leave the room.
Our group leader says the project is "done and dusted". Is it clean now?

It means completely finished, with nothing left to do. The phrase is common in British English.
Example: The report is done and dusted, so we can go home.
My teacher asked me to "flesh out" my story. Should I make it longer?

Yes, and also fuller. "Flesh out" means to add detail so that an idea or a story becomes complete.
Example: She fleshed out her outline with examples and descriptions.
My grandfather is still "hail and hearty". Is that the usual spelling?

The usual spelling is "hale and hearty", where "hale" means strong and healthy. "Hail" is frozen rain, or a word for calling out to someone.
Examples: My grandfather is still hale and hearty at eighty. Hail fell on the roof during the storm.
Does "gymnasium" start with "gim" or "gym"?

It starts with "gym", with a y, like the short word "gym".
Example: The basketball match was held in the school gymnasium.
Should I write "dialogue" or "dialog" for the talk between two characters?

"Dialogue" is the standard spelling in both British and American English, so choose it in schoolwork. "Dialog" is mainly used in American English and in computing, for example a dialog box.
Example: The dialogue between the two friends was funny.
Is it fine to write "and/or" in a formal letter?

It is accepted, but use it sparingly because it can be unclear. Often "or" alone, or a clearer sentence, is better.
Example: Students may bring a pen and/or a pencil.
My teacher greeted a guest with "How do you do?" What should the guest say?

It is a formal greeting, not a real question. The guest usually answers "How do you do?" too.
Example: How do you do? I am pleased to meet you.
Is a "public school" free for everyone?

It depends on the country. In the US it means a school paid for by the government. In Britain it usually means an old and expensive private school. In India it often means a private school.
Example: In the United States, a public school is free to attend.
My brother said he would "foot the bill" for dinner. Does he mean his foot?

No. It means he will pay the bill.
Example: Our grandparents offered to foot the bill for the family picnic.
The team tried to "cover up" the mistake. Did they put a cloth over it?

Not literally. "Cover up" means to hide a mistake or a wrong action so others do not find out. Hiding the truth is not a good plan.
Example: Do not try to cover up the error; tell your teacher.
Do "glance" and "glimpse" mean the same?

Not quite. A "glance" is a quick look that you choose to make. A "glimpse" is a brief view that you get, often by chance.
Examples: She glanced at her watch. We caught a glimpse of the tiger between the trees.
Do I write "soveriegn" or "sovereign"?

It is "sovereign". It ends in "-eign", as in "foreign", with the e before the i.
Example: India is a sovereign country.
The sports club asked us to bring a "holdall". Is it a special bag?

It is a large soft bag with handles, used for carrying clothes and equipment. "Holdall" is British, and "duffel bag" is a similar American term.
Examples: He packed his boots in a holdall. He packed his boots in a duffel bag.
What are square brackets [ ] used for in quotations?

Square brackets show that you have added or changed a word inside someone else's quotation, usually to make the meaning clear.
Example: The teacher said, "She [Anita] won the prize for poetry."
My friend asked "Shall we go?" Should I answer yes or no?

"Shall we" is a polite way to suggest something together. Answer "Yes, let's go" or "Not yet, please give me five minutes."
Example: Shall we start with the first question?
Is it "head master" or "headmaster"?

It is usually written as one word: "headmaster". The word for a woman who leads a school is "headmistress", and "head teacher" or "principal" works for either.
Example: The headmaster gave a short speech.
The company announced a pay rise "across the board". Does a board come into it?

No. "Across the board" means applying to everyone or to every case in a group, with no exceptions.
Example: The school cut homework across the board, so every class got lighter work.
My friends "egged me on" to sing. Did they bring eggs?

No. "Egg on" means to encourage someone to do something, often something unwise or daring.
Example: The crowd egged him on until he jumped into the pool.
Did I write it correctly: "the baby's berth was on Monday"?

No, it should be "birth". "Birth" is the moment a baby is born. A "berth" is a bed on a ship or a train, or a place for a ship to stop.
Examples: The baby's birth was on Monday. We booked a lower berth on the night train.
I always write "brocolli". Can you correct my spelling?

It is "broccoli", with a double c and a single l.
Example: We ate broccoli with rice and dal.
My British aunt said she will go to the "surgery". Is she having an operation?

Not necessarily. In British English "surgery" can also mean the place where a doctor or dentist sees patients. American English says "doctor's office".
Examples: The surgery opens at nine. The doctor's office opens at nine.
Do I put a comma after "Yes" in "Yes I can come"?

Yes. When "Yes" or "No" begins a sentence, a comma usually follows it.
Example: Yes, I can come to the match.
My grandfather says "much obliged". What does it mean?

It is an old-fashioned and polite way to say "thank you very much". Today it sounds formal or a little humorous.
Example: Much obliged for your help with the bags.
Can I say "He is knowing the answer"?

No. "Know" is a stative verb, so it is not used in the continuous form. Say "He knows the answer."
Example: He knows the answer to every question.
Our teacher hopes the new study plan will "bear fruit". Is this about trees?

Only in a figurative way. To "bear fruit" means to produce good results. It is also used literally for trees.
Example: We hope the new study plan will bear fruit before the exams.
The test results "bear out" what the teacher said. What does that mean?

"Bear out" means to show that something is true or to support it.
Example: The rain figures bear out the farmer's belief that this has been a dry year.
Is it a "bridle" or a "bridal" ceremony?

For a wedding it is "bridal", which means connected with a bride. A "bridle" is the straps that go around a horse's head.
Examples: She wore a bridal dress of red silk. The rider tightened the horse's bridle.
Is it "cafetaria" or "cafeteria"?

It is "cafeteria". It ends in "-teria", with an e after the t.
Example: The students ate lunch in the school cafeteria.
Is it "travelled" with two l's or "traveled" with one?

Both are accepted. British and Indian English usually double the l, as in "travelled", and American English usually uses one, as in "traveled".
Examples: We travelled to Goa by train. We traveled to Goa by train.
Do I use a comma after "however" in "It was cheap however it was poor"?

Yes, and a stronger break is needed too. When "however" joins two full sentences, put a semicolon or full stop before it and a comma after it.
Example: The shirt was cheap; however, it was poor quality.
What do I reply when a shopkeeper says "have a good day"?

Reply "Thank you, you too." It is a friendly way to end a talk.
Example: "Have a good day!" "Thank you, you too."
My parents want to send me to a "convent school". Is it a place for nuns?

Not exactly. In India, a "convent school" often means a school started by a Christian religious order, and many are English-medium. Students of different faiths often attend.
Example: She studied at a convent school in Shillong.
My aunt keeps her new neighbour "at arm's length". Is she being rude?

Not necessarily. It means keeping someone at a distance and not becoming close. People often do this to stay careful or private.
Example: He kept the salesman at arm's length and did not give out his number.
My brother needs to "cool off" after the argument. Does he need a fan?

No. Here "cool off" means to become calmer after being angry. It can also mean to become less hot.
Examples: Go for a walk and cool off before you reply. We sat under a tree to cool off.
I heard "a loud whale" from the baby. Is that the right word?

No. The word you need is "wail", a long, loud cry. A "whale" is a very large sea animal.
Examples: The baby began to wail. We saw a whale from the boat.
Is it "catastrophy" or "catastrophe"?

It is "catastrophe". It ends in "-phe", with "ph" and a silent e at the end.
Example: The flood was a catastrophe for the village.
Is it "aluminium" or "aluminum"? My textbook and my cousin's disagree.

Both are correct. "Aluminium" is the British and Indian spelling, and "aluminum" is the American one.
Examples: The tiffin box is made of aluminium. The recipe says to wrap it in aluminum foil.
How do I write what two people say in a story?

Start a new line each time a different person speaks. Put the spoken words in quotation marks, with a comma or a punctuation mark before the closing quote.
Example: "Where are you going?" asked Tara.
"To the market," said her brother.
My host said "make yourself at home". Can I sleep on his sofa?

The phrase means to relax and feel comfortable, but it does not mean you may do anything you like. Be considerate and ask if you are unsure.
Example: Please come in and make yourself at home.
My uncle said "I am having a car". Is that right?

In standard English use "I have a car". "Have" meaning "own" is a stative verb, so it does not take the continuous form. "Having" is fine for actions, such as "having lunch".
Examples: I have a car. I am having lunch with my friend.
Why did the teacher say Imran has "an axe to grind" about the exam rules?

It means he has a personal reason for complaining or pushing an idea, often a selfish one.
Example: Be careful with that review, because the writer has an axe to grind after losing the contest.
My teacher said not to "dwell on" my mistakes. Is she telling me to forget them?

Not exactly. "Dwell on" means to keep thinking or talking about something for too long. She means learn from the mistake and then move on.
Example: Don't dwell on the lost match; there is another one next week.
Is it "damage" or "damages" when a storm breaks a wall?

For harm to a thing, use "damage", which is uncountable. "Damages" with an s is a legal word for money awarded by a court as payment for harm.
Examples: The storm caused damage to the school wall. The court ordered the company to pay damages.
How do I write the number "ninteenth"?

It is "nineteenth". It keeps the e from "nineteen" and adds "-th".
Example: The sports day is on the nineteenth.
Is it a "plait" or a "braid" when hair is woven into three strands?

It is both. "Plait" is the usual British word, and "braid" is the usual American word.
Examples: She wore her hair in a long plait. She wore her hair in a long braid.
How do I use "e.g." and "i.e." in a school report?

"E.g." means "for example" and introduces some examples. "I.e." means "that is" and restates something more clearly. Put a comma after each in American style.
Examples: Bring sports equipment (e.g. a bat or a ball). Bring warm clothes (i.e. a sweater or a jacket).
How can I begin an email when I am late with my reply?

You can write "Apologies for the delay in replying" or "Sorry for the delay". It is short, polite and honest.
Example: Apologies for the delay in replying; I was away last week.
Is it fine to write "revert back to me" in an email?

The "back" is unnecessary, since "revert" already contains the idea of returning. Also, "revert" meaning "reply" is mostly Indian English, so "please reply" is clearer.
Example: Please reply to me by Monday.
My father told me to "grin and bear it" while waiting in the long queue. Is that good advice?

The phrase means to accept something unpleasant without complaining, because you cannot change it. It can be sensible for a short wait, but if a problem is serious it is better to speak up.
Example: The bus was late, so we had to grin and bear it.
Tanya "blurted out" the secret before she could stop herself. Did she do it on purpose?

Probably not. "Blurt out" means to say something suddenly, without thinking, often when you wish you had stayed quiet.
Example: He blurted out the news about the surprise party.
Is it "foul" or "fowl" in "fresh foul from the market"?

Here it should be "fowl", which means birds kept for meat, such as chickens. "Foul" means very unpleasant, or against the rules in a game.
Examples: The market sells fowl and eggs. The milk had a foul smell.
Is the plan of a trip an "itinery" or an "itinerary"?

It is "itinerary", ending in "-ary".
Example: Our itinerary includes two days in Jaipur.
The recipe asks for "mince", but the American site says "ground beef". Is mince a different thing?

They are close. "Mince" is British for meat that has been chopped very small, and "ground beef" is the American term for minced beef.
Examples: We made a pie with mince and peas. We made a burger with ground beef.
In an email, do I write "Dear Sir," and then start the next line with a small letter?

The next line should start with a capital letter, because it begins a new sentence: "Dear Sir," then a new line with "Thank you for your reply."
Example: Dear Mr Rao,
Thank you for your reply.
The notice says "sorry for the inconvenience". Who is saying sorry for what?

The people who wrote the notice are apologising because something, such as a delay or a change, causes trouble for readers.
Example: Sorry for the inconvenience; the library will be closed on Monday.
My friend said "I got 85 percentage in the exam". Is that correct?

Standard English says "I got 85 percent" for a score. "Percentage" means a share of a whole, as in "A large percentage of the class passed."
Examples: I got 85 percent in the exam. A large percentage of the class passed.
Is "blow your own trumpet" a compliment or a criticism?

It is mild criticism. It means to boast about your own achievements.
Example: Meera never blows her own trumpet, even though she has won three prizes.
My boss says I need to "put across" my ideas more clearly. What should I change?

"Put across" means to explain or express something so that others understand it. Use simple words, short sentences and a clear order.
Example: She put her idea across with a short, clear drawing.
My boss will "apprise" my work this month. Is that the right word?

No. The word is "appraise", meaning to judge the value or quality of something. "Apprise" means to inform someone.
Examples: The teacher will appraise your project on Friday. Please apprise me of any change in the timing.
Is "outragous" correct?

No, it is "outrageous". The e stays after the g, from the noun "outrage", so the ending is "-geous".
Example: The price of the tiny cake was outrageous.
My salad has "rocket" in it. Is that a space thing or the same as "arugula"?

It is a salad leaf with a slightly peppery taste. "Rocket" is the British word, and "arugula" is the American word.
Examples: Add a handful of rocket to the sandwich. Add a handful of arugula to the sandwich.
Is "I was tired I went to bed" a run-on sentence?

Yes. Two complete sentences are joined with no punctuation or linking word. Fix it with a full stop, a semicolon or a conjunction.
Examples: I was tired, so I went to bed. I was tired; I went to bed.
Is it "with regard to" or "with regards to" in a formal email?

The usual phrase is "with regard to", with no s. "With regards to" is also heard, but careful writers prefer the form without s. It means "about" and is common in formal writing.
Example: With regard to your request, I will reply by Friday.
At the wedding someone talked about my uncle's "co-brother". Who is that?

In Indian English a "co-brother" is usually the husband of your wife's sister. Standard English has no single word for this, so people say "my wife's sister's husband" or loosely "brother-in-law". The word is understood mainly in India.
Example: His co-brother came from Chennai for the wedding.
The report says the shop owners can see "the writing on the wall". What do they see?

It is an idiom meaning there are clear signs that something bad, such as a failure or a closure, will happen soon.
Example: Sales kept falling for two years, so everyone could see the writing on the wall for the old cinema.
The teacher asked us to "jot down" the main points. Should I write a lot?

No. "Jot down" means to write something quickly and briefly.
Example: Jot down the phone number before you forget it.
Which is correct for the pale sandy colour: "biege" or "beige"?

It is "beige", with the e before the i. It comes from French and does not follow the "i before e" pattern.
Example: She wore a beige scarf with her blue coat.
What is a "roundabout" in a road sign? Is it the same as a traffic circle?

Yes, it is a road junction where traffic moves around a circle. "Roundabout" is the British word, and Americans often say "traffic circle", although they use "roundabout" too.
Examples: Turn left at the next roundabout. Turn right at the traffic circle.
What is a long dash like — used for in a sentence?

The long dash is called an em dash. It marks a sudden break or adds emphasis, and it often comes in pairs around extra information.
Example: My brother — who hates mornings — woke up at five.
When do I use "please accept my apologies"?

Use it for a serious or formal apology, such as in a letter or an email to a customer or an older person. For small slips "I'm sorry" is enough.
Example: Please accept my apologies for missing the meeting.
Is "today morning" correct?

Standard English says "this morning". In the same way, say "this evening" and "tonight".
Example: I saw her this morning at the bus stop.
My teacher said winning the quiz is "a feather in your cap". Is that a gift?

No. It means an achievement you can be proud of.
Example: Getting the top rank in the district was a feather in her cap.
My cousin always "bottles up" his feelings. Is that a good habit?

"Bottle up" means to keep strong feelings inside and not show them. It is usually not a good habit, because talking to someone you trust often helps.
Example: She bottled up her worry until she finally told her mother.
Is "politican" the right spelling for a person in politics?

The right spelling is "politician". It ends in "-ician", as in "musician".
Example: The politician spoke to the crowd in the park.
On the form it says "ZIP code", but our parcel slips say "postcode". Same thing?

Yes. Both are the group of letters or numbers that marks an area for the post. "Postcode" is British, and "zip code" is American. India uses a six-digit PIN code.
Examples: Please write your postcode here. Please write your zip code here.
Do I put the title of a short poem in quotation marks?

Yes. Titles of short works such as poems, short stories and articles usually go in quotation marks. Titles of whole books are usually written in italics or underlined instead.
Example: We learned the poem "The Road Not Taken" in class.
Is "with respect" polite when I disagree with my teacher?

Yes, it can soften a disagreement, but it should be followed by a calm reason. Without that it can sound sharp.
Example: With respect, Sir, I found a different answer in the book.
My cousin said he will "give the exam" tomorrow. Is he handing something over?

In Indian English, "give an exam" means to sit or take one. In standard English say "take an exam" or "sit an exam".
Example: I will take my English exam tomorrow.
I am "at a loose end" this Sunday. Should I be worried?

No. It means you have nothing planned and are free, and perhaps a little bored. The phrase is mainly British; Americans often say "at loose ends".
Example: Sara was at a loose end after her exams, so she tidied her bookshelf.
Grandfather "dozed off" during the film. Did he leave?

No. "Doze off" means to fall asleep lightly, often without meaning to.
Example: I dozed off on the sofa while reading.
Is "hurridly" the way to spell it?

No, it is "hurriedly". The base is "hurry", and the y changes to i before "-ed", giving "hurried"; then "-ly" is added.
Example: She hurriedly packed her bag and ran to the station.
Is a person who serves in a shop a "shop assistant" or a "sales clerk"?

Both are correct. "Shop assistant" is British, and "sales clerk" is American. In India people may also say "salesman" or "salesperson".
Examples: The shop assistant found my size. The sales clerk found my size.
Why is "I" always a capital letter, even in the middle of a sentence?

It is a rule of written English: the pronoun "I" is always capitalised, wherever it appears.
Example: Yesterday I forgot my umbrella, and I got wet.
Can I write "I would appreciate it if you could send the file" to my teacher?

Yes. It is polite and clear, and it fits a formal request. Note that the "if" part uses "could".
Example: I would appreciate it if you could send me the notes.
My manager wrote "kindly revert by Monday". Does she want me to go back to something?

In Indian English "revert" often means "reply". She wants an answer by Monday. In standard British and American English "revert" means to return to an earlier state, so "please reply" is clearer for international readers.
Examples: Kindly revert by Monday. Please reply by Monday.
Parents asked for "a level playing field" in the school contest. Is it about sport?

Not only. It means fair conditions in which everyone has an equal chance.
Example: Giving every team the same time creates a level playing field.
The manager needs to "weigh up" both offers. Will she use scales?

No. "Weigh up" means to think carefully about the good and bad points of something before deciding.
Example: Weigh up the cost and the benefits before you choose.
Is "reminiscense" right, or does it end in "ence"?

It is "reminiscence", with "sc" before the ending "-ence".
Example: Her reminiscence of school days made us laugh.
My new cooker has a "hob". Is that the same as a "stovetop"?

Yes. It is the flat top part where you put pots to cook. "Hob" is British, and "stovetop" is American.
Examples: Put the pan on the hob. Put the pan on the stovetop.
