What mark goes between the numbers in "pages 10 to 20" if I want to write it short?

Use an en dash, which is a little longer than a hyphen, to show a range: "pages 10–20". A hyphen is also common in everyday typing, but the en dash is the proper mark.
Example: Please read pages 10–20 for homework.
At the party my friend said "help yourself". Should I wait to be served?

No. "Help yourself" invites you to take what you want, such as food or drink, without asking.
Example: The sandwiches are on the table, so please help yourself.
The notice says I passed with "first class". Is that a train ticket?

No. In India and in Britain, a "first class" degree or result means top marks. In India it often means 60 percent or more.
Example: She passed her B.Sc. with first class.
Dev told us he had "a close shave" on the road today. Did he visit a barber?

No. It means a narrow escape from danger or trouble.
Example: The cyclist had a close shave when a bus passed just beside him.
I have to "wade through" fifty pages of notes tonight. Will I get wet?

No. "Wade through" means to work slowly and with effort through something long or boring. Its first sense is to walk through water.
Examples: She waded through the long report. We waded through the stream.
Should I write "pamplet" or "pamphlet" for a small printed booklet?

It is "pamphlet", with "ph" in the middle, making the f sound.
Example: A pamphlet about the science fair came with the newspaper.
My British friend wears "dungarees" and my American friend wears "overalls". Is that the same clothing?

Mostly. Both are trousers with a bib front and straps over the shoulders. Be careful: in British English "overalls" can also mean a one-piece work suit.
Examples: The child wore blue dungarees to the farm. The painter wore overalls to protect his clothes.
Do I need commas in "My bag which is blue is new"?

Yes. When "which" adds extra information, put commas around it: "My bag, which is blue, is new." The commas show that the blue detail is not needed to identify the bag.
Example: The museum, which opened last year, is free on Sundays.
When do I say "pardon me" instead of "sorry"?

Say "pardon me" to excuse yourself politely, for example when you pass in front of someone or need their attention. It is a little formal.
Example: Pardon me, may I get past?
The teacher said I am just "mugging up" the lessons. Is it a compliment?

No. "Mug up" is informal and means to learn something by repeating it, without really understanding it. It is common in India and also used in British English.
Example: Don't just mug up the dates; try to understand the story behind them.
My boss asked me to say a few words "off the cuff". Do I need a shirt cuff?

No. "Off the cuff" means without preparation or notes.
Example: She gave a short thank-you speech off the cuff.
My friend said he would "swing by" my house this evening. Does he have a swing?

No. "Swing by" means to visit briefly, usually while on the way somewhere else. It is informal.
Example: Can you swing by the library and pick up my book?
Is it "firey" or "fiery" for a hot, angry temper?

It is "fiery". It comes from "fire", but the e moves: the word has "ie" before the r, so it is "fier" plus "y".
Example: The sky turned fiery red at sunset.
Is it a "letterbox" or a "mailbox" at the gate?

It depends on the variety. British English says "letterbox" for the slot in a door or a box for letters, and American English usually says "mailbox".
Examples: The postman put the card through the letterbox. Please check the mailbox for the parcel.
I like to type "COME NOW!" in capitals so people notice. Is that okay?

Writing whole words in capitals usually reads as shouting, so use it rarely. For emphasis, a stronger word or an exclamation mark is usually kinder.
Example: Please come now; we are about to start.
The shopkeeper said "I beg your pardon?" Was he angry?

Not at all. It is a polite way to ask someone to repeat what they said because you did not hear it. It can also be a formal apology.
Examples: I beg your pardon? I did not catch the last word. I beg your pardon for the mistake.
The letter says "intimate me about the date". Does it mean something personal?

In some Indian official English, "intimate" means "inform", so it asks you to tell the writer. In standard English, the verb "intimate" means to hint at something, so it can confuse readers. Use "inform me" instead.
Example: Please inform me about the date.
After our argument my sister said we could start with a "clean slate". What does she want?

She wants to forget the past mistakes and begin again as if nothing bad had happened.
Example: The new term gives every student a clean slate.
Mum wants to "stock up on" rice before the festival. Why "up on"?

"Stock up on" means to buy plenty of something so that you have enough for later. The "up on" belongs to the phrasal verb.
Example: We stocked up on fruit before the long journey.
I bought a "momento" of my trip. Is that spelled right?

The word is "memento", which starts with "mem-". It means an object kept to remember a person or a place.
Example: She kept a shell as a memento of the beach.
Is it "have a bath" or "take a bath"?

Both are fine. "Have a bath" is the usual British phrase, and "take a bath" is the usual American one.
Examples: I will have a bath before dinner. I will take a bath before dinner.
How do I punctuate an address on one line?

Put commas between the parts, such as house, street, town and state, and finish with a full stop only in a sentence. Usually no comma goes before the postal code.
Example: Our address is 12 Park Road, Mysuru, Karnataka 570001.
My friend asked "Do you mind if I open the window?" If I say "yes", do I agree?

No. "Do you mind?" asks whether it bothers you. Answer "No, not at all" to agree, or "Actually, I'd rather you didn't" to refuse politely.
Example: Do you mind if I sit here?
My friend writes "a lot of informations" in emails. Is that wrong?

Yes, "information" is uncountable, so it has no plural form. Say "a lot of information" or "many pieces of information".
Example: The website has a lot of information about the course.
Someone described Neha as "born with a silver spoon in her mouth". Is that an insult?

It can sound critical. It means born into a rich family and given an easy start in life. It may be said without unkindness, but it can suggest that the person has not had to work hard.
Example: He was born with a silver spoon in his mouth, but he still works at the shop every Saturday.
My father had to "flag down" an auto outside the station. How do you do that?

"Flag down" means to signal to a moving vehicle to make it stop, usually by waving your arm.
Example: We flagged down a taxi at the corner.
Is the spelling "dumbell" right for the exercise weight?

No, it is "dumbbell", with a double b and a double l. It is "dumb" plus "bell".
Example: He lifted a dumbbell ten times.
My mother's "purse" is in her "handbag". But my American friend calls the handbag a "purse". Why?

The words change between varieties. In British English a "purse" is a small holder for money, and a "handbag" is the bag. In American English a "purse" often means the handbag itself.
Examples: She kept her coins in a purse inside her handbag. She put her phone in her purse.
Is it "resign" or "re-sign" for signing a paper again?

Both words exist. "Resign" means to leave a job. "Re-sign" with a hyphen means to sign again. The hyphen shows the meaning "again".
Examples: He decided to resign from the club. The club asked him to re-sign the form.
Is "if you don't mind" polite when I ask a classmate to move his bag?

Yes, it makes a request softer. Add a "please" and a smile, and it sounds friendly.
Example: Could you move your bag, if you don't mind?
The teacher said the answer is not "cut and dried". Is it half right?

It means the matter is not simple or clear. Something "cut and dried" is already settled, with no room for doubt.
Example: The rules are cut and dried, so there is nothing to argue about.
